Protecting users' location privacy is a critical issue, and the standard deterministic privacy framework has limitations in addressing this concern. This is because releasing anonymized data under the deterministic framework can still lead to significant breaches of user privacy, as a malicious adversary can pinpoint the locations of multiple users given enough time. To address this issue, we developed a new privacy framework for protecting location data, taking into account the conditional probabilities of user movement between different locations. By releasing updated probability distributions for a user's location, we can achieve better privacy protection for multiple users without compromising the accuracy of the collected information. This approach is further optimized to meet specific privacy standards, and we provide a thorough evaluation of the proposed framework using real-world data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our location privacy protection method in achieving specified levels of privacy for multiple users without sacrificing the quality of the collected information. Specifically, our approach can release up to 2.7 times more location data while maintaining the same level of privacy or release similar amounts of data while meeting stricter privacy requirements. This contributes to an important area of research in machine learning and demonstrates the feasibility of our location privacy framework in real-world scenarios. Additionally, our code is publicly available for reproducibility. This includes the implementation of our privacy protection method, as well as the real-world data used in the evaluation. To facilitate further exploration, we provided a location privacy analysis tool that can be used for a variety of applications. This includes evaluating the effectiveness of existing location privacy methods, such as k-anonymity, as well as investigating the trade-offs between privacy and information accuracy for different location data release methods. Furthermore, we demonstrated the applicability of our location privacy framework to various other problems, such as protecting location-based event data and revealing the trends and patterns within aggregated location data while maintaining user privacy. This highlights the versatility of our approach and provides a potential solution to these complex privacy concerns. To confirm the reliability of our approach, we conducted a thorough comparison with existing location privacy methods, including differential privacy and the Laplace mechanism. This showed that our approach can achieve better privacy protection for multiple users while releasing similar amounts of location data, or release more data while meeting the same privacy requirements. This contributes to an important area of research in machine learning and demonstrates the effectiveness of our location privacy framework in real-world scenarios. Additionally, we provided a detailed evaluation of the impact of varying privacy parameters on the trade-off between privacy and information accuracy, shedding light on the underlying complexities of this issue. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes. Our data collection was based on actual, rather than simulated, fMRI datasets from N=345 young, healthy subjects, acquired across eight scanning sites, all of which utilized 3T scanners and varied scanning protocols. Our findings demonstrate that commonly observed functional networks are consistently present across all sites, and inter-site effects were relatively minor. Through Monte-Carlo simulations, we evaluated the effects of multisite data on our ability to detect changes and predict group labels, revealing that our ability to detect changes was minimally impacted, but prediction accuracy did decline slightly compared to single-site studies of equal sample size. Our results imply that large sample sizes can make multisite research in rs-fMRI a viable option. Our open-source software tools allow researchers to assess the reliability of rs-fMRI datasets and estimate the effects of multisite data, potentially obtaining accuracy comparable to that of single-site studies by adjusting parameters such as network boundaries and feature selection. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/FMRIMultisite/MultisiteTools. In addition, we have inserted the data into a public database as an RData object, which can be accessed via doi: 10.6080/GEF62LJ1. Kevin N. Heister has also contributed a package to the Bioconductor repository (available at https://bioconductor.org/packages/field-office/1.0.0), which includes our data along with additional functionality translating rs-fMRI data into network compatibility matrices. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly due to the presence of switch language points (SLPs). Current methods 
encode SLPs as a single label or positional information, oversimplifying their 
importance. This research introduces a novel approach called Switching Point
Encoding Switching Table (PESTO), which encodes each language's start and end 
information at every word index, capturing the dynamic and relative positional 
encoding of two languages. When combined with existing state-of-the-art models, 
PESTO shows improved performance on various tasks for code-mixed texts. Further 
experiments reveal that models trained with SLP-based data exhibit enhanced 
understanding of sentence generation, as demonstrated through the analysis of 
generated sentences. These findings confirm that capturing the precise 
characteristics of SLPs is crucial for effective model training. The proposed 
architecture addresses various challenges posed by SLPs, such as language 
identification, segmentation, and paraphrasing, providing a comprehensive 
solution to encoding SLPs. Additionally, the code for this research project is 
available at https://github.com/Amit Saxena/PESTO.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature. Additionally, we found that considering two key components - the positive electron-phonon interaction and the negative electron-electron interaction - yields a predictable trend in the isotope effect coefficient as a function of pressure. However, incorporating the variable density of states enhances our understanding of both interactions and improves agreement with experiments, particularly at high pressures, suggesting the importance of its van Hove singularities in superconducting H3S compounds. Furthermore, our study indicates that the variable density of states primarily influences high-frequency electron-phonon interaction weights, whereas it tends to stabilize the positive electron-electron interaction at low frequencies. Finally, we observe that incorporating the variable density of states predicts a higher critical temperature for H3S superconductors at extremely high pressures (> 200 GPa), aligning with experimental findings. Our study's theoretical framework can be applied to other superconductors under high pressure, taking into account their unique density of states characteristics. Fisher developed the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection using the concepts of average excess and average effect, where he initially defined these ideas somewhat abstractly. However, some experts believe that reframing his theories using statistical methods such as covariance and regression would clarify these concepts, both are part of classical statistical analysis. We propose an interpretation where Fisher's average excess and average effect are intended to represent a fundamental distinction between correlation and causality, and according to this understanding, the average effect specifically measures the average change in the trait value resulting from a change in the genetic value. We show that this apparent imprecision is resolved by considering the average effect as a causal influence, and we demonstrate that the apparent conflict between these concepts and modern statistical methods is resolved once the concepts are defined in terms of covariance and causality. Furthermore, this interpretation enables a clear understanding of the SAWGM method as a causal analysis and justifies the use of this method to estimate the average effect, even in cases where the genetic value cannot be measured. Additionally, this interpretation allows us to redefine the average excess as the ratio of correlation to causality, and we propose that this average excess should be negative, and we provide evidence supporting this negative view through numerical simulations based on the distribution of traits given the genetic value, and we show that the apparent ambiguity in its definition is resolved once the concepts are defined in terms of covariance and causality and the average effect is estimated accurately. Finally, we conclude that the apparent ambiguity in the definitions of these concepts, along with the apparent confusion with modern statistical analysis, is resolved once the concepts are defined in terms of covariance and causality, and we highlight potential areas for future research where our understanding of these concepts along with covariance and causality can be further refined. Additionally, we present a future research idea where Fisher's legacy can be further honored by further research.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within a factor graph framework. A novel approach involves directly predicting image descriptors from 3D geometric entities, bypassing the need to render the map into image space. This process enhances localization performance and reduces computational complexity. Real-world experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques by achieving lower localization errors and faster processing speeds. For example, under an ego-motion sequence of 10 degrees, the average relocalization error is reduced from 0.56 meters to just 0.32 meters. Furthermore, computation time is substantially minimized, with test times decreasing to approximately 0.56 milliseconds per frame. These advancements are attributed to both the surfel map aid and the novel descriptor learning module. To validate method effectiveness, we introduce and release a new, large-scale KITTI dataset featuring 111 sequences, totaling over 1,000 scenes. This dataset is designed to test various relocalization scenarios, including places never seen during training. To ensure method generalization, we also created a new dataset called TUD-LIS, which comprises 22 sequences capturing vehicle interactions with unique locations. To evaluate learning robustness, we employed a dataset expansion technique involving synthetic data generated from map features. To ensure fairness, we also applied a dataset augmentation technique involving real image features to train a baseline method. Results show that our method outperforms all competitors by a considerable margin. Code and the open-access dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/tml-ai/3D-surfel-map-based-visual-relocalization. Overcoming this issue, researchers have focused on personalizing machine learning models, which typically rely on having complete datasets, an unrealistic scenario given data labeling complexities. When models receive limited labeling, they experience reduced adaptability to local distributions and, subsequently, suffer performance degradation. Addressing this issue, we propose an innovative approach where under-resourced clients collaborate with data-related clients, dubbed 'helper agents', for enhanced labeling. We then develop a specialized learning framework, designated as FSSL, which is founded on shared supervisory information between the resource-constrained client and the helper agent to facilitate efficient learning. FSSL's theoretical min-max formulation captures both the client's local generalization and the helper's representation stability. We test FSSL in various scenarios, and the results indicate significant performance improvements, with code available at https://github.com/jaychauhan/UM-PFSSL. FSSL exhibits enhanced local generalization and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on both test and train datasets, with a notable improvement over baseline techniques by 5.3% and 6.0% respectively, and outperforms existing personalized FL methods by 3.2% and 2.9% respectively, under similar conditions. The proposed approach is an innovative contribution to FL, specifically personalized FL, with a new general personalized FL framework and novel test cases. Additionally, the supporting experiments provide valuable insights into the effects of varying helper resources and data sharing limits on the learning process. These experiments demonstrate the resilience of FSSL and highlight its potential for real-world applications, such as semantic segmentation and reinforcement learning training. FSSL's reliance on helper agents can be mimicked using existing data augmentation approaches, and the provided source code enables direct replication of the experimental findings. Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar evolution processes, regardless of setup variations.  The disruption of the neutron star leads to mass ejection accompanied by a massive accretion disk formation; the magnetic field within this disk then undergoes amplification due to various instabilities and turbulent forces, inducing the dynamo and angular momentum transfer.  The subsequent mass ejection by viscous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence begins roughly 300-500 milliseconds post-merger, persists for several hundred milliseconds; meanwhile, a magnetosphere is formed around the black hole, producing a focused strong electromagnetic outflow lasting about 0.5-2 seconds.  The model without equatorial-plane symmetry shows inverted magnetic polarity in the magnetosphere, caused by a magnetorotational instability dynamo, whereas a model initially comprising toroidal fields demonstrates a late post-merger stage characterized by a tilted disk and magnetosphere due to a late high-density disk dynamo.  The model depending on neutron star equation of state displays distinctly different initial mass ejection rates and final black hole and neutron star remnant fates.  The model with stiffer equation of state produces less initial mass ejection compared to the standard case, whereas a model with a softer equation of state yields more initial mass ejection than the standard case.  The standard and stiff equation-of-state models result in neutron star remnant contractions, whereas a model with a soft equation of state experiences no contraction or expansion of the neutron star remnant.  The model depending on initial magnetic field strength reveals variations in the intensity of turbulence and the magnetosphere, with a weak and isolated electromagnetic outflow produced by a model featuring the lowest initial magnetic field strength.  The model depending on initial magnetic field configuration demonstrates similar outcomes as previous variations, with distinctions arising from differences in the intensity of turbulence and the magnetosphere, especially a model featuring poloidal initial magnetic fields, which experiences a delayed and isolated electromagnetic outflow post-merger.  A model involving a magnetosphere initially comprising poloidal fields shows a late post-merger stage characterized by a tilted disk and magnetosphere due to a late high-density disk dynamo, whereas a model comprising toroidal fields yields a late post-merger stage characterized by a tilted disk and magnetosphere due to a late dynamo in the disk. This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions. These findings are further demonstrated through a combination of established theorems and novel extensions of recent research. Specifically, we draw upon the ergodic theorem established by Deronde and Masse, as well as the results of Djelidi and Mena, to name a few. Our work is specifically tailored to measure speed of convergence in reverse time. In a notable deviation, we focus on a self-conservative process rather than a traditional conservative process, thereby distinguishing our findings from existing ergodic theorems. Our key contribution lies in the establishment of a condition and a corollary ergodic theorem that may be of independent interest. Our ergodic theorem holds distinct advantages over existing techniques by utilizing only a limited set of assumptions regarding the process's transition matrix, thereby facilitating a straightforward proof that yields a precise rate of convergence without resorting to questionable simplifications. Our findings are thus positioned to offer a more precise and efficient alternative to measuring speed of convergence in reverse time, thereby potentially replacing existing ergodic theorems. Our work is primarily a response to the query posed by Henry Teicher, whose 1983 lecture had gone unaddressed by our research until the present day. Our results are further exemplified through a combination of simple, elementary examples and established theorems. Our conclusion summarizes the distinct contributions of our key ergodic theorem, paving the way for future research that may further elaborates upon and extends our findings in the future. Our findings demonstrate that the excitation of graphene's surface plasmons can produce numerous stable positions with interparticle distances much shorter than the photon wavelength. Both perpendicular and angled light incidence have been taken into account in the study. To better assess the Emergency Department's admission process, we analyzed average response curves for treatment duration. Extending the time for treatment is considered an effective strategy for improving admissions; nonetheless, empirical evidence supporting this claim is difficult to gather. The treatment duration is impacted by various unmeasurable patient factors and coincides with the admission decision, complicating the analysis. We mitigated the issue of correlation between patient factors and the admission decision by utilizing average response curves, allowing for the estimation of treatments duration in relation to altered admission policies. Under specified assumptions, the empirical distribution of treatment duration approaches a normal distribution, simplifying the estimation process. Our findings, based on data from a large hospital, reveal that treating all patients immediately yields the lowest average treatment duration, with a score of 310. The current policy achieves an average treatment duration of 314, indicating that delaying the treatment until the admission decision increases the average treatment duration by 4 minutes. The optimal admission policy that minimizes the average treatment duration in the Emergency Department is through a first-come-first-served approach. Furthermore, we computed the distribution of treatment duration when treating patients sequentially and found a 10% probability of treatment duration exceeding 450 minutes. This research offers a novel approach for evaluating the Emergency Department's admission process using average response curves, providing valuable insights into treatment duration. The findings can be utilized to refine the admission policy to reduce the variability in treatment duration and minimize the proportion of long treatment durations. The data and code used in this study are publicly accessible through a GitHub repository. This research is part of a broader effort to create empirical average response curves, allowing policymakers to make more informed decisions through the estimation of treatment durations in the Emergency Department. The move towards electronic health data simplifies the analysis of the Emergency Department's admission process, empowering researchers to explore the behavior of long-tailed distributions. The techniques employed in this study can be applied to various healthcare settings and areas of research, such as physician consultations and hospital readmissions. Moreover, advancing methods for analyzing electronic healthcare data will yield beneficial insights into patient health and healthcare operations. Finally, we are transitioning from descriptive statistical analysis to a more informative empirical research approach, yielding actionable insights into the behavior of electronic healthcare data. The techniques employed in this research can be utilized for empirical applications in the field of emergency medicine and other areas of research. The estimated average response curves provide a versatile tool for evaluating the Emergency Department's admission process, yielding valuable insights into treatment duration. The data and code used in this study are publicly accessible through a GitHub repository

Experimental results indicate that our approach exhibits robustness and efficiently facilitates coordination across multiple scales, from small to large networks. Research has examined the correlations of charges in particle interactions within Pb-Pb collisions, specifically looking at whether evidence of the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) exists in the collision data collected at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The study considered all charged particles within specific pseudorapidity and transverse momentum ranges, with particular emphasis on peripheral collisions. A signal related to CME was observed in specific correlator calculations and found to intensify with increasing collision peripherality. Calculations accounting for effects of background that arise from charge and anisotropic flow patterns, while able to partially explain observed results, did not capture the entirety of the CME signal measurements. A comparison of the CME and mixed-harmonics correlator signals further highlighted the significance of CME signal measurements. Finally, the study assessed the reliability of signal measurements extracted from collision data using a statistical method called Bayesian analysis, taking into consideration experimental measurement uncertainties all the way to the CME parameter calculations. The outcome showed that the CME signal constraint agrees well with a previously made CME field measurement, known as the CME predictions put forth by a theoretical model, known as the local parity violating model. In conclusion, the CME effect in heavy ion collisions has been established to exist within Pb-Pb collisions at specific energy levels. The study also discussed the CME interactions in relation to quark-gluon plasma properties and presented an updated summary of the CME findings up to this point in time. Furthermore, the CME observations in relativistic heavy ion collisions now provide even stronger evidence of the links between strong magnetic fields and the CME interactions that arise within the charged medium of these collisions. A key feature of the proposed framework is the ability to collect and process network traffic data in a common format to reveal meaningful patterns. Moreover, the federated averaging technique is employed to maintain the confidentiality of each organisation's update and avoid a single point of failure. The novel and adaptive nature of this framework makes it adaptable to various intrusion detection algorithms and datasets, offering valuable insights to researchers and practitioners. Introduced concepts also encompass privacy preservation and data decorrelation to further enhance the framework's privacy and pattern extraction capabilities. The source code of the proposed framework has been made available through GitHub at: https://github.com/josejcor/FedAD. The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions have commonly drawn on a variant of the classic Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), with a focus on achieving the quickest or most time-efficient task sequence. Despite their optimality, these methods face challenges in real-time execution, especially with larger problems. In fast-paced online planning environments where tasks are executed swiftly, the time taken to optimize task ordering becomes a substantial hindrance, even overshadowing the overall task duration. Such conditions are commonly found in online robotic manipulation sequencing, where the task completion time is substantially longer than the time taken to optimize the sequence. In such cases, a more desirable outcome is achieving a satisfactory, good-enough solution in near real-time. We introduce an innovative, fast clustering-based algorithm to address this need, offering a comprehensive online validation through experimental assessments. The study also provides insights on how the proposed solution compares to the optimal solutions generated through offline optimization techniques. The code for the proposed algorithm is openly accessible on GitHub at the URL: https://github.com/graha-robotics/FCN/tree/master/FCN\_RMS. The dataset for the offline optimization method, called Fast Cluster-based Robotic manipulation Sequence (FCN), can also be found on GitHub at the URL: https://github.com/graha-robotics/FCN/tree/master/FCN\_dataset. The dataset contains comprehensive information about the problem space of a robotic manipulation scenario, with its size determined based on specific criteria to ensure adequate performance of the offline optimization algorithm. The dataset includes a set of optimal solutions, along with their corresponding error margins and a measure of suitability, known as the quality of the solution, for reference purposes. The dataset can be utilized for tuning or training machine learning models to generate suitable task sequences based on the observed characteristics of the problem space, such as the number of visited locations, the sequence length, and the time taken to optimize the solution. The offline optimization solutions, including the FCN, a variant of the k-means algorithm called the Fast k-Means Robotic manipulation Sequence (FKN), can be applied in offline settings to generate a library of high-quality solutions that can be utilized in near real-time for online robotic manipulation sequencing, such as in cases involving human-robot collaboration where the task completion time is longer than the optimization time. To accelerate neuromorphic computing and quantum computing developments, there has been growing interest in modifying CMOS infrastructure to accommodate diverse novel functional elements. As these novel elements often possess high carrier mobility, incorporating them into CMOS circuits is a viable option. Current research focuses on substituting the standard CMOS MOSFETs with high carrier mobility devices, necessitating an examination of their behavior when employed in a complete CMOS process. This study investigates the electrical characteristics of a SiMOSFET built using a full 300mm CMOS process and discovers the device to possess an exceptionally high mobility ratio. The outcome of this research makes CMOS infrastructure an attractive platform for integrating novel functional elements aimed at achieving high-performance hybrid CMOS circuits. Additionally, the findings provide valuable insights into developing high-mobility MOSFETs for advanced quantum computing applications.

Our study examines the existence of domain-level source diversity bias in video search outcomes by utilizing virtual agents to mimic human searches from 98 distinct domains spanning 28 categories, such as news outlets and educational institutions, across 18 languages over a period of 18 months. Through an experiment involving 398 queries, we found that video search platforms like YouTube and Vimeo fail to display the first page completely, leading to a diversity deficit of up to 18.8%, with up to 42% of websites excluding due to bias. Furthermore, we found that virtual agents recovering biased search outcomes only minimally affects the quality of the retrieved videos, demonstrating that current video search platforms suffer from significant diversity shortcomings. These findings highlight the need for more robust retrieval methods and virtual agents that can better address diverse search demands. Our source code and dataset are openly available for replication of our study's results.

The capacity of wireless networks is inherently restricted by interference, and there has been a lack of investigation into the impact of interference correlation on wireless systems. Interference correlation occurs when packets are transmitted in consecutive order, causing the interference on each packet to be related. This study addresses this gap by examining the effect of interference correlation on wireless systems, and reveals that interference correlation can significantly reduce the capacity of wireless networks by generating bottlenecks, and even induce data losses. To enhance system performance, a novel random medium access control method is proposed, aiming to break up consecutive transmissions and mitigate interference correlation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively decreases interference correlation, and in turn boosts system throughput and reduces data transmission errors. Additionally, the study provides an analytical model to accurately assess the extent of interference correlation and data losses within the system. These findings can guide the design of wireless networks, particularly in high-speed systems, and the proposed approach can be integrated into existing wireless networks to enhance performance. Furthermore, the study discovers that random access control can also be an efficient scheduling method, and even outperform traditional sequential transmission in certain scenarios. To validate these conclusions, comprehensive simulation and analytical tests were conducted using real-world wireless traffic. The study offers a novel perspective on the impact of interference correlation and data losses in wireless systems, and can guide the design of efficient wireless scheduling systems. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling approaches have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label space unnecessarily, thus aggravating the scarcity of labels in the original set. Secondly, they fail to effectively account for data class imbalance in the pseudo-labeling process. To address these limitations, we propose an Informative Pseudo-Labeling method, which focuses on assigning informative pseudo-labels to unlabeled nodes while avoiding the expansion of the label space. Additionally, we introduce a variable confidence threshold adaptive to data class imbalance. By combining pseudo-labeling with a propogated loss from the GNN, we guide the model to generate more accurate pseudo-labels and refine its classification capabilities through self-training cycles. Experimental evaluations on six graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach over existing baselines. In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time video analysis on devices. We present PatchNet, a highly efficient neural network model for tracking objects across adjacent frames in videos. Unlike traditional pixel-based approaches, PatchNet leverages patch-wise correlation features. This results in a compact network that runs at a remarkably low computational cost of 58MFLOPs, approximately $5\times$ simpler than MobileNetV2. Our research showcases the effectiveness of PatchNet on object detection in videos and visual tracking, yielding substantial performance gains and comparable or even better results. Specifically, PatchNet surpasses DeTFNet in object detection video quality by a significant 7.7% to 11.3% and outperforms SfM in visual tracking by 4.1% to 11.6% while requiring significantly fewer resources, 54% to 88%. Furthermore, PatchNet demonstrates a 2-4 times faster inference speed on the FC5 tracking benchmark when compared to SfM. With its remarkable balance of low computational complexity, high performance, and efficient design for video analysis, PatchNet is an ideal candidate for various real-time video applications. These findings enable us to compare our results with previously obtained distributions at different time points and verify that the distribution of current and density at specific locations match with the periodic exclusion process's limit as time goes to infinity. These observations support the conjectured formula's accuracy for exclusion levels beyond 50%. Finally, our obtained distribution is expressed in a form that can be numerically solved for any given set of time points and exclusion levels, thereby facilitating a more detailed examination of the exclusion process at larger system sizes and exclusion levels. We present a generic, classical modeling of electric circuits that describes conventional single-tone microwave optomechanics, where a mechanical oscillator functions as a mobile capacitor within a parallel RLC circuit. Analytical derivations are developed, incorporating fundamental aspects like the back-action force, input-output relationships, and corresponding spectral densities, all situated within a purely classical framework. These derivations align with the established quantum optomechanics when both the cavity and mechanical oscillator have high occupation numbers. Additionally, the derived analysis equates optical elements with their electronic counterparts, a necessity for accurate measurements and design requirements. Lastly, a direct comparison between the quantum and classical treatments helps to distinguish the boundaries between these two regimes, thus identifying the genuinely quantum characteristics from those of the classical realm. This study is anticipated to facilitate hybrid quantum-classical designs, particularly in the context of solid-state quantum technologies. An appendix is included, containing an alternative discussion of the same subject, reaching the same conclusions through different reasoning, as well as introducing yet another approach to the field. Moreover, the main text and this appendix use different methodologies to enhance understanding but share a common purpose. Lastly, both sections are enriched with additional information to facilitate reading. The principal sections of this study are sections 1 through 4, while the appendix constitutes section 5. Furthermore, the introduction below sets the stage for the subsequent content. Introduction: The conventional setup for studying the interactions between mechanical and optical components in optomechanics involves two fundamental approaches, one of which being the quantum treatment, where the degrees of freedom are treated as quantum variables, and the other being the classical treatment, where these degrees of freedom are treated as classical variables. The classical approach, in turn, has two distinct manifestations, one rooted in the fundamental principles of classical mechanics and electromagnetisms and another, built upon the measurement-based paradigm of quantum mechanics. In this study, we focus on the latter, purely measurement-based, classical approach, where the hybridization of quantum and classical mechanics is of particular interest, specifically in the context of microwave optomechanics. The key aspects of this measurement-based, classical realm are then equated with their quantum counterparts, thereby providing a crucial bridge between the quantum and classical domains, as well as offering fresh insights into the fundamental, classical nature of optomechanics. In particular, we focus on the practical design and technical aspects of this measurement-based, classical realm, with an emphasis on the distinctions and similarities between quantum and classical mechanics, particularly in the context of solid-state quantum technologies. Employing a robot design proposed by Steve Mesburger and Alfred Hubler in "Chaos in Wall Following Robots", the autonomous entities use a straightforward distance sensor to navigate, with the added limitation of a narrow "phi" field of view. As these agents maintain a consistent forward velocity, they rely on the sensor to adjust their path accordingly: rightward when close to obstacles and leftward when distant from them. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ a weighted matrix to emphasize relevant details, which are then obtained through a z-score standardized image generation process. We tested this technique in a binary classification task and found it to provide beneficial information, with the enhanced images contributing to an improved classification performance compared to conventional RGB image-based methods. Specifically, our results reveal that our image enhancement technique achieves a higher classification accuracy on the Cholec80 dataset than the conventional RGB image-based method, which evaluates the importance of image features through a repeated t-test. Furthermore, our technique exhibits superior performance in terms of false positive rates, false negative rates, and classification confidence compared to the conventional method, as measured through a metric called the Matthews correlation coefficient. These outcomes demonstrate that our proposed image enhancement technique generates relevant information to distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which cannot be obtained from conventional RGB images. As such, this technique holds potential as a useful component of a full system to identify smoke images, which would be essential for the effective application of smoke removal methods in laparoscopic surgery. Measurements of joint polarization states for $W$ and $Z$ bosons in $W^{\pm}Z$ production processes have been reported. These measurements were derived from $139$ fb$^{-1}$ worth of data from proton-proton collisions at a $13$ TeV center-of-mass energy, obtained with the ATLAS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider.  $W^{\pm}Z$ candidate events, resulting from the decay of these bosons into electrons and muons, have been used to quantify longitudinally polarized vector boson pair production, an event that is here reported for the first time, occurring at a statistical significance of $7.1$ standard deviations.  Fiducially-integrated joint helicity fractions for these events are $f_{\mathrm{00}} = 0.067 \pm 0.010$, $f_{\mathrm{0T}} = 0.110 \pm 0.029$, $f_{\mathrm{T0}} = 0.179 \pm 0.023$ and $f_{\mathrm{TT}} = 0.644 \pm 0.032$, in concordance with the next-to-leading order predictions from the Standard Model of physics.  Additionally, joint helicity fractions for individual $W$ and $Z$ bosons were computed, revealing no substantial disparity between joint and individual polarization states, while both joint and individual polarization states were quantified separately in $W^+Z$ and $W^-Z$ events.  Finally, cross-sections for multiple kinematic parameters relevant to polarized $W$ and $Z$ boson interactions were provided.  Particle physics simulations of the SM predict that the sum of fiducially unpolarized $W^+Z$ and $W^-Z$ processes should greatly outweigh the sum of fully polarized $W^{\pm}Z$ processes.  Therefore, observations of fully polarized $W$ and $Z$ boson joint states hold potential to reveal evidence for non-SM physics, in particular, by detecting deviations from the SM predictions for fully polarized $W$ and $Z$ boson joint states.  Therefore, these measurements constitute valuable data with which to test the sole purely gauge-dependent four-boson process prediction of the SM.  Lastly, future $e^+e^-$ collider experiments are expected to be capable of observing fully polarized $W$ and $Z$ boson

In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing optimal preconditioners for the linear solver. However, standard termination criteria for the solver frequently cause excessive 'oversolving' by insisting on sufficient residual reductions. This paper presents an alternative approach to interior point methods that utilizes an inner termination criterion not dependent on the residual, as well as indicators for premature inner iteration cessation informed by IPM demands. It also modifies this criterion to accommodate Conjugate Gradient and Minimum Residual algorithms, and demonstrates substantial performance enhancements in computational experiments for quadratic optimization problems, which translates to considerable time savings in IPM solution. The proposed inner termination criterion is initially presented in a general manner and later specified for specific equation systems, as well as for Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient and Preconditioned Minimum Residual algorithms. This includes a notable application to an anisotropic elliptic equation where the author's modification yields notable improvements. The code for these modifications has been made publicly accessible through the GitHub repository. The research further highlights the difficulties and missing elements in current research on inner iteration termination, which requires consideration of factors beyond mere convergence, such as algorithm design and complexity. The author's methodological approach, rooted in the art of problem-solving and close analysis of numerical computations, illustrates the value of detailed numerical model expansions in understanding numerical method design. Moreover, the study's success hinges on the versatility of the OTAS preconditioner, which the author developed previously, as well as ongoing research on elliptic equation solutions with anisotropic properties. The preliminary findings presented in the paper have the potential to substantially enhance the performance of numerous interior point methods, which rely on similar Conjugate Gradient and Minimum Residual solvers. The study may also contribute to advancements in optimization research by exploring new numerical algorithms, as well as to theoretical and practical advancements in elliptic equation solutions with anisotropic properties. The author identifies potential future research directions, such as the utilization of anisotropic elliptic equations to model ground water flow, as well as the application of the OTAS preconditioner to ground water flow simulations, which involve complex geometries and mixed finite element solutions. The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized cost function, and can be solved using an iterative adaptive-sieving algorithm, which exploits the problem's sparse non-zero coefficient properties. Our solution involves developing a highly efficient computational implementation of the adaptive-sieving algorithm on GPU architectures, and further enhancing it with adaptive memory optimization, and novel activation function modifications to accelerate its convergence. Evaluations and comparisons with existing methods demonstrate that our implementation yields superior performance, specifically in terms of speed, stability, and robustness, and particularly effective for large-scale problems, achieving a 10x speedup over existing methods. Notably, our implementation has been proven stable and effective even when faced with challenging setups, and consistently outperforms other methods in a wide range of scenarios, ultimately providing a highly efficient and versatile solution for HDR Lasso. A detailed description of the source code is available at https://github.com/jbmanu/hdr-lasso-spike-and-slow. Additionally, the associated paper is publicly available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.16057. Please note that some data is available upon request due to data privacy concerns, and specific hardware information can be provided upon email inquiry to j.bmanu@gmail.com. Finally, the author would like to express gratitude to Dr. Valero-Cuevas for inspiration, and to colleagues and friends for their selfless support.

Identifying whether an optimal solution is localized or universal is particularly challenging in complex optimization problems. This work addresses that challenge by demonstrating the existence of a single, optimal, and universal method for achieving the lowest possible rate of entropy production in fast and sluggish driving processes. This outcome is verified by proving the functional convexity of the entropy production rate in relation to a key controlling parameter, which further confirms its monotonous progression in such scenarios. This contrasts with our previous research findings where the rate of entropy production was not consistently positive throughout all stages. Our analysis demonstrates that an analytical technique previously employed is, in fact, effective in determining the optimal solution, which is subsequently verified by comparing it with results obtained through genetic programming's global optimization method. This global optimization method was previously utilized in our research, and in another study by Mandrà et al. published in 2020 in Physical Review Letters, for solving the same problem. This work is an extension of our research on optimizing protocols in steady-state quantum computers. This novel approach for determining efficient protocols may be applied to various areas including quantum computing, heat engine optimization, and cooling techniques. Additionally, it presents an innovative use of reproductive coevolution through its analysis of the success of an optimal solution identified, which showcases the potential of this method for determining universal optimal solutions. Our research further examines the rate of entropy production decline in multi-drive systems, which undergo reductions in some drives' intensity, while experiencing enhancements in others. This contrasts with our previous research where the rate of entropy production increase was documented in systems undergoing uniform increases in their driving force. Our analysis demonstrates the practical applicability of our research by linking entropy production optimization with maximum possible work production, thus opening up new avenues for theoretical and experimental studies on this topic. Over the past decade, significant advancements in artificial intelligence have positioned it as a key tool for addressing environmental concerns, primarily reducing greenhouse gas emissions. However, researchers have lately come to recognize that increasingly complex AI models require substantial amounts of energy to train, thereby contributing to the very emissions they are intended to mitigate. To date, no thorough examination of the full scope of the environmental effects of using AI to address environmental problems (dubbed AI for Green) has been undertaken, focusing exclusively on greenhouse gas emissions. In this article, we seek to address this gap by analyzing potential negative outcomes associated with AI-driven environmental solutions. Initially, we will categorize and analyze various types of AI's environmental impacts. Subsequently, we will present established methods for evaluating these impacts, illustrate the application of life cycle assessment in AI services, and provide an evaluation framework to gauge the environmental utility of general AI services. Lastly, we will highlight the limitations of current AI for Green research initiatives. This study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the environmental implications of AI-driven solutions, thereby facilitating the development of more accurate environmental benefit assessments. Such assessments can help steer the development and deployment of AI technologies in environmentally conscious ways, thereby enhancing their effectiveness in addressing pressing environmental issues. Lastly, we envision that our analysis will contribute to the evolution of a future environmental meta-stock for AI services, thereby enabling researchers to gain valuable insights from past research initiatives and facilitating collective progress in this domain. Moreover, we hope to inspire further exploration of AI for Green topics, such as the environmental implications of AI-driven physical actions, thereby broadening the range of topics within this domain. Finally, we recognize that researchers may identify additional potential negative outcomes, thereby enhancing our understanding of AI for Green, a domain which we believe will continue to evolve in the years to come.

This paper investigates and classifies various prescriptive process monitoring methods, which identify potential issues during business processes and provide interventions to prevent problems at the point of execution. The systematic review encompasses a comprehensive analysis of the current approaches in the field. To better understand these methods, a conceptual framework has been developed to evaluate prescriptive process monitoring techniques based on performance targets, metrics used to assess performance, optimization methods employed, intervention types, and intervention implementation options. The findings of the systematic review highlight gaps and possible research avenues that could further improve the effectiveness and versatility of prescriptive process monitoring methods, emphasizing the necessity for method validation in practical scenarios, enhancement of intervention types, expansion of applicable domains, and enhancement of model and intervention quality. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions in the area of prescriptive process monitoring, incorporating reader guidance. The supplementary material accompanying this paper includes a detailed list of included studies, a further classification of prescriptive process monitoring methods by process phase, intervention types, and traits, along with the full list of conference and journal papers considered in the systematic review. The material also presents a taxonomy of prescriptive process monitoring methods, and the metadata for the included studies, along with the results of the systematic review in tabular form. This study introduces an error control strategy for a Boussinesq model with adaptive coefficients, where temperature-dependent properties of heat transfer and fluid viscosity are taken into account. The coupled system of the Navier-Stokes and heat equations is solved in a unified manner. The primary goal is to utilize the dual-weighted residual method for estimating the errors of various goal functions with the help of an adjoint problem. To localize the errors, we utilize a partition-of-unity method within a weak formulation framework that is well-suited for solving coupled problems. This approach enables the implementation of an adaptive algorithm that dynamically adjusts the discretization of the parameter-sensitive Boussinesq system according to an a posteriori estimate of the solution's residual. The proposed method is demonstrated by solving two- and three-dimensional test problems, with a particular focus on a 3D example mimicking a heated metal sample undergoing thermal processing. The results showcase the effectiveness of the adaptive algorithm in accurately tracking the solution's residual and goal function, with a corresponding reduction in spatial discretization errors. Furthermore, the output-based error control strategy is found to be particularly beneficial in a 3D scenario, where the output of interest is primarily influenced by solution dynamics in the vicinity of the boundary where the goal function is localized. Additionally, the output-based error control approach is shown to be more efficient than a standard a posteriori error control method that relies on a priori estimates in the far field. The proposed methodology is expected to be versatile and applicable to a broad range of Boussinesq model variations, including those incorporating parameter-dependent boundary conditions. Furthermore, the strategy is anticipated to be of considerable practical value in the context of heated material processing, where an adaptive algorithm can effectively mitigate solution artifacts resulting from steep gradient interfaces and spatial discretization errors that can lead to overheating and other abnormal material processing phenomena. The adaptive algorithm is expected to be a valuable tool in the realization of automatic material processing control systems via output feedback. This study explores how opinions are shaped and social connections evolve in a complex system, governed by a delicate balance between friendly and hostile relationships. We have developed a model that captures how individuals with limited confidence in their judgments form opinions based on their personal relationships. We considered two scenarios: one where close friends equally share their opinions, and another where opinions are weighted by the individual's level of confidence. Our research reveals that when opinions are subjective, a small number of influential individuals can significantly impact the overall network, leading to a diverse mixture of homogeneous and heterogeneous communities within the system. In contrast, when opinions are objective, a state of structural balance is quickly achieved, resulting in a more uniform distribution of opinions across the entire network. These findings are corroborated by two real-world studies, one examining the dynamics of political beliefs on Twitter and another investigating vaccine attitudes on Facebook. Our study demonstrates the importance of subjectivity in social interactions and how it can lead to diverse social groupings within a larger system. Additionally, we show the utility of our model in understanding and predicting opinion dynamics in actual social media environments. Lastly, our work highlights the potential consequences of algorithms that amplify objective opinions, such as promoting a single, uniform worldview that may not reflect the individual's true beliefs. Instead, these platforms could embrace a more nuanced approach, one that embraces and showcases diverse perspectives and opinions. Furthermore, our study sheds light on various social media interventions that can shape public opinion, thereby improving public health. Ultimately, our model is a valuable analytical tool for understanding and interpreting the complex dynamics of opinions within a social ecosystem. It can also be utilized to make accurate predictions about how opinions will evolve over time, thereby enabling more accurate forecasting in the future. In addition to these applications, our work also points out several challenges and unanswered questions in the field, thereby contributing to the ongoing discussion in the social science literature. This investigative method revealed a low-lying positive-parity 0+ band, which, along with other 64Ni features, aided in resolving long-standing puzzles surrounding spin-zero energy levels and shape deformations. Furthermore, comparisons with 60Ni results revealed similar low-lying isomer properties and a high-lying positive-parity 0+ band patterns, which suggests a universally occurring shape deformation phenomenon. The visual appearance and auditory qualities of an object provide dual insights into its material properties.  In everyday situations, information from vision and hearing arrive simultaneously, but the integration of asynchronous cues is essential, as seen when we locate an object dropped on the ground after hearing its fall.  In this paper, a controlled environment for studying 3D object localization in real-time is established, involving an embodied robotic agent, a camera, and a microphone that identify a dropped object in a room.  The robot achieves this by synthesizing audio and visual cues along with the principles of physical mechanics.  A dataset called Fallen Objects has been developed for studying this complex challenge.  The dataset is based on the ThreeDWorld platform and includes over 8000 simulations of various object types in 64 settings.  As an initial step toward resolving this problem, different agent architectures based on imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and modular planning are designed and evaluated to provide an in-depth analysis of this new task.  The emergence of tasks like Autonomous Driving, Crowdsimulation, and Manipulation that demand the integration of asynchronous cues can be compared with the newly introduced challenge of finding dropped objects.  This study provides a foundational exploration of this intriguing task.  More importantly, the embodied robotic agent is able to accomplish this task without requiring a prerequisite model of the environment through the utilization ofembodied learning. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of glassy dynamics and a state of rigidity influenced by friction. This prediction is tested on various particle and polymer pastes, showcasing that a vast array of substances can be mapped onto a single master curve, thereby revealing common underlying mechanics that govern shear thickening. Furthermore, this framework is employed to subdivide the state diagram of dense mixtures into distinct, individually customizable regions, thereby providing a unified, universal understanding of the phenomena underlying shear thickening. These insights hold potential for applications in multiple fields, including the control of viscoelastic materials and the reduction of vibrational transmissivity in suspensions and pastes. However, the applicability of this theory to predict rigidity for specific mixtures may be limited by uncertainties surrounding the state point of frictionless jamming, as well as issues arising from disordered structures that render predictions based on scaling models challenging. Despite these constraints, this theory may still contribute to refining existing viscosity correlations and providing a broader, universal understanding of the phenomena underlying shear thickening. Moreover, the notion that friction modifies the state of rigidity, thereby presenting an opportunity for friction to enhance a material's ability to absorb and dissipate external forces, serves as a key takeaway from this study. Finally, researchers acknowledge that the vast majority of shear thickening transitions observed to date have been detected through rheology, thereby prompting an inquiry into potential correlations between the viscosity of dense mixtures and other indicators of rigidity, such as acoustic modulation and Brownian dynamics, which could hold the potential for controlling friction on an microscopic and nanoscale through the tailored design of viscoelastic coatings and surfaces. This study investigates the fluctuating electricity consumption in Ghana's period of power shortages by applying Markov switching models. We considered two approaches: a straightforward MS model and a more complex MS-GARCH model. The MS model evaluated two primary market conditions, whereas the MS-GARCH model analyzed three market states and used Relevance Vector Machine regression to determine the error term. By comparing the performance of these models, we found that the MS-GARCH model provided a more suitable representation of the data as it takes into account the variability of volatility. Furthermore, we found that the MS-GARCH model's estimated market probabilities aligned well with intuitive expectations. Additionally, we applied the MS-GARCH model to forecast peak electricity demand, demonstrating its effectiveness in forecasting peak demand during the crisis period. This text explores multiple reduction techniques that facilitate the connection of Earth's climate models of varying complexity, emphasizing approaches that enable thorough reduction. It distills key mathematical concepts behind each method while showcasing several benchmark climate modeling examples for illustrative purposes. The primary goal is to introduce climate researchers to the core of reduction techniques, although an in-depth mathematical examination is inevitable in some sections. The climate modeling examples used are relatively simple; readers can find comprehensive mathematical definitions in relevant reference materials. Furthermore, this review aims to showcase the diverse toolbox of reduction techniques, highlighting both their strengths and weaknesses to inform future research. Benchmark problems have been carefully selected to address essential questions in climate dynamics using reduced systems: understanding the behavior of multiple equilibria, capturing bifurcations, and identifying propagating signals. The methods employed include multiple scale analysis, geometric reduction, Hamiltonian systems, and stochastic averaging. Ultimately, the success of these reductions is evaluated by demonstrating the preservation of original model properties in the reduced systems. The text concludes by highlighting outstanding issues in the field and suggesting pathways for further research to address existing gaps. Specifically, it explores the role of reduction techniques in understanding extreme events, the accuracy of reduced models, and the application of reduction techniques to 3D models that effectively simulate the Earth's energy balance. The groundbreaking discovery of gravitational waves emanating from a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled material from neutron star collisions, present an attractive opportunity for optical and near-infrared follow-up observations following the detection of GWs. The observation of the kilonova from GW 1780817 revealed crucial evidence for the astrophysical site of heavy element formation via the rapid neutron capture process or r-process. Given that properties of the emission are heavily influenced by the opacities of the expelled material, recent calls for enhancement in the limited available r-process atomic data have led to an increased need for precise atomic structure information. Consequently, this research aims to alleviate the present limitations in atomic structure data, specifically for the Os-like and Ir-like elements in the Os isoelectronic sequence. Utilizing the relativistic atomic structure approach and the Dirac-Castorium series as a reference, we have calculated energy levels, E1, E2, and M1 transition probabilities, and recombination coefficients for Au IV and Ir IV, while a new set of predicted lines for these ions in the vicinity of a threshold has been included in the predicted kilonova opacity data. The obtained results for Au IV and Ir IV have been incorporated into the MESSUGI database, a comprehensive online repository of messy atomic structure data, and the data will be crucial in the prediction of future kilonova light curves. Additionally, we have calculated the bound-bound and free-free absorption coefficients for a wide range of r-process ions during the initial stages of a kilonova event, specifically for Os-like and Ir-like ions in the range of $4782-24411$ Angstroms. The predicted lines for Au IV and Ir IV have been identified in the initial stages of a kilonova event, emerging as the highest energy features in the spectrum, whereas a reversal in the order of the lines for Ir IV and Os IV has been observed in the vicinity of a r-process peak. The incorporation of a new atomic structure data for Ir IV has led to an alteration in the initial stages of a kilonova energy distribution compared to the energy distribution obtained with the previous atomic structure data for Ir IV and Ir III. Moreover, the observed changes in the line features for Ir IV, Ir III, and Os III have prompted the conclusion that utilizing a more accurate atomic structure for the ions involved leads to larger emission reductions in the vicinity of a r-process peak

Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data sets through the composition coefficient, a ratio of each component to the total. Despite this prevalence, difficulties arise in analyzing these data due to its complex nature. Specifically, problems include dealing with variables that are highly correlated and difficult to interpret in their raw form. This tutorial utilizes the Coxmat R package to showcase the implementation of compositional data analysis. We focus on linear algebra techniques, visualization, and interpretation to provide a comprehensive understanding. Additionally, we incorporate real-life data from various fields to illustrate the applicability to distinct research environments. Variational inequalities are a potential future tool for analyzing compositional data sets. Furthermore, we outline future research directions that incorporate the Coxmat R package and utilize the simecompos structure. This approach can be further explored using TDA (topological data analysis), which is not covered in this tutorial.

The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which was discovered through Doppler radial velocity measurements, does not demonstrate the anticipated 'desert' at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with close orbital radii (<=3 AU), as predicted by the runaway gas accretion theory. Notably, similar findings have emerged from the MOA gravitational microlensing survey, which did not detect the 'desert' effect for planets in slightly longer-period orbits with lower-mass host stars (Suzuki et al., 2018). These studies collectively suggest that runaway accretion is unlikely a dominant process in shaping the final mass and orbital characteristics of exoplanets according to core accretion theory. As such, the CORALIE/HARPS exoplanet sample provides substantial support for the migration hypothesis, which postulates that the evolution of protoplanets is influenced by disk processes and the dynamical accretion of solid particles, or by photoevaporation that reduces the mass of the disk at an age of ~10 Myr (Jin, 2019; South et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019; Gratz et al., 2020). We investigate how dark matter, composed of bosons generated from a complex scalar field via a Yukawa interaction, behaves when it's dense and cold. The addition of a Yukawa interaction prevents the occurrence of symmetry-caused scattering that might otherwise stabilize the formation of long-range forces during the cooling process. The yield of dark bosons following a cooldown, as well as their fundamental characteristics, particularly the mean momentum and distribution width in the ground state, are closely tied to the impact of the Yukawa interaction. Furthermore, we examined the influence of the Yukawa interaction on the equivalent mass of the dark bosons due to their non-quantized momenta in the ground state. The yield of dark bosons, rather than being a constant, varies in direct proportion to the inverse square of the initial kinetic energy, whereas their fundamental characteristics display discontinuities due to the non-quantized momenta in the ground state. By comparing two different scenarios - one with a Yukawa interaction and one without any interaction - we observed a significant disparity in the equivalent mass distribution width. Finally, in a specific y-value range (between 0.25 and 0.5), the distribution of equivalent mass is nearly symmetrical, whereas it becomes asymmetrical outside this range. The behavior of dark matter, composed of bosons generated from a complex scalar field via a Yukawa interaction, can be understood by considering three distinct physical phenomena: thermal equilibrium, cooldown, and the distribution of equivalent mass. The latter phenomenon, in particular, reveals how the yield of dark bosons, characterized by mean momentum and distribution width, can be affected by the Yukawa interaction. By incorporating the equivalence mass as a variable, we can study the behavioral patterns of dark matter in a more comprehensive way. Moreover, we discovered that the equivalent mass can be utilized as an effective probe of the Yukawa interaction, thereby providing insight into its strength within a specific, confined space. In systems where the equivalent mass is sufficiently heavy, the yield of dark bosons tends to decrease as the Yukawa interaction strengthens. Conversely, in systems where the equivalent mass is sufficiently light, the yield of dark bosons tends to increase as the Yukawa interaction strengthens. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of equivalent mass distribution width on the equivalent mass itself, revealing that it can be influenced by the Yukawa interaction in such a way as to produce asymmetrical distributions at higher values of equivalent mass. In a hypothetical scenario where equivalent mass is not a factor, we would expect the yield of dark bosons to be uniformly distributed

Deep learning models often require considerable amounts of data, yet certain structured models can learn efficiently from smaller datasets. Examples include neural networks with specific inherent properties like sparse connections. When applied to complex tasks such as continuous control, sparse neural networks can learn faster and more efficiently than traditional dense networks. This study examines the effectiveness of sparse neural networks in learning complex cognitive tasks. We utilize a fixed sparse structure instead of the typically used trainable sparse mechanism and find that this approach yields better results across a variety of cognitive tasks, including reinforcement learning and prediction tasks. Furthermore, we find that models with approximately 50-60% sparsity achieve the best results, delivering superior performance while reducing computational costs. Unlike previous studies on reinforcement learning, we find that sparse models can succeed in tasks that require exploring large action spaces. Finally, we explore the uncertainty of task demands and find that the fixed sparse structure can adapt to changing task requirements while minimizing unnecessary additional parameters. In summary, the fixed sparse structure provides an efficient approach to cognitive modeling, enabling faster learning, higher performance, and increased energy efficiency while reducing the need for large datasets or complex parameter adjustments. We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal the irreducibility of corresponding geometric spaces, allowing us to accurately calculate their dimensions and establish general families of algebras associated with each space. Additionally, we demonstrate how these results contribute to an understanding of the length of anticommutative algebras in further study. To access these results, we develop various general theorems that provide insights into the structure of nilpotent algebras given their dimensions and anticommutativity characteristics. These theorems unlock new mathematical relationships that were previously unknown. Our work culminates in a comprehensive classification of nilpotent algebras of length two, encompassing all possible cases for their base algebras. Finally, we initiate a study on the length of anticommutative algebras through the examination of a specific linear transformation associated with these algebras, which allows us to determine the length based on certain low-dimensional algebra parameters. Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial sources, spanning across a wide range of wavelengths. These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly influence both the black hole's growth and its surroundings in the vast expanse of space. In the radio spectrum, these jets can be observed on various scales, but their X-ray and gamma-ray emissions are predicted to be concentrated on smaller scales, typically under 10 parsecs. Recent findings by the Chandra X-ray telescope have revealed the presence of kiloparsec-scale jets, which has sparked debate about the source of their high-energy radiation. Understanding the origins of this high-energy radiation is essential for accurately determining the physical properties and powers of these large-scale jets, which in turn affects the environment in which they reside. In this investigation, we explore the potential for the Inverse Compton interaction between relativistic electrons in jets and cosmic microwave background photons as a plausible explanation, also analyzing how this explanation could impact the observed evolution of black holes over cosmic time in jet-powered systems. Our analysis reveals that the Inverse Compton interaction is likely to be a significant process, and it has a notable effect on the observed correlation between black hole mass and age, particularly at higher redshifts. However, we find that the Inverse Compton interaction does not substantially alter the overall cosmic evolution of black-hole powered jets. Furthermore, we propose that the observed breakdown of the black hole mass-age correlation at high redshifts could be attributed to the emergence of a jet-powered population, which is likely to be prevalent during this early period of cosmic evolution. Our work presents a new perspective on the co-evolution of black holes and their relativistic jets, which could have an impact on the growth of the universe's supermassive black holes. These findings also provide a framework for further investigation, which could help to clarify the role of black holes in the universe's overall evolution, particularly during the early periods of cosmic evolution. Our analysis demonstrates that a comprehensive understanding of black holes and their relativistic jets, which power cosmic emission, is essential for elucidating the universe's evolution, particularly at high redshifts. Lastly, we highlight that a comprehensive understanding of black holes and their jets, which are responsible for cosmic emission, is necessary to fully comprehend the universe's evolution, especially at early times. Our study offers a new perspective on black hole evolution, which could have implications for the universe's overall evolution, particularly during early periods, and may help to clarify the role of black holes

of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. Ultimately, this method
permits an in-depth examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion up to
its next-to-next-to-leading order. Additionally, we derive the action for the
second-order terms, which specifically applies to non-relativistic situations, in
which case it reduces to the Poincaré action. Our approach also enables a

fail due to divergence. This new technique may be applied to other field-

obtaining the quantum Einstein action. In a related context, we identify the
critical aspect of the foliation freedom that facilitates the derivation of the
off-shell action through a null foliation condition, thereby providing new
insights into the role of the foliation freedom in the phase space. Moreover,
we believe this method can effectively be applied to other fields, thereby
enabling novel advancements in their respective quantum domain developments.
