Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surrounding the optimal input method for retrieval and the ultimate application have been ongoing. In this research, we present an alternative approach by focusing on using 3D sketches as input and envisioning a virtual reality (VR) environment for retrieval. We aim to allow users to freely access 3D models through air-drawn sketches in a VR setting. As an initial step, our study contributes four aspects: implementing a tool to collect and retrieve 3D sketches in VR, gathering the first dataset of $167$ sketches in two categories from ModelNet, developing a novel approach to generate synthetic human-like sketches, and evaluating the performance of different approaches. We observed that in the context of sketch-based retrieval, volumetric point-based methods excel due to the sparsity and abstract nature of VR sketches. We believe our work will serve as a foundation for future studies, and the associated VR interface, code, and datasets can be found at https://tinyurl.com/3DSketch3DV. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Furthermore, we've derived an XP algorithm for converting an upward planar embedding into a linearized one, extending previous results on planar graphs. Our work also includes two new XP algorithms for graph bipartization based on the number of source vertices and treewidth parameters. Finally, we've identified NP-completeness for the source vertex parameter in the upward embedding and bipartization problems. Our research contributes valuable insights into the interaction between parameterized complexity and embedding constraints. Our experimental evaluations of the algorithms show promising efficiency for various practical examples. Our study also leads to new theoretical outcomes and proposes new problems for further investigation. The source code for the experimental evaluations is available at https://github.com/graphdrawing/upward-drawing. The MemoNav's graph memory module aggregates the top two most relevant features from past experiences, weighted according to their proximity to the current position, as well as their predictive value in reaching the objective based on a proposed reward function that estimates the likelihood of encountering desired features.
The close proximity reward component ensures that the agent prioritizes nearby memories with higher feature overlap, demonstrating their efficacy in reaching the objective more efficiently.
We evaluate MemoNav on a variety of tasks that necessitate the retrieval of diverse paths in both indoor and outdoor environments, comparing its performance to existing methods. MemoNav consistently outperforms the competition by accurately navigating to objectives up to 25% more frequently than alternative methods. Additionally, MemoNav successfully navigates to unseen objectives using previously encountered paths, showcasing its generalization capabilities in visual-based navigation. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. Furthermore, we identify a distinct entanglement anomaly and investigate its origin, revealing that it stems from the distinct ways operator growth is arranged in SU(1,1) and SU(2) systems. Finally, we demonstrate that information capacity is inherently tri-modal rather than bi-modal as commonly observed, showcasing the intricate connection between operator growth and the information-carrying capacity of coherent states. Overall, this research emphasizes the importance of leveraging symmetry to explore the intricate patterns underpinning operator growth and the information-carrying dynamics in Lie-symmetric systems. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered through the measurement of the electric dipole transition strength from the Hoyle state to the ground state. The goal of this investigation is to quantify the direct decay component from the Hoyle state to the 0+ ground state through the measurement of the electric dipole transition strength, $\left|C_{0+}^{(1)}\right|^{2}=0.042(11)$, which represents about 8% of the total decay strength. The remaining 92% of the strength was attributed to the two-body component of the Hoyle state. The 180 keV proton spectrum showed agreement with the predicted transition distribution based on the theoretical $\langle p\rangle$ distribution. The measurement of the direct decay component of the Hoyle state, which consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital, has been verified. In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access) and secret key generation in information-theoretic secure settings. We establish a crucial observation that in channels which exhibit positive information measures in response to feedback, there exists an optimal approach to achieving the ultimate transmission rate, known as the zero-rate boundary. This involves encoding based solely on the current state, without considering future states or feedback information. Consequently, we derive an approach for evaluating the transmission rates under look-ahead access and devise a secretion rate assessment tool for secret key generation, both of which align with previously established bounds in relevant research. Additionally, we provide a clear illustration of our findings through an examination of a specific channel model, known as the discrete-time Advisory Gaussian channel. Furthermore, we expand our analysis to consider the scenario in which multiple encoders, possessing different levels of knowledge about the channel states, communicate with a single decoder. In this multi-private setting, we develop a approach for key generation and demonstrate its relevance to the transmission of confidential information over channels with private states. Finally, we abstract our findings and offer a broader interpretation, connecting our work to the broader field of distributed information-theoretic problems. This research contributes to the advancement of multiple ENIGMA tasks outlined in a broader report. This work addresses Task 1.2 (exploring feedback in information-theoretic channels) and is connected to Tasks 1.3 (investigating the interaction of local secrecy and transmission rates) and 2.2 (analyzing the secrecy and transmission rates in a multi-private setting). This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to verify factual information and locate supporting evidence within tabular scientific data. The comprehensive dataset comprised 981 manually crafted tables and an automatically generated collection of 1980 tables, encompassing over 178,000 statements and more than 11 million annotated evidence references. This task comprised two primary sub-tasks. Sub-task A required participants to verify whether a statement was substantiated, contradicted, or remained inconclusive relative to a given table. Meanwhile, sub-task B involved pinpointing the specific table cells that served as evidence to support the given statement. Ultimately, a total of 69 teams from diverse academic backgrounds submitted their proposals, with a subset of 8 teams successfully completing both sub-tasks and an additional team completing sub-task A alone. Notably, we received corrected submissions from 49 teams in total. This paper will detail our approach to addressing SEM-TAB-FACTS, a task that posed significant challenges due to its intricate nature, stemming from the intricate relationships between tables, statements, and evidence, as well as the abundance of ambiguous tokens associated with them. Despite these complexities, several teams were able to achieve accurate results for verication sub-task A, with their overall f-1 scores ranging from 0.41 to 0.61. In regard to cell-ranking, a task posed by sub-task B, teams exhibited a considerable degree of variability in their performance. A team achieved a relatively high ranking of 0.79 in macro-f1, while the lowest was 0.19. This paper also showcases supplementary information that could have been utilized to enhance performance, as well as some intriguing team proposals that incorporated additional data sources such as unannotated scientific articles, pre-trained models, and table embedding. Additionally, we provide participants with access to the data used in sub-task B, enabling them to explore the intricate connections within the tables and develop novel strategies to address the task. Finally, we outline our plans to expand on this research in the future, a future that includes incorporating SEM-TAB-FACTS to a larger dataset encompassing various data types, as well as introducing a related natural language inference task. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics. 

--Roderich Tumulka, "The Viennese tradition of understanding quantum mechanics", arXiv:1709.06728v2, 2018, Sec. 2.2.2, emphasis added.

Existing research quotes Reinhardt Rudy regarding Sommerfeld's influence on Heisenberg's matrix mechanics and the complex numbers requirement. Additionally, the discussion draws from Wolfgang Yourgrau and Stanley Mandelstam's 'Discussion of the principles of quantum mechanics', 1963, in which they Heisenberg's matrix mechanics and the subsequent Born-INFERNAL structure of the matrix, leading to the electron energy eigenvalues. 

The analysis also touches on Paul Dirac's development of electron spin quantum theory and the challenges he faced in representing observables as infinite matrices, requiring infinite dimensional mathematics, leading Dirac to express states and operators with complex coefficients. Yourgrau and Mandelstam noted that Born-INFERNAL structure, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, relies on complex numbers, and concluded by highlighting that 'this sophisticated mathematical tool' cannot be replaced by simpler concepts. 

The discussion is part of a larger research paper examining the underlying principles of quantum mechanics, where the authors, Tumulka, Yourgrau, and Mandelstam, engaged in a long-standing debate regarding the necessary complexity of quantum mechanics, ultimately agreeing on the crucial role of complex numbers. As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to test and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different architecture designs. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper proposes a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC for RISC-V multi-core platforms that incorporates multiple computing-in-memory accelerators for neuromorphic computing. The authors also investigate and demonstrate various simulation architectures for integrating these accelerators, comparing the efficiency gains against conventional sequential simulation approaches. The results show that using 4 and 8 cores can achieve simulation speeds up to 2.3 and 4.6 times faster, respectively, while utilizing a high-throughput CPU for tasks like page mapping and data copying can further enhance efficiency by a factor of up to 9.2. The developed simulation platform is freely accessible on GitHub, allowing researchers to experience and build upon the technology for themselves. The platform includes a multi-core platform model, a memory-inclusive in-memory computing unit model, a spike-based neuromorphic computing model, a kernel-based neuromorphic computing model, and an example neuromorphic kernel that can be used as a reference for others. The authors also provide a kernel compiler that makes it easy to create new kernels from existing RISC-V assembly code, streamlining the process of simulating and evaluating neuromorphic computing designs. The proposed simulation platform is versatile and compatible with various extensions, such as floating-point units, Vectors Extension, and Load-Store Acceleration, offering a flexible solution for simulating and comparing different architecture designs for neuromorphic computing. The research outcomes will likely contribute to the advancement of neuromorphic computing by enabling multiple architecture simulations, whereas previously such testing was only feasible for a single design. The simulation platform can be utilized for simulations up to 100 million instructions on a 64-core host system, opening up new avenues for research and simulation. The authors' simulation environment can be adapted for simulating various applications, such as deep neural networks and spiking neural networks, by compiling the kernels from their respective programming models, thus expanding its potential applications to a broader range of use cases. Moreover, the proposed simulation platform is compatible with various simulation tools, such as regression testing and profiling, for evaluating and simulating the behavior of neuromorphic computing designs under real-world regression tests. The outcomes will likely enable multiple architecture simulations to be carried out concurrently

The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW introduced an innovation in DTW's development. Building upon PrunedDTW's early abandoning and abandoning decisions, a refined variant of PrunedDTW was created. This new model achieves pre-terminating decisions both before and during the series comparison process. Moreover, a modified PrunedDTW variant was designed, taking into account the relaxation of a previously stringent condition related to series alignment. This revised variant is now integrated into the CDTW distance. The proposed approaches are then used in an experimental analysis of similarity search performance with a significant impact on runtime efficiency. As a result, the new algorithms demonstrate superior performance, full correctness, and a reduction in runtime that is proportional to the number of neighboring candidates considered. The development of these algorithms marks a significant advancement in the evolution of DTW-based distances, providing a practical solution for the deployment of DTW-based methods in large-scale similarity search applications. The proposed techniques are now openly available as open-source software at a public repository. The code was validated through comprehensive testing, which is documented in a publicly accessible collection of test cases. The studied methods were evaluated on a widely used dataset, along with two other previously existing variants of PrunedDTW, and two other prominent distances: the IED and LCP distances. The results of this analysis demonstrate that the new algorithms outperform the competing methods in an experimental analysis of similarity search performance. The improvement in runtime is attributed to the early abandoning of series comparisons in a significant number of neighbor searches. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. In this study, we introduce a novel conceptual feedback approach that reinforces key teaching principles. By comparing our approach to traditional testing tools, this research evaluates student performance, instructor feedback, and instructor satisfaction to determine the effectiveness of conceptual feedback in teaching software testing. The results indicate that conceptual feedback leads to more efficient testing, fewer redundant test cases, and fewer unexecuted test cases among other outcomes, demonstrating its potential to improve the educational testing experience and enhance the effectiveness of instructional material. Consequently, conceptual feedback can encourage instructors to revise or create new educational test suites that promote best testing practices. Additionally, this research can motivate tool developers to introduce conceptual feedback features that support teaching principles and provide valuable insights to instructors. To further validate our findings, the research outcomes can be utilized as a validation metric in empirical studies focused on the impact of testing education. This results in a more detailed analysis of network behavior and improved accuracy in the representation of intricate DNNs. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 6-fold rotation symmetry, indicating epitaxial relationship, achieved through a low-temperature, van der Waals epitaxy process. This result suggests that contamination-free growth may be an elusive goal in epitaxial growth, particularly with complicated materials such as those involving Gd. Further work is needed to realize truly remote epitaxy. Nonetheless, this study demonstrates that graphene can serve as an effective substrate for growing materials with high lattice mismatch through careful temperature control. Meanwhile, experimental and theoretical analysis was employed to investigate the epitaxial relationship between the grown film and substrate, revealing an unexpected flexibilty in remote epitaxy that allows growing certain materials on graphene, even those requiring matching with a substrate's surface structure. Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced service quality by the ISPs. To model these negotiations, we use a Stackelberg game, where the Content Provider decides the distribution of its profits and the ISPs determine their level of investment effort, while in another scenario, we look into how Content Providers and ISPs collaborate, with ISPs deciding on how to split the profits fairly through a Nash Bargaining model, resulting in improved outcomes for all parties. Numerical findings indicate that Content Providers profit from splitting their profits evenly, whereas ISPs gain more from investing in high-speed networks, with, however, a peak investment effort by the Content Provider. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Content Providers and ISPs can both benefit from a fair distribution of profits, with, notably, an increase in the profit-split ratio leading to improved outcomes for both parties, and observing similar trends for the Content Provider's best response curves for both models. These results provide valuable insights for negotiations between Content Providers and ISPs, with implications for network infrastructure investment. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a quantum system and associated physical states. This process essentially inverses itself through a universal factorization. We demonstrate that the GNS construction, along with a related functor, defines a categorical adjunction at the level of 2-categorical structure. This reflects the universal factorization as a composition of functors that isolate the essential mapping between a collection of observables, a representation of its algebra, and an isomorphic mapping of Hilbert spaces. This adjusted perspective on the GNS construction clarifies the construction's abstract universality and provides a strong formal foundation for further abstract mathematical analysis of observables and states in quantum systems. This new view also accommodates constructions like compactimentation, a procedure that removes physically redundant degrees of freedom from a given quantum state, revealing a natural duality between collections of physical observables and their associated algebras through a contravariant functor that pairs these two concepts in a universally natural way. This duality further strengthens the abstract framework by showing a natural relationship between collections of observables, their algebras, and the associated Hilbert spaces. We established a natural mapping between this duality and the compactimeation procedure, which is currently only defined on a select class of quantum systems called Weyl algebras. This abstract framework also yields a natural definition for Weyl algebras and their associated observables through a construction called a co-Weyl algebra, which is universally natural in the category of C*-algebras. Furthermore, this abstract framework provides a strong definition for compact quantum systems, which are defined as any collection of physical observables for which there exists a natural mapping to the Weyl algebra, and yields a natural construction for the algebra of physical observables in any quantum system. This abstract framework also naturally incorporates the concept of gauge symmetry, which is a naturally closed subset of the collections of physical observables in any quantum system. Finally, this abstract framework provides a strong definition for the charge of an element in a quantum system through a construction called a local gauge group, which is universally natural in the category of C*-algebras. This abstract framework for collections of physical observables in quantum systems, along with its associated algebraic structure, is a strong foundation for further abstract mathematical analysis of these systems. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables seamless incorporation of quantitative strategies, including short-selling and leverage. Further enhancements to the model's flexibility are achieved through the utilization of kernel smoothing. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. Novel applications of the developed portfolio return distribution are presented, including measuring portfolio risk, modeling option prices, and analyzing liquidity, all of which contribute to the advancement of contemporary finance research. A user-friendly Python package, pendle, is included in the supplementary material for easy implementation of the proposed methods. It has been thoroughly tested on various datasets, including NYSE, NASDAQ, SNB, and the STO, as well as on bespoke lists of large-cap, small-cap, and liquidation portfolios. Datasets of historical portfolio returns are also provided. The time required to compute the first eight moments of the probability function for a portfolio of 200 stocks depends on the specific configuration and hardware, but is shown to take less than one second for a wide range of scenarios. This computational efficiency is further exemplified by the generation of precise option prices in a second for even the most complex cases. Efficient kernel weights for various kernel types are provided, along with guidance on installing the pendle package via a pip installation script in the supplementary material. It is noteworthy that the development of the pendle package facilitated a substantial reduction in the overall code size of the accompanying material, with the total number of lines in the included code amounting to approximately 29,000 lines. Furthermore, the pendle package has been designed for maximum usability, with a clear documentation of its components and a comprehensive guide to its functionality, along with multiple example applications that demonstrate its efficacy. A detailed index of the package's contents is also included in the supplementary material. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise interfering with the doctor's ability to hear the sounds properly.  To address this issue, this study investigates methods for improving the signal quality of cardiac auscultation sounds to enhance diagnostic accuracy.  The research involves analyzing and comparing the performance of various noise reduction methods, specifically focusing on the effect of convolutional distortion caused by background noise on the diagnosis of heart conditions.  The study finds that some signal processing methods cause the cardiac sounds to be distorted beyond recognition, hindering their effectiveness in clinical settings.  To mitigate this issue, this study proposes the use of objective metrics, such as the frequency resolution measure, to assess the quality of the cardiac sounds and guide the development of noise reduction methods that prioritize integrity of the sounds over mere noise suppression.  The findings of this study indicate that the correlation between signal quality metrics and the effectiveness of cardiac auscultation sounds, measured by their frequency resolution properties, can be utilized to design effective noise reduction methods.  The research also involves investigating the use of deep neural networks as automatic cardiac condition diagnosis tools, and discovers that these networks utilize the degraded cardiac sounds, resulting from the convolutional distortion caused by background noise, to make diagnoses.  The study ultimately demonstrates that the effectiveness of noise reduction methods, such as the frequency resolution-based approach, is linked to the quality of the cardiac sounds, and proposes a diagnostic approach that combines the quality of the signals and the effectiveness of the frequency resolution-based noise reduction method to achieve the best results in cardiac condition diagnosis.  The findings of this study are validated through simulations of a healthcare professional's ability to diagnose heart conditions based on cardiac sounds obtained from a specific location on the chest, and are found to be applicable to various situations, including diagnosis of mitral regurgitation and Starr-Edwards prosthetic valve disorders.  The research ultimately contributes a new approach for evaluating the performance of noise reduction methods in clinical settings by considering the quality of the cardiac sounds, and demonstrates the effectiveness of frequency resolution-based noise reduction in achieving the best results in cardiac condition diagnosis.  The study also sheds light on the role of deep neural networks in automatic cardiac condition diagnosis, and suggests a new diagnostic approach that combines the quality of the signals and the effectiveness of the frequency resolution-based noise reduction method to achieve the best results in this field. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup was employed to demonstrate complete heat blockage and simultaneous efficient heat transfer through a common reservoir under distinct electron phases. Furthermore, a geometric tunneling approach in a quantum Hall double dot system confirmed these results, exhibiting a detailed energy-dependent heat transfer pattern. These innovative findings pave the way for the development of highly efficient heat management and thermoelectric devices at the microscopic level. These waves, typically triggered by pacemaker-generated activity, serve as a means of transmitting information, with their velocity determined by the disparity in oscillation rates between the pacemaker and surrounding medium. Given the disparity's direct correlation with synchronization capabilities, understanding and accurately predicting pacemaker-generated wave speed is essential. Although numerical methods can be employed to study this phenomenon, analysts have turned to analytical approximations in similar contexts, such as scroll-wave dynamics. A fundamental concept, von Neumann entropy, measures disorder or uncertainty in random systems, significantly influencing numerous scientific disciplines. The complexity of determining entropy from a quantum state makes it intractable for large systems, leading researchers to explore the feasibility of approximating this value using quantum algorithms. The existing solution, while accurate for limited-sized systems, becomes computationally burdensome for larger ones. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we have developed two new quantum algorithms that efficiently estimate the entropy of chaotic or nearly chaotic states with a lower error rate compared to prior approaches. These algorithms defy the widely accepted notion that data processing cannot be compressed in such scenarios, instead achieving an optimal balance between computational resources and output precision. The possibility of achieving even higher precision, albeit with increased computational expense, also presents further research avenues in this area. The proposed protocols have the potential to be further improved using techniques not previously explored to reconcile the trade-offs between resources, error margin, and entropy margin – the difference between the known entropy value and the minimum entropy value for a given state. The potential for sublinear quantum algorithms, where the number of iterations scales sublinearly with the system size, presents an intriguing possibility, albeit without providing a complete algorithm at present. The origin of this challenge is rooted in the quantum version of the central limit theorem, which suggests that the density matrix of a chaotic state becomes Gaussian, featuring known variance but undeterminable mean for large system sizes. The ability to approximate this mean without requiring the full computational resources for a given error rate would break the long-standing barrier, enabling sublinear algorithms and potentially even a classical version. The proposed protocols, while falling short of this ideal solution for now, remain a vital part of the ongoing research in approximating the entropy of complex quantum states. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our method exhibits a $10^2$ to $10^5$ times computation speed improvement over previous approaches while achieving superior performance, as evidenced by our synthetic and real-world experiment results. This research is facilitated through an open-source C++/Python framework called 'diffrender,' allowing for versatile scene illumination and visibility representation. This platform includes various rendering modules for common image-based inverse problems, as well as prototypical problem-solver modules that offer a simple, high-level interface for implementing analysis-by-synthesis optimization. Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow. Building on long-term traffic data collection, this paper develops an innovative framework to estimate the average and statistical distribution of origin-destination demand while accounting for the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' unique preferences. The framework incorporates stochastic programming and probabilistic origin-destination demand, expressed as a multivariate probability distribution, with the latter being estimated through kernel density estimation. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in providing accurate probability distributions of origin-destination demand and link flow, thus enhancing the reliability of network flow assessment. Furthermore, the methodology showcases a practical application in the state-of-the-art Freeway Performance Measurement Systems, revealing notable day-to-day variability in origin-destination demand and a strong correlation with link flow's probability distribution. The applicability of this methodology extends to a variety of transportation networks and demand modeling scenarios. In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity in the system, these global phases exhibit a temporary state of stability, akin to that observed in nearly conservative systems. The obtained results are also compared to the outcome of a simplified phase model where the oscillations' amplitudes are eliminated under an adiabatic process. The relevance of these findings to the behavior of Bose-Einstein condensates sharing a well-like potential is discussed. Additionally, the presence of dimer nonlinearity in the system is explored to introduce asymmetry in the condensate and thus modify its locking pattern. The outcome of this interaction is then contrasted with that from a binary mixture of condensates possessing different chemical potentials. The phase locking patterns obtained from both situations exhibit notable contrasts. Lastly, the possibility of trapping the condensate within a smaller area by adjusting a parameter is investigated and demonstrated to produce an array of oscillators exhibiting temporal chaos. The obtained results offer insights into the locking patterns that can be expected in Bose-Einstein condensates sharing a well-like potential and also suggest methods for generating localized periodic and chaotic waves within such systems. The phase coherent state and its collapse through the creation of localized waves can also be implemented in digital hardware by either FPGA or VLSI technology. The hardware implementation can further extend our understanding of this phenomenon by exploring its behavior in systems of higher dimensions. The equations of motion for such systems can be solved using various numerical methods like Runge-Kutta, further validating the observed results. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms on complete graphs reveals that these algorithms can generate uniform spanning trees in tandem. This realization enables a faster, hybrid method that leverages the strengths of both algorithms to expedite uniform spanning tree generation in complete graphs. Furthermore, a novel, two-stage approach is developed to adapt and explore this hybrid strategy across a range of graph structures, showcasing its efficacy and efficiency in examples, such as transitive graphs, where it outperforms Wilson's algorithm by generating a uniform spanning tree 25% faster. This research also proposes two new metrics: 'exploration efficiency' and 'branch utilization,' which provide valuable insights for assessing spanning tree algorithms. The study confirms that the hybrid strategy is the fastest known method for generating uniform spanning trees and also examines its applicability to reaching a stopping criterion in algorithms like Wilson's and explores its potential to improve these algorithms' performance. The research delves into the theoretical underpinnings of 'exploration efficiency' and establishes a mathematical relationship between 'branch utilization' and tree size, which holds potential for future investigation as an area of conjecture. Finally, the study showcases the generated code, which showcases the hybrid method's superiority in a real-world application on network datasets. The new insights from this research may facilitate the enhancement of the random spanning tree algorithm used in network simulation software, such as JGraphT. The study also proposes two new methods for evaluating uniform spanning tree algorithms: assessing tree generation time and analyzing the branch paths to provide insights into these algorithms' workings. The research concludes by highlighting the theoretical and practical advancements it has achieved. The relevant source code for this project is available at https://github.com/abimgan/wilson's.git. Currently, large music datasets featuring three modalities are scarce, limiting the ability to learn effective representations for cross-modal applications. To bridge this gap, our research expands on existing musical notation, combining it with audio synthesis and generated sheet-music images to create a dataset with precise alignments among audio, visual, and text-based components. This aligned MusicTM-Dataset allows for the development of unified representations across multimodal data. Comprising sheet-music images, lyrical text, and synthesized audio, the dataset is comprised of three modalities, each represented by advanced models. This paper outlines the development of the MusicTM-Dataset and the process of modal representation, followed by an examination of the impact of multimodal fusion on music content retrieval. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of our dataset in a range of cross-modal tasks through numerical evaluation, ultimately enhancing the performance of existing music applications and future research in this area. The MusicTM-Dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/dddzeng/MusicTM-Dataset.

We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only achieves a range of rotational transform targets but also surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume. Our research reveals that stellarator design is characterized by a fundamental tradeoff between flexibility, quasisymmetry, and nested flux surface volume. We aim to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the optimal objectives in stellarator design. Additionally, our approach's results are shown to be resistant to minor variations in coil placement, which my be utilized for outer coil design optimization. We propose an outer coil design that incorporates the planar control coil concept, allowing for precise quasisymmetry achievement, and demonstrates the possibility of achieving rotational transform targets across a wide range through modular coil design. Furthermore, we identify the possibility of exhibiting excellent quasisymmetry and substantial nested flux surface volume within a considerable range of rotational transform values, specifically for rotational transform targets between 0.25 and 0.5. To achieve outer coil design optimization, we suggest introducing new integrability objectives related to flux surface linking, which could provide a valuable reference for the stellarator design. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps with elliptical geometries that favor specific polarization modes. Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results reveal a unique method for polarization control with potential applications in spin-based photonics and research on complex optical systems with adjustable coupling properties. Additionally, this technique allows exploring the emergence of polarization-symmetric and -antisymmetric modes arising from exciton-polariton coupling. A comparative analysis of the system's behavior in single and coupled condensates is presented. It is shown that coupling leads to mode mixing and symmetry breaking, depending on the trap's anisotropy and coupling strength. These effects are extensively explored and their implications discussed. Finally, a forward-looking perspective on polarization photonics research is provided, highlighting the ensemble manipulation of polarization-degenerate modes. Such an approach could facilitate the development of complex optical networks with high scalability. Lastly, a schematic illustration of polarization manipulation is presented, demonstrating how optical traps with specific phonon modes can be used to create complex polarization patterns. These findings open the door to advanced polarization photonics and contribute to the advancement of exciton-polariton-based research with vast applications in spin-optics and other advanced photonic research. The  COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. Consequently, the health minister in South Africa updates the public every day on COVID-19 infections, including affected individuals' demographic and travel details. Meanwhile, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases provides daily updates on testing numbers, case counts, and fatality rates via infographics but often fails to release patients' ages or other critical transmission details. Recognizing the need to effectively share this information, the University of Pretoria's Data Science for Social Impact research team developed an open-access data platform comprising a data warehouse and an online dashboard, enabling transparent and efficient data sharing. This endeavour revealed challenges pertaining to data availability, credibility, and governance within the public sector. This research aims to address these concerns through a case study on COVID-19 data in South Africa, encompassing the successful creation of a data ecosystem, an examination of associated risks, and a proposed data-driven framework to inform public policy-making. Furthermore, the study identifies lessons learned and proposes a data-driven approach to address broader societal concerns. Ultimately, this research seeks to inspire other organizations to emulate this model, prioritizing data sharing to promote social responsibility. It is hoped that this research will contribute to the development of a data-driven culture within the public sector and facilitate evidence-based decision-making in public policy-making processes. Additionally, this project may serve as a prototype for socially conscious data projects. The research data and dashboard are openly accessible at [https://github.com/data-science-for-social-impact/covid19-SA](https://github.com/data-science-for-social-impact/covid19-SA). The data warehouse and dashboard were officially presented at the University of Pretoria's Research Day 2020, an online event. This research received recognition through an oral presentation awarded by the data owners, the Department of Health in South Africa. Consequently, this project enabled our research team to establish a data-driven relationship with the department, addressing challenges related to data availability, credibility, and governance within the public sector. The research outcomes from this study were disseminated through academic networks and the relevant data owner community, ultimately leading to several subsequent research opportunities, including a planned publication and further data integration initiatives. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. This is strengthened from a previous constraint applied to the sums of the first four elements of subset B. Moreover, it's shown the new constraint can be applied without reference to the elements of subset B, merely to the sums involved. Finally, a conjecture is proposed that subsets A and B, of size k, meet the aforementioned criterion if the sumset A plus B is bound by 2k. This is particularly reflected in the case where subset B consists solely of ones. It's noted that proving this would resolve a long-standing problem regarding the additive combinatorial phenomenon known as the 'Freiman's root' hypothesis. Furthermore, it's conjectured that subsets A and B, of size k, that meet the criterion must comprise A as an additive subgroup of the sumset A plus B. In medical contexts, diverse information often arises from various sources, which when combined enables healthcare professionals to form more precise opinions. For retinal analysis in particular, recent advancements have led to increased use of multiple imaging methods: standard two-dimensional fundus photographs and more detailed three-dimensional imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography. Our study employed three distinct multimodal data fusion strategies centered on deep learning to tackle challenges in retinal analysis: early combination, intermediate fusion, and hierarchical integration. Noting that early and intermediate fusion approaches typically fail to exploit information shared by different data sources to their full extent, our hierarchical method focuses on fusing characteristics from various dimensions within a network, while also uncovering connections between disparate datasets. We implemented these strategies on classification tasks involving glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy using a mix of public and proprietary OCT-based datasets, which demonstrated that our hierarchical method performed optimally and laid the groundwork for improved diagnostic procedures. Furthermore, our novel approach to fusion enabled novel features to emerge which were not apparent in individual datasets on their own. Our work directly addressed the notable gap in knowledge regarding effective fusion strategies for diagnostic medical imaging. Additionally, we explored the feasibility of integrating data fusion with domain adaptation to broaden the applicability of diagnostic models to diverse datasets. Our newly-proposed hierarchical fusion strategy combined with domain adaptation emerged as the most effective approach, which provided a positive response to a question posed in the STARE challenge regarding early detection of retinal pathological changes. Our methods, which can be found on our website, are accessible to the public as a resource. Ultimately, our findings validate the hypothesis that diverse, dimensional data can be effectively integrated through a hierarchical approach centered on a deep learning-based fusion strategy. As such, our hierarchical fusion with domain adaptation stands as the most effective means of merging dimensional data for the purposes of retinal analysis in a diagnostic context. Our work, which is comprised of a novel fusion strategy, a fresh set of fabricated data, and a newly-discovered ability to adapt various datasets, has ultimately enabled us to perform complex tasks including the early detection of retinal abnormalities, a previously unconquered challenge. Additionally, our findings directly address a previously posed question regarding the detection of retinal abnormalities, which provides a significant breakthrough in our understanding of dimensional data fusion. Lastly, our findings provide a significant understanding of the functional dynamics of retinal cells through a new set of fabricated data in the context of dimensional fusion. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis suggests that the placement and size of lung lesions could serve as vital signs relevant to disease severity. This study investigates whether lung lesion counts and sizes within X-ray images can forecast severe COVID-19 symptoms. Our analysis reveals a link between these features and the progression of the disease but notes that they are insufficient for predicting ICU admission. To resolve this issue, we identify additional image characteristics relevant to ICU admission and combine them with lung lesion information, resulting in a robust model capable of predicting ICU admission with 70% accuracy, outperforming a baseline model by 10%. Notably, our study highlights the predictive value of non-lung-related image characteristics, such as patient pose and image focus, which could compromise model reliability in real-world scenarios. Consequently, we recommend utilizing supervised learning approaches over unsupervised methods for predicting ICU admission from X-ray images, due to their superior performance and implicit regularization. Code implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/keunwoocho/predicticase.eyJ.

To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, and require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting new approaches to representing utterances semantically and clustering them effectively. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training strategy that leverages a large amount of unlabeled data in conjunction with labeled external data for representation learning. Secondly, we design a new contrastive loss to capitalize on self-supervising signals from unlabeled data for clustering. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the superior performance of our method over existing approaches in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings. For instance, on the Yelp dataset, our model achieves an accuracy of 82.95% for unsupervised discovery and 97.35% for semi-supervised discovery, surpassing the best existing methods by 12.40% and 2.30% respectively. The code and model are available at https://github.com/JD-19/New-ID.

This estimate enhances the previous upper bound given by Neil and Sullivan, which was $r^{1+\frac{\log_2r}{4}+o(\log_2r)}$. Our research further shows that $r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$ grows at a rate comparable to $r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+\frac{\log_2\log_2r}{4}}$, effectively validating the conjecture proposed by Henderson and Thorold. Our method of validation also yields an explicit upper bound of $48\frac{\log r}{\log\log r}$ for the width of the smallest $r$-subgroup of a finite nilpotent group of order $r$, which further supports Henderson and Thorold's hypothesis. Additionally, our investigation reveals that our subgroup estimate is particularly relevant to abelian groups, with the possibility of a further enhanced bound of $24\frac{\log r}{\log\log r}$ in such cases. Our study uses a combination of analytical techniques, including transference principles and Stirling approximations, to achieve these estimates and bounds. Ultimately, our work offers a straightforward, universally applicable approach to estimating the number of subgroups in a finite group and their widths, which can be useful for both upper and lower bound assessments. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted not only via further von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimally weak measurements. We exemplify these outcomes using a Bell-diagonal state. Moreover, our research showcases that the relationship between QCC and TQD can be utilized to determine the measurement operator in weak measurement experiments. It's also established that QCC is a more suitable quantity than TQD when discussing the influence of quantum correlations in weak measurement procedures. Lastly, our research highlights that QCC can be viewed as a measure of quantum entanglement between the system and its environment following a weak measurement, and this point has significant practical implications. These findings contribute to a deeper comprehension of the role of quantum correlations in weak measurement procedures. They also offer a novel approach to analyzing and implementing this measurement method that only employs weak measurements, thereby facilitating efficient extraction and utilization of quantum information. Moreover, our research demonstrates that the quantum nature of an arbitrary state can be fully mapped onto the environment via a series of infinitesimally weak measurements, thereby paving the way for future applications in quantum information technologies. Finally, our results also underscore the distinctness of weak measurement, which only employs infinitesimally weak measurements, from other forms of quantum measurement, such as continuous measurement, and highlight its important practical implications. They also offer a new perspective on the quantum-blackbox scenario, thereby expanding our understanding of this phenomenon, which is a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics. Additionally, our research exhibits the potential for future applications in quantum information technologies by employing quantum entanglement between the system and environment, and also sheds light on its intrinsic nature. Moreover, our results also disclose a previously unnoticed connection between quantum discord and quantum entanglement, which are key concepts in quantum information theory. They also suggest a way to determine both of these important quantities via a series of infinitesimally weak measurements, thereby facilitating their practical application in quantum information technologies. Moreover, our results also highlight the essential difference between quantum discord and quantum entanglement, which are the two crucial quantities in quantum information theory.

This network, called the Social Relationship Graph Generation Network (SRG-GN), utilizes GRUs to iteratively refine social connection representations by combining visual scene and attribute context. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive integer multiplications with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling significant resource savings when full precision is not essential. Additionally, we incorporate error propagation rules to ensure a specified error margin for MCM results. Our proposed ILP models for various MCM configurations are available in an open-source tool, integrated with the FloPoCo VHDL code generator, providing a complete flow from coefficients to hardware design. Thorough experiments were conducted to assess the models, followed by a detailed analysis of how design metrics impact actual hardware implementation. Our study demonstrates that optimal MCM designs transferred to FPGA and ASIC platforms demonstrate functional equivalence with the expected error tolerance. Our work closely ties hardware and algorithmic design, offering practical guidance to address the optimal MCM problem. Our research thoroughly evaluates the recently developed DNN-based MCM optimizers as an alternative to ILP models and reveals their advantages in some scenarios. Our work successfully addresses the multiconstant multiplication problem while minimizing hardware costs, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between algorithmic and hardware design. \textit{Editor's Note: The paper was returned to the third iteration. The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology continues to be fundamental in 
high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, where significant progress has been 
made over the past decade in advancing the field. This progress could soon lead 
to upgraded existing facilities, enhancements to facilities still under 
construction (such as PIP-II), well-established proposals, or newly emerging 
ideas like the FCC-ee and future proton intensity upgrade at Fermilab, among 
others. Innovations in RF technology not only contribute to HEP but also extend 
beyond to fields such as nuclear physics, basic energy sciences, and other areas, 
as evidenced by European XFEL, LCLS-II and related facilities, or SHINE, 
EIC, and FRIB. Therefore, an extensive R&D program focusing on RF technology 
is needed to tackle challenges in accelerator-based applications and introduce 
new, promising technologies. This R&D would address technical difficulties, 
such as improving performance and cost-effect of accelerating cavities for 
high-brightness linacs, and exploring applications of hollow nanocavities, 
dielectric accelerators, and other innovative approaches. Additionally, the R&D 
would address common problems with applications having high-power proton or 
ion beams, such as heavy-ion accelerators or a future EIC, or those involving 
electrons, such as a future FCC-ee or CFHEP proposal. This report to Snowmass 
2021 presents an comprehensive assessment of the state of RF technology development 
and outlines a broad-range R&D program, encompassing areas of focus like 
Higgs-factory, future proton colliders, and high-intensity hadron accelerators, 
as well as areas like linear colliders, free-electron lasers, and heavy-ion 
accelerators. The R&D recommendations are structured according to specific 
challenges, with an emphasis on the level of effort (small, medium, large), 
the likely impact on the specific project or area (high, medium, low), the 
required resources (short-term, mid-term, long-term), and the potential risks 
involved (none, manageable, high). The report further discusses broader R&D 
opportunities and challenges common to multiple projects/areas, proposing a 
strategy to address these and recommending specific actions for implementation.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC research will require supplementary data obtained from a lepton collider to fully comprehend. This text outlines the underlying principles of electron-positron colliders, a muon collider's proposed energy enhancements and the intricate technical difficulties in constructing such a collider. A feasible solution involves utilizing an existing particle accelerator tunnel and incorporating an advanced muon accelerator chain to achieve an incredibly high energy of 20 TeV per nucleon. Achieving this level of advancement will likely involve breakthroughs in accelerator physics and technology. Nonetheless, constructing a muon collider is a viable and feasible project that can be completed with a total cost of $6-10 billion, providing researchers with a sturdy platform to explore unknown regions of the Standard Model and potentially decisive evidence of new physics. It is emphasized throughout this presentation that a muon collider is not only an essential tool but an irreplaceable component of a comprehensive research strategy in the field of particle physics. This talk summarizes the findings of an extensive report issued by the muon collider working group within the context of the National Science Foundation's (NSF) funded study on a future particle physics facility. The full report is available for download at http://www.fnal.gov/pub/www/collaborations/muoncollider/publications/FPC_Muon_Collider_White_Paper.pdf. We calculate the intensity of cosmic background radiation resulting from the Hawking radiation of primordial black holes. The temperature of this background is given by the average Hawking radiation temperature emitted by these black holes. To find the intensity, we apply the concept of blackbody radiation, normalizing the flux by the Planck function, and then multiply by the speed of light. The resulting intensity matches previous research findings. Furthermore, we have derived a relationship between the primordial black hole mass and the star formation efficiency, which may help to explain why we have not observed the expected cosmic background radiation. The intensity of this background is significantly influenced by the efficiency of star formation because more massive black holes result from higher efficiency star formations, leading to a higher intensity background. We have also considered the effect of eROSITA's sensitivity in detecting primordial black holes through their Hawking decay within our Milky Way. The intensity of this background within our galaxy, resulting from Hawking radiation of PBHs of mass $\sim 5.5 \times 10^{29}$ kg, exceeds the cosmic background intensity by a factor of approximately 1.25. eROSITA's sensitivity could potentially detect the Hawking radiation of PBHs within our galaxy, which may help to clarify the mass range of PBHs participating in galaxy halo accretion. The intensity of this background could be significantly affected if the masses of PBHs participating in galaxy halo accretion lie in the range $\sim 5.5 \times 10^{29}$ to $1.0 \times 10^{31}$ kg. In this mass range, the intensity of the background would exceed the cosmic background intensity by large factors. We have also considered the effect of star formation efficiency variations, which could lead to a dense cloud of low-mass PBHs that would strongly affect the intensity of the cosmic background radiation. The resulting intensity would exhibit a discontinuous change at an efficiency value of approximately $10^{-16}$ due to the PBH mass cutoff in this efficiency range. The intensity of the background in this range of efficiencies lies in the range from approximately $10^{-2}$ to $10^{3}$ times the cosmic background intensity. We have also used the constraint on PBHs in our galaxy from their impact on the galaxy's rotation curve, which may help to clarify the mass range of PBHs participating in galaxy halo accretion. To enhance performance, our innovative VSP architecture features a five-stage pipeline design that increases circuit evaluation parallelism. Moreover, a custom-designed Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) was created to decrease processor gate count, accompanied by comprehensive toolchains allowing for arbitrary C program compilation into our custom ISA. To further boost performance, CMUX Memory-based ROM and RAM implementations over FHE were developed. Experimentation results confirm the effectiveness of the pipelined architecture and CMUX Memory approach in significantly accelerating VSP processing speed. We made the VSP source code available and achieved remarkable results, with each instruction taking under 1 second to complete, a substantial improvement over current existing processors over FHE. The VSP prototype has outperformed the best competing processor, executing nearly 1,600 times faster. VSP has boldly bridged the gap between efficient and secure computing capability for general-purpose sequential processing over FHE. VSP has paved the way for efficient and secure functional evaluations in various emerging homogeneous and heterogeneous distributed computing scenarios such as intelligent edge, metaverse, decentralized AI, and blockchain. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to CSPs with constraints that have a single value, but it is extended to work with the more relaxed constraints. The results are based on the assumption that the LP relaxation is integer soluble, which holds for the considered graph classes. The method uses a new efficient solution technique that reduces computation time. The technique can also be applied to obtain a PTAS for the complementary problem, minimum CSPs with specific value restrictions. The findings are validated through experiments on generated random instances. The research is theoretically significant, and the experiments provide practical insights into the complexity of the problems. The PTAS is implemented as an efficient algorithm that can be used in computational experiments. The research validates that the PTAS can be efficiently used to solve CSPs with specific value constraints in many cases. The findings are not restricted to CSPs but can also be applied to other problems, such as minimum vertex cover or maximum independent set, on graph classes with limited connectivity. The technique presents new perspectives on the approximation of general-valued CSPs and opens up new research directions in the field. The PTAS presents an innovative solution to the problem of approximating general-valued CSPs and can be used in computational experiments to analyze its performance. The efficiency of the PTAS is verified through experiments on random instances, which demonstrates its applicability to the problem. The research is a significant contribution to approximation algorithms and presents new insights into the complexity of general-valued CSPs. The PTAS is a versatile algorithm that can be used in various applications and presents an efficient solution to the problem of approximating general-valued CSPs. The research validates the efficiency of the PTAS and presents new perspectives on the approximation of general-valued CSPs

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weight matrices in pre-trained language models to evaluate sentence structures. Further experiments demonstrate the significance of linear projection matrices in self-attention for accurate parsing. Consequently, the unsupervised models were transformed into few-shot parsing models, FPOA and FPIO, to learn better parsing matrices with limited annotated trees. On the Penn Treebank dataset, the unsupervised model UPIO achieved parsing results on a par with current best techniques on short sentences. Meanwhile, the few-shot parsing model FPIO surpassed previous comparable models, trained on only twenty trees instead of fifty. Importantly, both models showed superior cross-lingual parsing capabilities on SPMRL languages, outperforming earlier methods on most of these languages. Notably, the few-shot parsing model FPIO showed exceptional performance with only twenty labeled sentences on certain languages, thereby exhibiting strong generalization abilities. The models' and source code's availability can be found at https://github.com/alecys/parsing-from-self-attention.

High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated annotation tools are scarce, making relevant object categories more easily identifiable in such images. By leveraging this advantage, we introduce a groundbreaking approach to semantic segmentation, which harnesses the enhanced color and spatial information in HSI images to simplify object annotation. Our novel framework, HSI-HS, excels at object recognition by analyzing each pixel across various spectral bands and then applying a histogram-based technique to simplify the annotation process. Our model's effectiveness is demonstrated through HS segmentation tasks using the Cityscapes dataset, where it displays impressive performance even without any labels, ultimately providing enhanced semantic segmentation and object recognition accuracy. Thorough evaluation metrics, including the mean frequency class intersection over union, reveal our model's stability and best performance when compared to conventional segmentation methods. Our code and related information are openly accessible on GitHub. Experimental findings validate the significant advantages of HSI-HS over conventional segmentation techniques, achieving improved performance in semantic segmentation and object recognition tasks. Additionally, the associated code and related information are openly available on GitHub.

This study reveals intriguing results from a survey of rapidly rotating, cool and luminous stars that have reached the end of their primary life cycle. The research shows that these stars experience a significant loss in rotational velocity by about 50% during a relatively short period, typically taking less than 100 million years. The unusually rapid spin-down of these stars defies the predictions of traditional angular momentum conservation models and instead suggests that these stars experience an unusually high amount of internal mixing that causes a significant loss of rotational velocity. The rapid spin-down of these stars bears a striking resemblance to the characteristics of stars that have been affected by planetary engulfment, although the data collected does not provide conclusive evidence to support this theory. Further research is needed to determine the underlying cause of the rapid spin-down of these stars. The data collected as part of this study is based on a comprehensive analysis of 63 rotating, cool and luminous stars that have reached the end of their primary life cycle and is part of the SPHERICAL III survey. The data collected reveals the detailed physical characteristics of these stars, including their rotational velocity, age, mass and size, and is accessible through the URL spheical-63.html. The research also relies on a sophisticated theoretical model that combines both core contraction and external wind-driven angular momentum redistribution to explain the rapid spin-down of these stars. The theoretical model, when applied to the data collected, comes surprisingly close to matching the observed data, although it does require an unusually high amount of internal rotation that is difficult to explain using traditional astrophysical models. The research does offer an exciting opportunity to further explore the underlying physics of the rapid spin-down of these stars, with potential applications to the theory of planetary engolfment.
