In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-LIN, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after a constant delay in a linear-time algorithm. The proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and operations involve shifting, masking, arithmetic, and comparison. The success of this foundation will be built upon the notion that if an arithmetic operation takes more than a constant number of steps, it can be performed in no more than a constant number of steps after another, with the expense of an additional constant step for handling overflow. This led to demonstrating that, in the current RAM model, linear-time computability is only possible if it can perform a specific set of basic arithmetic operations, including multiplication, division, modulo operation, and specific cases of exponentiation. These findings demonstrate that, even within a widely accepted computation model, a secure theoretical foundation requires a thorough reevaluation of basic assumptions about the underlying computation operations. Additionally, these results reveal new insights into the bounds of linear-time computability and the complexity of specific problems, while also paving the way for further investigations into the minimum storage requirements for achieving linear-time computability. Furthermore, this research may contribute to resolving another prominent open issue - determining whether LIN is a decidable class in the RAM model. A positive solution to this problem would require developing a new algorithm for computing distance in integer metrics on a unit cube, with the additional constraint of using only single arithmetic operations, further highlighting the complexity of this problem with these new storage and computation capabilities. These results also reveal a surprising relationship between the computability of LIN and the feasibility of performing a division operation with only a single step, both of which are critical for achieving linear-time computability. Finally, this research may facilitate a rejuvenated investigation into the bounds of linear-time computability and the feasibility of performing a division operation with only a single step. The proof technique developed in this research may also be applied to other problems, with substantial modifications, in order to obtain these new results. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to identify meaningful patterns, thereby auto-producing negative samples that improve the latent representation of the current item and enhance neighboring nodes. Due to graph-based self-supervision, the models learn to emphasize relevant historical interactions and the co-occurring items users have engaged with, thereby empowering the models to make more informed predictions. Experimental results showed a substantial improvement over baseline sessions-based recommendation models and superior performance when applied to real-world datasets compared to a method that utilizes a plain grid search to generate negative samples. Notably, the models benefited the most from this novel approach when the target items were chosen from a limited set. This work was inspired by co-training in the context of graph neural networks and expanded its applicability to session-based recommendation, thereby initiating a new graph neural network baseline for the field. The proposed method was further validated through an analysis of its effectiveness from both theoretical and practical perspectives and through an examination of its components, which revealed the critical role each played in its success. Finally, the authors provided a theoretical explanation for the success of graph-based self-supervision and the critical role the session graph appeared to be taking in the process. The proposed framework was then evaluated through a range of experiments, which showed it outperformed other state-of-the-art session-based recommendation models. The novel approach was further demonstrated to possess superior practical value through a set of additional experiments designed to examine its practical effectiveness, which showed it consistently produced a higher accuracy than baseline session-based recommendation models and provided more relevant item predictions. The authors then addressed potential ways to enhance the consistency of the proposed method, which would further expand its practical applications. The relevance of the proposed session-based graph neural models could be enhanced through the utilization of additional external session connections that it does not presently utilize. This could be accomplished by exploiting the links between close-by sessions that the models do not presently consider. The authors then provided a comprehensive summary of the proposed graph neural models and addressed how they could be extended to address additional challenges affecting real-world recommendation systems, such as sparsity, cold-start, and ethics. Under specific conditions for the group ring element $v$, the proposed construction allows for the creation of non-trivial group LCD codes, with additional constraints enabling the development of reversible group LCD codes. A variety of binary group LCD codes are presented, including optimal and reversible group LCD codes with various parameters. Furthermore, this research proposes a method for estimating the minimum weights of group LCD codes, providing a lower bound for their weight. The existence of reversible group LCD codes with prime-order multiplicative identities is also investigated. Our findings indicate that certain group LCD codes do not possess reversible or additive properties, yet can possess a high level of self-duality. Finally, this research highlights potential applications for group LCD codes in authentication schemes and presents a code example that surpasses the current known bounds for optimal binary group LCD codes. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory. Specifically, the integrals evaluate scattering amplitudes in pure Yang-Mills theory, a connection first noted by Benedetti and Billi. Our integrals may also be seen as extending the concept of 'hard' particles in the stochastic motion of graphs, a notion analysed by the mathematicians Kapranov and Gogi and the physicist Kapranov. Together with the work by the mathematicians Eguchi, Ojima and Zagier, our results provide a novel explanation for the equivalence between metric and algebraic structures on graph complexes, revealing an underlying graph-theoretic rationale for the magic relations that enable the computation of period integrals. Furthermore, the magic relations emerge as an extension of a fundamental principle in graph theory, one which simplifies their earlier comprehension and provides novel insights into their deep underlying mechanics. Lastly, our integrals may be seen as generating a subgroup of the homology group of the moduli space, one whose cohomology would likely be generated by the periods, a notion whose computation would be reducible to evaluating the integrals at specific 'on-shell' configurations, a possibility first noted by the physicist Kapranov. Our theory extends the concepts of 'hard' and'soft' particles, a distinction whose significance extends beyond the world of graphs to the general linear group and motivic Galois groups, groups whose study is central to the works of the mathematicians Borel, Hensel and the physicist Kapranov. Our integrals may also be seen as giving rise to a generalised 'on-shell' condition for the homology groups, one whose satisfaction would allow for the computation of the cohomology via the periods, a notion whose feasibility would reduce the computation of the cohomology to the simpler problem of integrating the forms across 'on-shell' configurations, a possibility first noted by the physicist Kapranov.

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in real-world conditions such as occluded or partially hidden situations, it has been demonstrated that deep neural networks drawing inferences from visual properties of individual objects, also incorporate information from surrounding context.  This context can serve to alleviate potential ambiguities in object features.  Notably, studies have revealed that when trained on category-level tasks, individual objects within a category tend to be mapped to distinct representations, implying that objects are viewed as collections of distinct, category-orthogonal features.  This study examines the extent to which such category-orthogonal object characteristics serve as a foundation for context-driven inferences in object categorization, revealing that when two objects share few category-orthogonal attributes, they are more likely to be correctly identified even in scenarios where one or multiple object parts are obscured.  This predictive capability was found to decline for objects sharing numerous category-orthogonal attributes, regardless of the occlusion level.  This research provides a systematic understanding of the role of category-orthogonal object features in visual inference capacities of neural networks trained for object categorization.  Additionally, it introduces a quantitative metric, referred to as the category-orthogonal attribute success rate (COASr), for evaluating predictive capabilities in diverse occlusion conditions.  This COASr metric was found to possess high correlation with the predictive capabilities of a network in multiple object categorization scenarios, thereby serving as a useful asset in evaluating and forecasting the performance of a neural network under varying levels of occlusion.  This study further validates the utility of attribute-based methods for assessing and forecasting visual inference capacities of deep neural networks in complex real-world conditions.  Finally, it provides an X-ray depiction of the object attributes that facilitate successful inferences in such scenarios, offering insights into the role of individual attributes in visual processing.  This research further acknowledges the crucial role of multi-layered object features in visual understanding and has introduced the concept of success rates for evaluating and forecasting attribute-based visual inference capacities.  This study further presents evidence supporting the notion that deep neural networks trained on object-level categories (i) exhibit enhanced performance in comparison to those trained on object parts, and (ii) display better generalisation capabilities across a wide array of object categories regardless of the occlusion level of the object part. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with additional free fermion modes and bulk chiral modes. Consequently, the extension of the non-Hermitian topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ is no longer valid in the presence of correlations. We also demonstrated that correlations can regulate the transport of topologically protected edge modes, leading to anomalous transmission when the system is in the extended phase. Our work provides a foundational framework for the study of correlated non-Hermitian topological systems, enabling the exploration of topological properties through correlation functions and clarifying the transport characteristics of correlated non-Hermitian systems. Furthermore, our findings may be extended to higher-dimensional systems and the study of unconventional superconductors. Statements about the breakdown of quantum tunneling and long-range nonlocality are also presented. Lastly, under certain conditions, we reveal that correlations can give rise to indicated phenomena that have no natural occurrence. Our study offers a crucial insight into the relationship between correlations and nonHertmitian topological systems. It clarifies the transport characteristics of such systems and provides a foundational framework for the study of correlated systems. Moreover, it points out that correlations do not enhance the topological classification of one-dimensional systems, whereas correlations do regulate the transport of topologically protected edge modes and can give rise to anomalous transmission in some cases. Our study may be generalized to multi-dimensional systems and extended to the study of unconventional superconductors. This paper utilizes the cyclic parent array concept to develop Golay complementary arrays (GCAs) of polyphase versions. By combining two GCAs, one of which is a traditional Golay code, a Golay complementary array is formed. The paper presents a generalized approach for constructing polyphase GCAs of orders $m \times n$, with specified values of $m$ and $n$, and defines the cyclic parent array as a specific type of bipolar array. Two novel constructions of polyphase GCAs are presented: the first allows any $m \times n$ value, given $m \geq 2$ and $n \geq 2$, and the second allows $m = n$ values, with additional possibility of making GCAs non-polyphase in certain cases. The paper showcases some of the possible GCAs resulting from these constructions. A significant finding is that it is feasible to create a polyphase GCA for nearly every $m \times n$ value. However, there are some restrictive conditions on the possible values of $m$ and $n$ for constructing polyphase GCAs. The paper specifically finds that for an $m \times n$ polyphase GCA to exist, the following conditions must be met: $m$ must be even, $m$ must be a multiple of 3, or $n$ must be an odd multiple of 3. Furthermore, it has been found that $4 \times 4$ and $5 \times 5$ polyphase GCAs cannot be constructed. The proposed methods also possess the potential for further generalization and the development of new techniques for constructing polyphase GCAs. Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previously collected data from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 104.6 fb^-1. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. The constraints on non-standard interactions with electroweak vector bosons align with the standard model predictions in on-shell and off-shell regions. Assuming the standard model coupling structure, the Higgs boson width is constrained between 0.4 and 5.4 MeV, while the simulated expected range is between -8 and 12 MeV. The constraints on the Higgs boson width remain comparable with the consideration of tested non-standard interactions. When considering non-standard interactions, the Higgs boson off-shell coupling deviates from the standard model in on-shell regions, and this deviation is quantified as 1-2 standard deviations. Furthermore, the research explores the sensitivity in detecting discrete conformal symmetry in the Higgs boson system using off-shell production. The off-shell production proves to be a sensitive probe of the Higgs boson properties, and the analysis sets a limit on the Higgs boson width, thereby testing the discrete conformal symmetry in the Higgs boson system. The results from this research also provide limits on the Higgs boson coupling with a light pseudoscalar, and these limits range from 0.42 to 3.89 times the standard model coupling, depending on the pseudoscalar mass. The research further refines the precision on the Higgs boson off-shell coupling and sets the current most restrictive limits on the Higgs boson width near its rest frame. The analysis across the Higgs boson mass range reveals that the Higgs boson coupling to vector bosons exhibits dependence on the momentum transfer, and this effect is most pronounced in the Higgs boson off-shell region. The research provides the most up-to-date limits on the Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons in the four-lepton final state analysis. The analysis also provides the first direct observation of Higgs boson off-shell coupling in the four-lepton final state and the most restrictive limits on the Higgs boson width near its rest frame. Consider the set $\mathcal{S}$ of squares and let $\mathcal{W}$ be a subset of natural numbers such that when you combine these two sets with addition, the result encompasses all natural numbers greater than or equal to some finite number $N_0$. Now, the $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$ denotes the count of all possible pairs of $s$ from $\mathcal{S}$ and $w$ from $\mathcal{W}$ whose sum is equal to $n$. Previous studies have shown that the total count of these pairs minus the total natural numbers up to $N_0$, i.e., $\sum_{n=1}^{N} \mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$, is less than or equal to $N+1$, with the lower bound of $\frac{N}{4}$ asymptotically achieved when the size of $\mathcal{W}$ is a constant multiple of $\sqrt{N}$. Here's an enhancement: when the size of $\mathcal{W}$ is a constant multiple of $\sqrt{N}$, the sum of the counts of all possible pairs whose difference is also zero, i.e., $\sum_{s,w}s,\ s\in\mathcal{S},\ w\in\mathcal{W},\ s+w=0$, the result can be further optimized and is now aspirationally capped at $\frac{N}{2}$. This optimization reaches an aspirational upper limit of $2\frac{N}{4}$ for the original problem stated earlier. Following a straightforward transformation, the generalized problem can be applied to any additive complement of the squares with the same achievability limits. Additionally, the transformation can also apply to any additive complement of the cubes with the achievable limits that are twice the current known limits. Finally, the known lower and upper limits for the size of $\mathcal{W}$ when its elements sum up to half the total natural numbers have been verified and the size of $\mathcal{W}$ has been proven to be greater than $\sqrt{N}$. These findings provide an optimization and an extension to the previously known results which were first published by Chen and Engels in 2015. Furthermore, these results can also be applied to higher powers of natural numbers with the same achievability limits. The key proof involves the application of the Fourier Analytic Method

In this study, a valley degree of freedom-associated interference phenomenon is observed in silicon's local oxidation process, and valley-dependent spin exchange interactions become apparent. To shed light on these interactions, a theoretical model is developed, allowing for the calculation of valley-associated interference patterns and magnetic properties at the atomic level. The results of these simulations reveal a magnetic contrast developing between adjacent silicon atoms as a result of valley-associated interference, and this phenomenon is found to occur prior to the formation of an oxide layer. Additionally, the effect of an oxide layer is valley-associated interference, and this interference can give rise to distinct valley-associated interference patterns. The study finds that an oxide layer can either enhance or suppress valley-associated interference, contingent upon the position of the atom relative to the layer. The observed results offer an explanation for previously documented magnetic properties displayed by silicon wafers, and the theoretical model developed in this study has the potential to be applied to a broad range of materials exhibiting valley degree of freedom-associated interference. Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. For instance, we aim to resolve a significant conjecture by proving that Aut(X) is an algebraic group when X is a non-affine toric variety. Additionally, we propose another conjecture stating that if Aut(X) is a linear group, then X is either rational or of non-compact conjugate linear nature. Furthermore, we present a mysterious open question by asserting that Aut(X) is compactly generated when X is a compact homogeneous variety. Finally, this research involves providing a precise mathematical representation of transitivity degrees for specific groups acting on specific varieties, such as CP(n) and P(n), while exploring related problems and conjectures involving projective spaces. These concepts are further discussed in Chapter 2. Meanwhile, Chapter 3 involves analyzing a distinct set of techniques to compute transitivity degrees for specific groups acting on specific varieties, such as CP(n) and P(n), while exploring related problems and conjectures involving projective spaces. Lastly, Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 are complementary in their approaches to computing transitivity degrees. Specifically, Chapter 4 involves presenting a distinct computational strategy for determining transitivity degrees. It achieves this by employing a unique graph-theoretic method to calculate degrees for specific groups acting on projective spaces. This research is particularly notable as it offers a new algorithmic approach to computing transitivity degrees, thus providing an innovative solution to a long-standing problem involving graph decomposition. Ultimately, this study is a comprehensive collection of new ideas, approaches, and insights to computing transitivity degrees, along with a set of open problems and conjectures, which are further outlined in Chapter 5. We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality. Furthermore, we show that a cut-free version of the Scott model's denotational semantics aligns perfectly with a corresponding operational semantics defined using univalent type theory's lifting monad, thereby illustrating the compatibility of constructive and predicative approaches to domain theory. This research draws on insights from topos theory and provides a new perspective on adapting these insights to univalent type theory. Finally, we hope that our proof that a predicative and constructive Scott model works involves a significant and intriguing application of this research, showcasing the potential for domain theory to be developed entirely from a logical and type-theoretic perspective, even in the absence of classically inclined set-theoretic foundations. Materials related to this work, including a fully formalized proof script, can be found on the corresponding GitHub repository. The proof script combines elements from both Coq and Lean proofs. Additionally, this research benefits from the inspiration and guidance provided by Amr Ahmed's doctoral dissertation. Amr's dissertation has been adapted into a paper, also available on arXiv, and we extend our gratitude to Amr for sharing his work and expertise with us. We also extend our gratitude to Thomas Bredekamp for his feedback on this research, and to Amr Ahmed and Michael Isaacson for engaging in a productive discussion with us on the topic of predicative domain theory. Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints into a Continuous Control Barrier Function, rendering them invertible and straightforward to optimize.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and accuracy in generating collision-free trajectories. Moreover, the CBF-QP approach exhibits a favorable trade-off between prediction time and computational complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate the flexibility of this framework by adapting it to address additional safety constraints related to the presence of narrow passages. Overall, the developed strategy provides a practical solution for the underlying control helicopter. The associated code for replicating the results in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/f-n-a/MRA-CBF. Additionally, the 3D visualizations of the mobile robotic arm's safe navigation are displayed on an online interactive platform at https://n3d.io/214443/. This platform also includes a demo of the underlying CBP-QP framework. For a more comprehensive description of the key components in this research, please consult the associated knowledge outline at https://public.iai.eu/documents/2022-thesis-knowledge-outline.pdf. Specifically, Section 3 discusses relevant prior research, while Section 4 presents the proposed approach in greater detail. Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity. Both exact and approximate matching approaches are taken into account to optimize performance. Empirical evaluation reveals that using graphs for text summarization yields satisfactory results, supporting the utility of this strategy in real-world applications. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a scaled limit and invariance under vertex blow-up. Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their pivotal roles in investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection, and the implications on the puzzles of excess positrons and the widespread TeV gamma-ray excess. Lastly, we outline the prospective research avenues for the upcoming gamma-ray satellite, CTA, and the ongoing and future on-ground observatories.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. Our evaluation reveals that our implementation surpasses existing methods and achieves impressive accuracy rates of 98.4% for rain, 97.2% for snow, and 94.2% for fog. Furthermore, we explore the practical outcomes of employing our model in an vehicle-mounted camera system for weather monitoring. It is designed to facilitate the development and assessment of robust deep learning algorithms across various weather scenarios. Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Furthermore, our results suggest a causal link where science and economics are interconnected, while institutions tend to follow closely behind. It's worth noting that our findings are robust to various different specifications, thereby providing strong evidence for the existing dynamics among these groups. Our study offers a novel approach to understanding the complex interactions among diverse interest groups within this field. To further reinforce our conclusions, we also explored the impact of influential climate change-related events on the interests of these various groups, revealing that science often serves as the primary driver for both institutions and economists, as well as providing valuable insights into the dynamics of public interest as it evolves over time. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current models relying solely on sensor data often lack enough information to accurately represent the system dynamics across different environments and flexible materials. To address this limitation, we propose a novel method using the Koopman operator theory to integrate dimensionality issues, based on an infinite-dimensional spectral geometric approach. To ensure the model remains valid in real-time, our approach involves an adaptive algorithm that updates the system's dynamic model in real-time, enabling more effective control of soft grippers. Through simulations and experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method, achieving a successful grasp rate of 88% for a multi-fingered gripper model and 82% for a single-fingered gripper, both within three seconds of the start. These results validate our approach as a suitable control method for real-world soft grippers automation. One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods. We demonstrate a novel approach for determining the optimal manifold that yields superior performance compared to existing methods, such as the Fisher Information Matrix. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the generalization of any first-order optimization algorithm, including SGD and QA, to Natural Gradient Descent. Our proposed method exhibits superior performance in several high-precision quantum simulations and machine learning tasks, significantly outperforming the existing methods by several orders of magnitude. Additionally, our approach allows for the integration of prior knowledge into the optimization cost function, thereby expediting convergence and achieving better results. Our code is publicly available for reproduction of the results. Our work bridges the gap between optimization theory and practical algorithm development, providing a new framework for algorithm design that prioritizes performance and interpretability. We anticipate our approach to revolutionize the design of black-box optimization algorithms, thereby enhancing the understanding and performance of numerous existing methods. In particular, our generalization of NGD to SGD will empower researchers and engineers to develop more performant algorithms for a wide array of applications. We illustrate the efficacy of our approach through rigorous numerical simulations and showcase its immense potential for further development. Our approach enables the simultaneous optimization of multiple cost functions, thereby expediting convergence and enhancing the understanding of optimization methods. A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies. A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the data requirements for a desired level of accuracy. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. 
Our goal was to confirm the efficacy of LSTM in sentiment analysis and to provide a
benchmark for future researchers by offering a well-documented, high-quality dataset. 
Additionally, we have made the code and data sets publicly available for the sake of
transparency and to facilitate the replication of our work. It is hoped that this effort will
contribute to the advancement of research in this field. The source code can be found at:
https://github.com/Abdullah-7/LSTM_Twitter_Sentiment_Analysis. The data can be found at:
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1k9p1T4U0p0T9pU0p0p0u0p0p0p0p0?usp=sharing. 
It is intended that this project will serve as a valuable educational resource for those
new to natural language processing and sentiment analysis. The project involves tasks and
guidelines tailored to address the needs of students and novice researchers. Our goal is to
make the materials and code base available to the widest possible audience.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety.  To address this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations.  We propose a framework for
training role-specific dialogue models by using a few examples of role-relevant
dialogues.  To optimize our models for role consistency, we employ a data augmentation
technique and a contrastive loss method.  We tested our approach by creating a
dataset of role-consistent dialogues and evaluated it against various open-domain
dialogue benchmarks.  Our model outperformed the benchmark models, achieving a 9.5%
enhancement in conversational consistency, according to an evaluation metric called
Consistency Score, with a notable 400% improvement in conversational style,
as assessed through a style similarity metric called Style Score.  Additionally,
our model demonstrated a 0.54 increase in human satisfaction, obtained through an
evaluation of consumer satisfaction, while maintaining a comparable level of
conversational naturalness, obtained through an analysis of word error rate (WER). 
Our work on role constraints for open-domain dialogue systems represents an
innovation in the field, offering a highly natural and conversational
character to chatbots while enhancing their role-specific dialogue traits in a
scalable manner.  The source code for our model is available at

called the Role Consistency Dataset, can be accessed via

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework that facilitates causal understanding among communicating nodes. Within this system, nodes engage in an emergent communication process, utilizing sequential messages to convey meaning. To effectively decode the intended information, receivers within this dynamic process must evolve through an learning process, guided by the receivers' predictive capabilities. A neuro-symbolic reasoning strategy emerges to address the receivers' semantic uncertainty issue. A key innovation of this research involves the creation of an evolutionary graph, mapping communication signals to their corresponding semantic meanings. A neural network-based classifier is then designed to optimize the evolved graph, enable causal reasoning, and enhance semantic communication. Through the implementation of an example causal query task, our findings illustrate the priority of emergent communication signals over traditional data transfer methods and the superiority of the evolved semantic communication approach over direct data transfer methods. Furthermore, simulation results confirm that the proposed semantic communication system can reduce the data transfer volume by up to 80% and enable causal reasoning among nodes. The proposed approach provides a versatile solution for the neuro-symbolic communication of complex causal information among nodes. The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Various complex algorithms have been applied to tackle this issue, despite there being a straightforward, less computationally intensive solution available - one grounded in statistical naivety. We propose a straightforward approach, which not only reduces computational expenses but also provides a noticeable enhancement in prediction accuracy when integrated with Long Short-Term Memory models. In this research, we present a hybrid word predictor, which synchronizes the statistical Naive Bayes model with latent information, for enhancing prediction results.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two single-colloid particles that move freely in a fluid environment with an inherent viscosity that varies significantly in different areas. Our study centers on understanding the behavior of this dimer when one of its components has a high and the other a low activity level. We have developed a statistical model that enables us to analyze various parameters, including the interplay between their relative activities, position, and applied forces. Our key findings include the presence of unique steady-state arrangements, where the dimer is situated in an optimal position to experience the maximum possible interaction between its components due to the varying activity levels in the environment. Additionally, our model predicts a wide range of movement patterns at higher activity levels that are characterized by a dimer transition state. Our work should facilitate further research on this dimer system through experimental applications and provide a foundation for exploring the behavior of more complex structures composed of multiple colloid particles. It also presents an exciting opportunity to observe these outcomes using advanced technology. We believe that our study will contribute valuable insights to the broader field of active colloid research, enabling novel applications in the future. A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparisons with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large stochastically generated network of 257 fractures. The model exhibits satisfactory convergence in all tests, demonstrating its effectiveness for simulations involving complex fracture networks. The primary outcomes of this work can be utilized to simulate a broader range of natural porous media systems. Additionally, the code developed here can be modified to simulate various types of fluid flow by integrating new kernel modules. The simulated results can serve as a reference for benchmarking other methods and models, particularly those based on more simplified representations of fracture networks. This work can also facilitate the exploration of other applications of discrete fracture models, such as geostatistical modeling of reservoirs and carbon sequestration sites. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second issue, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is realized through a temperature reduction scheme in a simulated annealing process. To this end, a temperature function is proposed that leverages a measure of formation stability, derived from a centroid-based point set registration technique. The technique applies thin plate splines to calculate the average or centroid of a formation, represented by a set of 2D points, with their velocities. The stability measure triggers a temperature decrease when the desired formation is approached. The implementation of this technique via Python yields promising results in various test scenarios, even when facing demanding conditions such as high reformation velocities. The technique outperforms existing methods by achieving lower collision avoidance reformation times and lower formation instability rates. The results validate the efficacy of a novel training approach for annealing simulations and the use of a registered formation's velocity average for collision avoidance reformation. In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue related to stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools from the existing literature to establish necessary first and second-order integrals, along with a modified fractional Stochastic Fubini theorem. By utilizing these innovative strategies, we successfully develop the necessary mathematical framework to investigate this specific control issue, which includes deriving the maximum and minimizing values of the given function. Consequently, we apply the established theoretical framework to a practical example, demonstrating its applicability in a real-world context. Lastly, we touch on the issues related to the delayed term's discontinuity and possible solutions. This study's key contributions are the introduction of the fractional White noise calculus and the modified fractional Stochastic Fubini theorem. They both play crucial roles in the entire analytical process. Lastly, the employed methods and obtained results are then applied to the solution of a delay-based control issue. It is worth noting that the technical difficulty in this project lies in handling the fractional Brownian motion's properties under navigation. These challenges necessitated the introduction of an innovative approach to utility functions and the creation of an hybrid calculus of fractional White noise. Our investigation indicates that even though the fractional Brownian motion meets the requirements for being a cadlag process, it still fails to satisfy either a local martingale or a semi-martingale criterion, necessitating the use of the fractional White noise calculus to make the process "martingale-compatible". Similarly, the modified fractional Stochastic Fubini theorem is utilized to establish the integrability requirements for the optimal control issue, playing a crucial role in the analysis of the mean-field type control problem. Ultimately, this study signifies an significant breakthrough in the mean-field type control problems involving fractional stochastic processes. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over relying on existing, manually generated labels. Furthermore, we discovered that Wikipedia editors' behavior provides more accurate labels compared to crowdworkers who lack the same level of contextual understanding and agreement as editors. Our study delves into the correlations between editing behaviors and quality labels, showing the potential for our approach to contribute to a comprehensive quality assessment metric that also considers other essential factors. As a byproduct, we created a dataset of high-quality sentences from good articles, as well as a large corpus of low-quality sentences from articles in need of improvement, totaling over 33,000 sentences, over 21,000 of which are labeled automatically. This dataset, along with our method, can aid in enhancing article quality using machine learning, while also providing insights into the patterns in editing behaviors that contribute to our labels. Moreover, our work can contribute to the ongoing discussion on trustworthiness and the weight of different types of Wikipedia content. To ensure the reliability of our results, we employed various methods to validate our labels, evaluate our dataset, and analyze our model, such as comparing our labels to those generated by existing machine learning models, as well as assessing the consistency of our edits with Wikipedia policies through the use of edit distance. Our work has been reviewed and approved by human validators, as well as tested for biases and weaknesses in a controlled study, conducted in accordance with ethical standards. To conclude, our research presents an innovative approach to automatically labeling low-quality content in Wikipedia by examining editing behaviors, while also providing a comprehensive dataset and new metrics for measuring quality that can be utilized independently, as well as enhancing the performance of machine learning models seeking to improve article quality. These contributions can aid in further research on Wikipedia quality, while also paving the way for new applications in natural language processing, specifically in domains involving large-scale content production and quality assessment. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our approach is validated by comparing it to other black-box knowledge distillation methods on multiple datasets, and the code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang1999/ZeroShotDBNBD. Experimental results demonstrate that decision-based black-box knowledge distillation outperforms other black-box methods by significant margins in terms of compression ratio and performance. For example, our approach achieved a top-1 accuracy of 53.34% on the CIFAR-100 dataset when training a compact model to be the same size as the original network, whereas standard black-box methods resulted in a top-1 accuracy of 42.88%. Additionally, our approach was the only one that allowed for zero-shot knowledge distillation. Our contribution is threefold: first, we propose decision-based black-box knowledge distillation; second, we introduce a quantitative method for measuring sample resistance to other classes; and third, we introduce pseudo-samples based on network decision boundaries, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our work lays the groundwork for future studies on black-box knowledge distillation to explore the theoretical and practical limitations of our approach. Moreover, our method may have potential real-world applications in areas such as mobile AI and AI-based image recognition. By allowing for the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible to be modeled, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation presents an attractive solution for training deep neural networks in resource-constrained settings. The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, offering clear group-theoretic criteria for classifying classical T-duals and providing explicit, continuous-trace algebra computations for the resulting non-trivial Dixmier-Douady classes. Ultimately, we demonstrate that any solvmanifold can be represented as a $C^*$-algebra bundle of noncommutative tori, which we explicitly compute, while the monodromy of the original torus bundle is translated into a Morita equivalence among fiber algebras. This new perspective enables us to identify instances of ramified T-duals and the emergence of classical T-duals from non-trivial cases through a reduction of Morin's nilmanifolds. We also provide a new geometric interpretation of the T-dual construction for almost abelian solvmanifolds in terms of a commutative $C^*$-algebra associated with the solvmanifold's monodromy, which we explicitly identify and construct. We further extend our formalism to certain cases involving ramified abelian symmetries found in string theory, such as orbifolds, while we introduce an example illustrating a solvmanifold with a non-trivial first Betti number possessing a classical T-dual, while we point out an open problem concerning classical vs. non-classical T-duals and the simplicity of noncommutative tori. Additionally, we present several specific almost abelian solvmanifolds across various dimensions across which the classical T-dual is a bundle of noncommutative tori, along with the explicit codes for the algebraic data involved in the T-dual construction as computed using the author's algebra package 'algebras'. Finally, we present a call for the development of a standard package for symbolic computation with noncommutative $C^*$-algebras, which we believe would greatly benefit the field by providing a common platform and uniform tools for such computations. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from the pool of credible peer experiences, enhancing each other's policies and thereby accelerating the learning process. We validate the efficacy of our approach with successful experiments on both simple and complex tasks, such as multiple-asset portfolio management and control of a complex quadcopter. Quadcopter training times were dramatically reduced, with the learned policies exhibiting impressive generalization when applied to novel environments. Furthermore, our methods demonstrate robustness to various types of noise when applied to portfolio management tasks. These experimental findings support the claim that Co-Imitation Learning can efficiently utilize the learning credits of multiple agents to speed up training, especially on complex tasks. Moreover, our framework ensures the reliability of the knowledge shared among the agents, eliminating the issue of contaminated knowledge that contamines single-agent imitation learning. This novel approach opens up new avenues for multi-agent collaboration in learning. The code and simulation data are publicly available at https://github.com/agarwalrco/co-imitation-learning. The quadcopter videos can be found at https://agarwalrco.github.io/co-imitation-learning/.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in multi-stage search decoding, which can be applied to both convolutional and polar codes. Furthermore, we investigate various computational approaches for PAC codes, including early termination, multi-stage search, and tree search algorithms, and present a dynamic computing-memory tradeoff framework. Experimental results confirm our theoretical findings, showcasing the tradeoff between error-correction performance and computing complexity for PAC codes, as well as the optimal performance of the scaled cutoff rate metric with minimal computations. The proposed scaled cutoff rate metric also offers improved error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes over conventional convolutional codes with iterative decoding, and exhibits a computing complexity similar to that of polar codes with tree search. Furthermore, our results indicate that the computed PAC codes approach the optimal performance of the corresponding convolutional code, with enhanced error-correction performance due to the polarized cutoff rate metric. Additionally, we analyze the impact of the computed path height on file segmentation, and present a precise expression for the expected path height, which surpasses the conventional heuristic bound by a logarithmic factor. Moreover, we investigate the memory-computation tradeoff for PAC codes, and derive a precise expression for the expected memory requirement, which surpasses the conventional convolutional code bound by a factor of $\log_2(\log_2(N))$ for a sequence of random PAC codes of length $N$. Finally, we present a novel bound on the relative compute-energy of PAC codes, which surpasses the conventional polar codes bound by a factor of $\frac{\log_2(\Delta)}{\Delta}$ for a sequence of random PAC codes of length $\Delta$. Furthermore, our results indicate that search complexity is directly proportional to the code rate, search depth is directly proportional to $\log_2(r)$, and there is an inverse proportional relationship between compute-energy and the code rate. This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By converting these joints into a template-based hand model called MANO, our system can reconstruct the entire hand. To track objects, we use an efficient module that generates object SDF data from the first frame and performs optimization-based tracking. Then, to resolve ambiguity caused by occlusions, our system adopts joint optimization for both hands and objects. In our training process, our system only uses simulated, highly variable synthetic data for ease of generalization, making our system more versatile. Our method performs well on real in-the-wild hand-object interaction datasets such as HO3D and DexYCB without further adjustments and significantly surpasses state-of-the-art depth-based hand and object tracking methods while operating at a high 9 FPS rate. Our released code and data are now available for public use at https://github.com/SamehAldabous/HandTrackNet. Keywords: Hand Tracking, Object Tracking, Hand Object Interaction, Depth Point Cloud, Reconstruction, Tracking and Reconstruction. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated by its high 51.64 and 52.19 CMPE on the HO3D and DexYCB datasets respectively, as well as its robustness in various challenging situations such as occlusions, fast hand movements and radical changes in hand and object poses. Our released code and data are now available at https://github.com/SamehAldabous/HandTrackNet.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose and track key points even in the presence of significant pose changes. Alternatively, a keypoint detection and end-effector pose estimation method can be employed for enhanced inferences. Both methods exhibit exceptional performance in direct pose estimation tasks, and are highly adaptable to new environments with minimal retraining. Moreover, they excel in a variety of applications, including predicting critical points, mapping tasks, and predicting success in complex manipulator tasks. To validate our system's effectiveness, calibration was performed using real-world Point Grey and Realsense depth cameras under both indoor and outdoor conditions, yielding remarkable results. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Neural-Factory/robotextrinsics. Supplemental material can be found at https://neural-factory.com/ExtCal. Existing calibration methods employing fiducial markers are impractical for real-world use due to their reliance on simulated models, whereas our extrinsic calibration system relies solely on real-world depth data. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. This improvement in detection through targeted focal units selection is validated across various simulation settings. Further, a novel test based on this concept is proposed for identifying interference in networks. We examine the performance of this new test in a simulated environment and observe that it yields superior results compared to standard approach. Crucially, selecting focused units yields more accurate inferences of treatment interference and enhances the validity of these inferences. Consequently, this technique presents a more efficient solution for detecting treatment interference in networks compared to the traditional experimental approach. We present a package named detei in R for the purpose of performing these novel tests on designated networks. The package detei can be accessed at this website: https://github.com/gneudeteki/detei. The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude of 24.5 for galaxies. Our research utilizes the ShapePipe pipeline to generate accurate galaxy shape data for weak gravitational lensing applications, incorporating data from UNIONS/CFIS's initial six square degree subset. A comparison of shape data from different pipelines reveals ShapePipe's reliability, with the results demonstrating reasonable duality between the co-maps of redshift and galaxy orientation. Employing the SDSS photometry, we generated weighted average shape maps in quadrants of $4500\sq. arcmin$ with an angular resolution of $3\sq. deg$, and discovered a mean galaxy bias of $1.65$ with an uncertainty of $0.03$. ShapePipe's implementation, along with the corresponding shape product, are available at https://github.com/JulianMehrkens/ShapePipe_public.git. Furthermore, the shape data has been released publicly on GitHub and Zenodo, referenced by doi: 10.1101/2021.05.13.445 604. Additionally, the corresponding source code and shape data can be accessed through https://github.com/JulianMehrkens/ShapePipe_public.git and Zenodo: doi: 10.1101/2021.05.13.445604.

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\alpha + ib$. Veech demonstrated that, for specific real numbers $\alpha$ and $b$, the set of numbers of the form $n + ib$, mod $1$, is evenly distributed. More recently, it was determined that an analogous result can be achieved for the mod $3$ form, and a general framework for achieving mod $q$ forms has been developed, allowing for the calculation of bounds related to Hausdorff dimension. A key aspect of this new framework is the use of a specific set of lattices, defined by the numbers $1, \sqrt{3}i$, and $1+\sqrt{3}i$, which have the advantage of requiring the computation of only a limited number of points to achieve the desired precision of the approximation. Furthermore, it was found that achieving the mod $q$ forms requires the computation of a specific number of points, which is shown to be no more than a multiple of the logarithm of $q$. Additionally, a mod $q$ form of the Weyl's equidistribution theorem can be achieved when $q$ is a product of two distinct prime numbers, which has to do with the computation of certain integrals and their connections to Jacobi action of Hecke algebra, especially in the case where $q=3$. A new method for achieving the mod $q$ forms has to do with the use of the Veech's unitary tree, which has the advantage of allowing for the computation of the rotation numbers of irrational rotations of the form $\alpha + ib$ without having to solve Diophantine equations, while also providing a new method for approximately solving such equations, which has to do with the computation of the Hausdorff dimension of the set of bad diophantine approximation, which has long been known as the set of $\omega(\sqrt{3})-bad$ numbers, and has recently been studied extensively by J. Martin. A significant consequence of the new method for achieving the mod $q$ forms has to do with the unitarity of the rotation matrix, which has the advantage of allowing for the computation of the boundedness of the rotation, which has long been known as the $3x1$-problem, and has recently been studied extensively by M. Sock

We prove that for a singular local complete intersection k-rational variety, k-Du Bois, k-rationality and k-Du Bois properties coincide. Furthermore, we demonstrate the k-rationality or k-Du Bois property for certain types of local complete intersections, including those with codimension two or three, and also hypersurfaces with specific properties. These findings are derived from an underlying theorem relating the rationality of local zeta functions to vanishing cohomology. Additionally, we explore the rationality of local zeta functions for certain types of monomial ideals. Crucially, our approach does not rely on the resolution of singularity theorem or the characteristic zero analogues, allowing it to yield singular varieties with positive characteristic that satisfy these conditions. This methodology is a key adaptation from the prior work of S. Gusev, M. Szyma\'nski, and C. H. Woracek. Another significant observation relates the rationality of local zeta functions to the vanishing of tight log forms, a concept introduced by J. Herzog and A. Thompson. This observation is particularly significant as it enables the separation of singularities into two distinct groups: those with vanishing tight log forms and those without, which exemplifies the complexity of the problem. Finally, the paper includes extensive appendices that contain supplementary results and crucial estimates necessary for the proof of the key theorem. One such appendix involves an independent discovery of an important estimate by M. Szyma\'nski, which is instrumental in establishing the k-rationality of certain monomial ideals. Another appendix contains a previously unpublished work by C. H. Woracek that is essential to the proof of the key theorem. Yet another appendix contains an alternative demonstration of the key theorem via an alternative method, along with other complementary results. Lastly, the paper concludes with a comprehensive bibliography and a list of open problems along with proposed solutions. One such problem involves confirming whether an example of M. Brodmann and C. H. M\"uller, which involves a monomial ideal with a rational but non-vanishing local zeta function, can indeed be generalized to codimension three. Another problem involves verifying whether an example of M. Szyma\'nski, which involves a monomial ideal with a rational but non-vanishing local zeta function, can be generalized to hypersurfaces. We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the time-evolution operator are employed to determine the critical temperatures and exchange integrals, revealing an unexpected anisotropy of the latter. This unique combination of BKT physics and tunable magnetic anisotropy can contribute to the development of novel quantum technologies like quantum computers, where practical applications of BKT physics could be explored. Additionally, this research provides insight into the complex effects of magnetic anisotropy on 2D to 3D phase transitions in geometrically challengeable systems. Ultimately, this study presents an innovative strategy for producing supratranslational long-range order in a two-dimensional system through the deliberate introduction of magnetic anisotropy. Lastly, the researchers suggest that another BKT system could be designed with a critical temperature of around 1 Kelvin by utilizing a pyrazine-based copper compound with weak interlayer coupling. However, this would require decreasing the exchange coupling to near its quantum limit by adjusting the hydrogen bonding between layers. Ultimately, this novel quantum-synthetic system could facilitate original experiments to study the robust BKT physics that persists in the limit of very weak magnetic anisotropy. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by TuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note its exceptional performance with respect to throughput, energy consumption, and latency. TuRaN represents the first TRNG that can simultaneously achieve low latency, high throughput, and low power consumption while maintaining continuity. As such, it has the potential to significantly impact the field of information security. Leveraging TuRaN could enable the development of secure internet of things systems capable of withstanding sophisticated attacks due to their enhanced resilience against predictability exploits. Moreover, TuRaN could significantly reduce the resource requirements of secure systems, thereby facilitating the deployment of security features in resource-constrained devices. To facilitate easy implementation, we provide sources for TuRaN that can be directly used in firmware or hardware designs. The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination number affect the underlying physics. Additionally, we observed the potential for superconductivity or Mott-like behavior to occur under certain conditions. Lastly, we outline the experimental implications of our findings.
