A higher education system or similar opportunities serve as key milestones that allow individuals to enhance their social standing. To examine the behavior of societies that provide limited opportunities to their members, we develop a theoretical model that focuses on the decision-making processes of both the ruler and the ruler's children. The ruler determines the number of opportunities available based on the likelihood that her children will be successful. If the chances of success are low, the ruler may choose to limit the number of opportunities, as this makes it less likely that children will leave the system in search of better prospects elsewhere. However, if the chances of success are high, the ruler may opt for a "first-come-first-served" policy, as this increases the likelihood that children will remain within the system in search of better opportunities. Our theoretical results are supported by empirical analysis of college admissions in the United States, where we find that societies that provide limited opportunities to their members are more likely to implement merit-based admission systems. The transition from preferential admission to merit-based admission has led to improved social mobility in these societies. Conversely, we discover that societies that provide an abundance of opportunities are more likely to implement a "queue-based" admission system. Our research suggests that the design of opportunity allocation systems, particularly higher education systems, plays a pivotal role in determining social mobility and motivates rulers to make informed decisions about opportunity allocation to benefit their children's future prospects. Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of the design of opportunity allocation systems in determining social mobility and suggests various policy implications. If rulers prioritize the well-being of their children, they should strive to create opportunity allocation systems that encourage children to remain within the system by limiting access to external opportunities and providing equal access to opportunities within the system. Furthermore, we discover that opportunity allocation systems with elements of randomness, such as lottery systems, may also encourage children to remain within the system by limiting the allure of external opportunities. On the other hand, merit-based opportunity allocation systems enhance the chances that children will leave the system in search of better opportunities, as these children are more likely to find better opportunities elsewhere. Our research suggests various policy implications for college admissions, as well as other opportunity allocation systems, such as immigration policy and welfare policy, where rulers make decisions about the duration of opportunity allocation to beneficiaries. Our study also highlights the importance of program design, as this determines the effectiveness of such policies in achieving desired outcomes. To illustrate the relevance of our research to real-world issues, we examine college admissions in the United States, as well as immigration policy and welfare policy

The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.

Additionally, we observe that Delegated RingCT can accommodate distributed ledger technology at a larger scale due to its considerably faster transaction processing capabilities. Consequently, we suggest that Delegated RingCT can provide an effective compromise between anonymity and the practical requirements of a decentralized cryptocurrency. If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics. 

We define a subclass of linear systems as solvable in n^o(1) log^k n space if there exists an approximate solver for its specific instances that requires at most n^o(1) log^k n space; our main result states that if such solvers exist, we can also solve a broader class of linear systems in n^o(1) log^k n space. 

Our proof relies on a novel reduction from one approximate solver to another, using a concept called 'approximate compactness'. We note that our reduction does not rely on specific computational models such as the László Székely's combinatorial algorithm, or randomization, making it applicable to a wide range of input representations. 

We define another subclass of linear systems as solvable in n^o(1) log n space if there exists an approximate solver for its specific instances that requires at most n^o(1) log n space; our main result states that if such solvers exist, we can also solve a broader class of linear systems in n^o(1) log n space. 

Our space-complexity results are a direct consequence of our application of the known time-complexity results to space-complexity settings, utilizing a concept called'space compression'. 

Finally, our findings show that approximating the logarithm within a certain precision is necessary for solving certain linear systems in approximate space, providing the first such lower bound in the literature. 

From a technical standpoint, our proof involves the use of space-efficient data structures such as the priority queue and a new variant of the ball sort algorithm which utilizes the size of the array for sorting, as well as space-efficient sampling algorithms. 

We note that our results and methods are primarily focused on understanding the theoretical bounds and may not yet translate to practical solutions for solving linear systems in approximate space. 

Ultimately, our findings provide a framework for testing the correctness of approximate linear system solvers that operate in near-logarithmic space, by reducing the task of testing such solvers to another solver for a specific subclass of linear systems with known solutions

Current research on LDPC codes usually assumes the independence of degree distributions and various correlated distributions, but fails to provide a comprehensive theoretical framework. To address this gap, our study develops degree-degree correlated LDPC codes and provides a comprehensive framework for designing associated degree-degree product distributions. We show that any degree-degree product distribution can be achieved through various constructions of correlated LDPC codes, including ensemble and single-code methods. Our work also explores the impact of degree-degree correlations on the decoding processes of LDPC codes, particularly in discussions surrounding the asymptotic and near-asymptotic performances of LDPC ensembles under different channel models. Furthermore, we investigate how to design degree-degree correlated LDPC codes with optimal or superior error-rate performance compared to traditional LDPC codes, and provide numerical examples to verify our findings and demonstrate their practical applications in enhancing the overall performance and code design flexibility of LDPC codes. Overall, our study contributes to the further development and understanding of LDPC codes and their applications in error-correcting codes. Additionally, the novel techniques and ideas presented in this work can be extended and adapted for the design and analysis of other advanced coding ensembles, enriching the field of low-density parity-check code design.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may facilitate the development of in-context learning, even when each domain doesn't result in in-context learning alone. Lastly, a pretraining corpus related to a downstream task may not always ensure a high in-context learning performance for that specific task, especially when it comes to the few-shot setting, and that language modeling performance and in-context learning do not always correlate as one might expect. Our study provides valuable insights into the characteristics of a pretraining corpus that's necessary for in-context learning to emerge, and it also highlights the importance of a thorough evaluation process through a nuanced understanding of the task at hand. Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of forming gas clouds disintegrates and spreads throughout the cluster. To investigate this process, we conducted 3000 particle simulations of a developing gas cloud within a typical galaxy cluster environment, examining how a varying initial disk density and magnetic field strength affect the evolution of the gas cloud. Typically, within a few million years, the gas cloud shatters into numerous dense fragments, which expand at different rates while retaining magnetic field strength. This fragmentation process increases the surface area of gas, ultimately leading to a higher rate of heat loss and further instability. Depending on the strength of the magnetic field, some systems experience a "thermal equilibrium" where the growth of the gas cloud's volume due to cooling is balanced by the loss of mass to the surrounding ICM, creating a "cooling flow". A high magnetic field recovers the equilibrium faster, while a low magnetic field allows the gas cloud to continue growing in mass and creates unusual, sinuous shapes in the gas cloud due to the continued fragmentation. Thermal conduction accelerates this process, resulting in a loss of structure and the rapid expansion of the gas cloud due to the rapid heat transfer. In magnetic field-free environments, the gas cloud's surface area increases rapidly, leading to a rapid increase in mass and a loss to the surrounding ICM due to a high mass flux density. In summary, the rapid break-up of galaxy cluster forming gas clouds is likely to cause widespread, rapid gas loss and a loss of initial, intricate structure, while maintaining steady, long-term 'cooling flows' requires the presence of a strong magnetic field. Moreover, the widespread, rapid expansion of gas due to the disintegration of forming galaxy cluster clouds may aid in the maintenance of a high star formation rate in the central nebulae by continuously supplying new, high-density gas clouds. This, in turn, may help to explain the apparent age discrepancy between the central nebulae and the surrounding galaxy cluster. Finally, the extension of our simulation results to larger galaxy cluster masses reveals that the rapid, widespread expansion of gas due to the disintegration of forming galaxy cluster clouds may ultimately lead to a'strangulation' star formation suppression phase. To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage diverse data streams. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and an optimal resource allocation algorithm to manage computation and radio resources in a sustainable MN. We show that these mechanisms allow BSs to dynamically adjust resource pools to meet the needs of changing mobile and IoT traffic, thus preventing unnecessary resource over-provisioning, a problem that typically leads to wasted resources in a shared MN. A numerical analysis confirms that our proposal reduces the likelihood of resource over-provisioning and resulting waste by more than 90%, thus extending the life of computation and radio resources in a shared MN. We present detailed core network management procedures to support these optimizations and provide a comprehensive framework for managing sustainable MNs. Moreover, we define a metric called the sustainable network life cycle, which calculates the number of replacements needed for each resource type based on a MN's current and future traffic patterns. Our simulations show that a dynamic BS resource management approach significantly increases the sustainable life cycles of computation and radio resources by more than 120% compared to a static resource allocation method. Furthermore, we show that our proposed dynamic resource management approach provides better results for multiple MN configurations and traffic scenarios, thus confirming its efficacy in managing future mobile networks. The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The AU sequences are then used to develop synthesis models, and the effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through the analysis of subjective and objective scores on the Zerospeech 2019 challenge database. The results show that acceptable quality speech synthesis at a low bit rate can be achieved with the proposed units. However, the synthesis quality could be improved by supplementing the approach with additional training data and a more advanced model. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot. It successfully completed a 10 km hour inverse dynamic simulation and a 0.1 km hour direct dynamic simulation, all while producing visually appealing and physically feasible outcomes. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques. Additionally, steady-state amplitudes were determined using two different expansion techniques in the context of a weak excitation case. The study found steady-state solutions that depend on the average angular velocity, pitch angle, and frequency and amplitude of excitation, among other factors. It was observed that when excitations are minimal, regular oscillations occur; however, as excitations increase, irregular movements emerge and are further exacerbated when vertical and horizontal excitations coexist. Moreover, the results reveal regular movement patterns that conform to specific geometric shapes (Lissajous and cardioid patterns) under specific conditions of excitation. Experimentation using a digital camera and slow-motion filming showed the existence of irregular movements, which were predicted through numerical simulation. The study found that regular movements are favored when vertical excitation prevails and, interestingly, the occurrence of regular movements when both vertical and horizontal excitations are present can be manipulated by adjusting the ratio of these excitations. It was also discovered that regular movements of a specific geometric shape (Lissajous) are favored when the ratio of excitations lies within a specific range and, alternatively, regular movements of a different geometric shape (cardioid) are favored by another excitation ratio. Ultimately, the occurrence of regular versus irregular movements can be dictated by the ease with which the pivot changes its vertical position. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we modified the velocity-based model by adding a current correction term, which aligns the response of this model with the dipole-based model and achieves agreement with the converged standard band theory. This correction term, scaled by the system's size, accounts for the discrepancy arising from the finite tight-binding basis and ensures gauge invariance in the limit of a infinitely large system. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effective cancellation of singularities in the TB models' interaction operators through the Kontoulis trick, eliminating the need for convolution and replacing it with a sparse, locally acting operator. This simplification results in a significant reduction in computational complexity without loss of physical precision. To facilitate practical implementation, we introduced a set of locally balanced, maximally localized Wannier functions that capture the low-energy physics of the materials with enhanced resilience to perturbations and long-range effects, allowing for the achievement of a converged band structure with a smaller basis set. Additionally, we developed a novel approximation of the dipole tensor that replaces frequent matrix multiplication with a more efficient, sparse index-based approach, leading to substantial computational efficiency improvements for single and double precision calculations. Finally, we integrate these methodological developments into a modular, flexible, and high-performance tight-binding code named JULIP-TB, which includes a range of tight-binding simulation tools. This code provides accurate first-principle insights into the optical responses and non-linear excitations of materials. It also offers a range of additional features and functionalities that enhance the efficiency and scalability of tight-binding models, including the calculation of material inducible responses and the determination of non-linear optical properties. This analysis will involve examining the distribution of the complex parameter $\gamma$ on the Cayley plane following the transformation of its values under the Cauchy distribution. This investigation stems from a corresponding study on the normal distribution, which employed the Poincaré half-plane; in this context, the Poincaré half-plane's geometry can be mapped to the Cayley plane through a conformal transformation. As a result, the findings for the Cauchy distribution will be expressed in terms of the Poincaré half-plane, allowing us to revisit and reinterpret the normal distribution's results through a different geometric lens. Furthermore, this study will quantify the geometric properties of the Cayley plane, such as the Hausdorff dimension of its sets, thereby contributing to the development of geometric probability theory. To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance of high-accuracy and high-speed in mind.  The movement of many high-accuracy motion systems over the long term is limited by wear and tear.  The main challenge here is that traditional control designs which focus on long-term performance often result in performance losses in the short term due to uncertainties.  One way to address this issue is to use a control method that takes changes in system parameters into account in real-time.  Although this approach does result in more accurate long-term performance predictions, it does introduce some complexity.  In order to overcome this limitation, a new system design is proposed which decouples the short-term and long-term performance metrics.  The result is a control method that is both simple and effective, and has been successfully tested on an linear motion system with precision adjustments for the industry.  The movement of the tested system is similar to that seen in many other high-accuracy motion systems which experience performance losses due to friction and wear over the long term of operation.  The effectiveness of the proposed control method was evaluated in simulation using an model which accurately represents the dynamics of the motion system, and was also put through real-world testing on an in-place linear motion system in the industry.  The performance of the proposed control method far surpassed that of traditional control methods in both simulations and real-world tests.  The new control method does result in some minor changes to system parameters, but these changes can be mitigated through a process known as "calibration", and do not impact the movement of the system in any way.  The same problem of LPV sequential loop closing for other high-precision motion systems which experience performance losses due to wear and long-term movement patterns could be addressed using the new control method, and is the subject of ongoing research by the authors.  The movement of these systems is limited by wear and tear over the long term of operation, and is often accompanied by performance losses due to friction and wear, as well as changes in system parameters which must be taken into account in real-time in order to achieve more accurate long-term performance predictions.  The authors have also developed a new system design which decouples the short-term and long-term performance metrics, and is both simple and effective.  The result is a control method that is both simple and effective, and has been successfully tested on an in-place linear motion system in the industry, and could be applied to other motion systems in the future.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Furthermore, PRNet's view-agnosticity enables zero-shot generalization to unseen categories. With its adaptability and performance across diverse datasets, including real-world datasets such as NUI-Field, NUI-Wild, and RW-Real, PRNet represents a versatile registration method for a broad range of applications. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/mu-Systems/PRNet.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Existing methods often adapt known classes' knowledge to unknown modalities, but since we don't know which classes exist, this approach is ineffective. To overcome these challenges, we suggest employing seamless image synthesis to create labeled imaginary data from the unseen modality, allowing us to segment synthetic data from the known modality instead. However, generating perfect synthetic data is impractical, so we instead propose training a model that can segment real data from both known and unseen modality sources, processing samples from multiple modalities in an alternating sequence to avoid mode confusion. Our method has several advantages: it doesn't necessitate identifying which classes to use, can process samples from multiple modalities simultaneously, and can segment the unseen modality without labeled data by segmenting synthetic data. We test our method by segmenting the MRI modality, demonstrating its effectiveness on multiple public datasets. Our code and datasets are publicly available for verification. The authors' codes can be found at https://github.com/ghome23/CyclicSegGAN and the datasets at https://neurology-in-figures.github.io/LabelFreeMRI.html. Our paper has been accepted for publication in ICCV2021 and SFOR2022, with a published version at arXiv:2104.07837 and arXiv:2111.07197. Our models have won several contests, including LabelFreeMRI challenge at MICCAI2021 and ImageJAX challenge at ICIP2021, and our paper on LabelFreeMRI has received the 2nd best paper award at MICCAI2021. Our models also won the 1st place in FlowPrediction challenge at STAC2022, and our paper on LabelFreeMRI also received the 1st place in LabelFreeCT challenge at MICCAI2022. Experimental results demonstrate that our method performs better on higher-resolution data and achieves comparable results to fully supervised methods when high-resolution data are available for supervision, while significantly outperforming existing unsupervised domain adaptation methods when high-resolution data are not available for supervision. Moreover, our method also performs better on lower-resolution data without supervision than traditional domain adaptation methods. Moreover, our method also performs better on multi-modality dataset than single-modality supervised dataset, demonstrating its ability to learn more general and transferable segmentation knowledge. Additionally, our method also performs better on variety of clinical tasks including tumor segmentation, multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation, retinal vessel segmentation

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$. Furthermore, we identify the necessary and sufficient conditions for these operators to meet the required criteria. It is also shown that the convergence in compact uniform norm of the operators $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, as $\psi$ undergoes a specific transformation, can be equated to the convergence in the same norm of the composition operators $C_\varphi$. Our investigation also involves establishing sufficient and necessary conditions for the C-normality of another class of operators, specifically those involving a Moore-Dirac operator, under a given conjugation operation. These findings broaden the existing results in the field by providing more general outcomes. Our work may also provide insights into the relationships between conjugation operations, function conjugations and their relationships with linear operators. Neural network-based point cloud models have shown exceptional performance in handling raw sensor data for object detection and state estimation applications. Despite achieving significant improvements, these models remain prone to inaccurate predictions in incomplete or partially occluded environments. A widely adopted solution, domain adaptation, has limitations in tackling missing data within the same domain. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called Transformation-Specific Point Cloud (TPC) smoothing, which leverages a set of established transformation models to fill gaps in the sensor data. Our method proves to be an effective domain adaptation technique, outperforming existing methods in dealing with incomplete or partially occluded data. The proposed technique is versatile and can be applied to various domain adaptation scenarios with a wide range of parameters. Additionally, we conduct an ablation study and provide an open-source implementation to facilitate further research. Experimental evaluations confirm the proposed method's efficacy in enhancing the performance of point cloud models, especially in predicting missing data and handling partial occlusion. Notably, our method achieves a 10% relative improvement in prediction accuracy in comparison to a leading domain adaptation method. The proposed technique demonstrates a flexible and effective solution to handling incomplete or partially occluded point cloud data, setting a new benchmark in the field. To further validate the method's efficacy, we provide a video supplement to the paper, examing its performance in various scenarios. The method's potential applications extend beyond object detection and state estimation, and it can be used in various domains such as self-driving cars, robotics, and drone navigation. The repository can be accessed at https://github.com/achchauh/TPC. The proposed technique is an effective domain adaptation method that can be used to enhance the performance of point cloud models in various applications. To validate the method's efficacy, we conducted a series of experiments employing a range of parameters, and provided a video supplement to the paper to examine its performance in different scenarios.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen-pearl (EPRP) experiment is improved upon by developing two more robust versions,'strong' and'super' EPRP experiments, which exhibit greater Bell nonlocality than their weaker counterparts. Specifically, the strong EPRP experiment showcases a greater amount of Bell nonlocality through both higher maximal violations of Bell inequalities and greater distances from the clifford limit, all while maintaining a comparable cost structure as the original EPRP experiment. Furthermore, the super EPRP experiment surpasses the strong version in this regard, with the added advantage of requiring fewer measurements per party than the strong version without losing Bell nonlocality. These enhanced EPRP experiments present a new benchmark for quantum communication applications and serve as valuable resources for testing the nonlocality of complex quantum systems, rendering the original EPRP experiment and its 'weak' version strong and super EPRP experiments, respectively. Additionally, a possible implementation of the strong EPRP experiment on optical systems using postselection is proposed. Lastly, a theoretical framework for a new type of Bell nonlocality known as 'incomplete Bell nonlocality', which deviates from the traditional inequality-based paradigm, is introduced via a pivotal example of the super EPRP experiment and subsequently demonstrated in multiple complete and incomplete scenarios. A fundamental distinction between Bell inequalities and other forms of nonlocality such as particle splitting and teleportation, as well as no-hiding mechanisms, is also established. Finally, a future research goal is outlined by the developer of the EPRP idea, which aims to achieve a Bell nonlocality free from postselection, thereby resulting in a perfect Bell nonlocality without inequalities. A note on copyright has also been added.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, the study illustrates the ability to map detected communities in the low-dimensional phase space, even in cases where the system's dynamics are unknown. In a real-world application, the approach successfully segmented the atmospheric data into meaningful regions, enabling researchers to analyze the Amazon rainforest's spatial divide. Additionally, the analyst can reconstruct the long-term spatial patterns and explore the variability in the forest's ecosystem over extended periods. In another test, the time-series data of individual variables from electrical power and airline industries were successfully grouped into relevant categories, and the approach was further validated through the application of influence-based clustering to attractorial subspaces derived from atmospheric and electrical power data, resulting in the formation of intricate structures that reflect the underlying dynamics of the systems. Overall, the proposed method facilitates the analysis of dynamic data, thereby enabling researchers to gain new insights into the behavior of complex systems. Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a modern variable-based approach, whereas Arthur highlights the significance of infinitesimals in calculus, leading him to adopt a logic-based representation.  In contrast, I argue that an intuitive arithmetic handling of infinitesimals provides a precise mirror of Leibniz's actual calculus.  This mirror-effect can be achieved by translating key concepts within a calculus language designed by Robinson.  By examining the roles of variables, bound and free, in a context enriched with arbitrary sequences, we can gain a deeper understanding of Leibnizian concepts such as sequence, infinitesimal, and rate.  Furthermore, infinitesimal movement emerges as a natural consequence of these fundamental notions, eliminating the need for a distinct definition.  By comparing the variable, bound-free, and intuitionistic approaches, we can identify unique aspects of each that illuminate Leibniz's thoughts on calculus, revealing a unified picture of calculus based on sequences, infinitesimals, and gradual change. In contrast, I argue that this assertion distorts the true nature of Leibniz's calculus by prioritizing a variable-based approach over an arithmetic one, as advocated by Arthur.  By reconsidering the fundamental structure of this calculus in terms of sequences, I show that its core concepts revolve around sequences, infinitesimals, and gradual change, as equally essential to understanding Leibniz's thoughts on calculus. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation has been explored, particularly the labeled distillation method. This approach minimizes errors by directly learning from correct labels, thereby accelerating the distillation process. However, previous studies discovered that labeled distillation training often resulted in underperforming models compared to supervision from a single high-quality teacher. To address this issue, we propose a new method called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), which combines multiple teachers and learns effective student models through iterative correction. Moreover, PILE allows the assignment of greater confidence to ensemble logits from high-quality teachers and the incorporation of hyper-logarithmic numbers of teachers, thereby extending the applicability to a wide range of scenarios. PILE's efficiency is demonstrated through a substantial reduction in computational costs of up to 10x and 4x less memory usage compared to other approaches, while achieving superior performance on large-scale ranking tasks. Our research not only offers insights into label-free knowledge distillation but also provides a practical solution to address the computational limitations of this approach. The source code of PILE is publicly available at https://github.com/epam/PILE.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively. The weights' signs can be positively or negatively constrained, depending on the matrix's sign. The weights of the Dirac masses can be interpreted as eigenvalues of a matrix involving a Toeplitz matrix and a circulant matrix, whose entries are determined by the Fourier components up to the cutoff frequency, the torus's circumference, and the point at which the Dirac masses' supports terminate. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. It is interesting to note that local critic training can also be applied to parallel data training, expanding its potential applications. To explore this idea, we will examine the properties of clouds located far from their host galaxies' centers, specifically those associated with the Central Molecular Zone in the Galaxy. These clouds are enveloped by compact filaments that emit radio signals at 22 GHz, typically associated with methanol ice. The rate of star formation within these clouds will be compared to the average GFN (star formation rate to gas mass ratio) in the Galaxy, with the aim of uncovering the link between radiation density and star formation. To assess the impact of radiation, we will analyze the behavior of a model cloud, adjusting variables such as radiation intensity, gas temperature, and density to observe their effects. The findings of this simulation will be presented in a graphic comparison to real data from the Central Molecular Zone. The discussion will conclude with a consideration of the relevant factors that might prevent the formation of new star clusters in the Galaxy's Central Molecular Zone. The analysis will also raise questions about the stability of gas-free standing shocks, particularly those triggered by ionization fronts in cloud edges, and the effect of radiation pressure on dust grains. The ultimate consequence of this exploration will be a deeper understanding of the interplay between starlight and star formation, a concept encapsulated in the phrase "starlight in darkness: the birth of stars." This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. Furthermore, this paper outlines a general framework for applying NS-based entropy estimation that can be applied across various challenges and unsolved problems. A publicly accessible Python package has been developed to facilitate the method's implementation. It's also available online at https://ntsc.github.io/NSEntropy/. This work builds upon prior research on NSEntropy, expanding its applicability while maintaining comparable computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method typically achieves accurate results with minimal computational overhead, suitable for tasks in real-time or near-real-time. Future work is suggested to expand the method's reach into other areas of entropy estimation. The code for this research is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/ntsc/NSEntropy/README.md. A detailed tutorial is also available at https://ntsc.github.io/NSEntropy/tutorials.html. This work is backed by funding from DARPA and the Air Force Research Laboratory. A corresponding paper on this research has been published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research, volume 23. Additionally, the authors present an alternative approach to NTSC that uses Reversible Neural Estimators (REs) for comparing the performance of NSEntropy and RE-based methods on generating random samples from unknown distributions. REs fail to achieve comparable results with NSEntropy in many cases; however, the RE approach outperforms NSEntropy in some scenarios involving the prediction of future outcomes from past data. The RE method successfully captures the long-term structure of the distribution; nevertheless, it incurs a higher computational cost due to the additional memory requirements of maintaining a reverse model. The authors hypothesize that the suitability of either NSEntropy or RE might depend on the specific latency constraints of the underlying application, with RE being more suitable for tasks with higher latency tolerance. A publicly accessible Python package has been developed to facilitate the comparison between RE-based and NSEntropy-based entropy estimation, and it is available online at https://ntsc.github.io/RENE/. The code for this research is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/ntsc/RENE/

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion in raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By recognizing this trait, an effective criterion for biolocomotion detection is proposed. Alternatively, an alternative approach based on a deep learning model is presented to classify biological movement using a larger and more comprehensive dataset. Additionally, this document explores the uses of biolocomotion, discussing its potential impact on multi-robot systems and the differentiation of living and non-living objects. A final consideration is presented for future research in this field. A freely downloadable video dataset, known as the Biolocomotion Dataset, is provided to support further research on this topic. The dataset comprises a comprehensive collection of biolocomotion videos, alongside non-biolocomotion footage for comparison. Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations. Our work sets the stage for future investigations into incorporating additional power network constraints. The source code for this work is openly available on GitHub.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Furthermore, it's shown that the widespread use of short, artificially curated data sets in research can result in biased models that fail to correctly simulate physical behaviors in a variety of untested conditions. Utilizing an open-data and open-science approach, this research encourages the adoption of rigorous experimentation in computational physics discovery and promotes the use of comprehensive, experimentally validated datasets that can help in the in-depth analysis of discrepancy modeling and further advances in this area. It's thus hoped that this work will inspire new insights in the physical understanding of a phenomenon that has been studied for centuries. Finally, a future challenge is issued to the AI and ML research community: develop a data-driven model of object fall that's equally accurate as the law of gravity without receiving any formal instruction or credit. The code and datasets utilized in this research are publicly available at https://github.com/adv-physics-discovery/falling-body and https://github.com/adv-physics-discovery/autophysics-GBM. The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A key variant explored in this paper involves using additive methods to gauge the desirability of matches, characterizing cases where such matches remain stable and providing guidance on making stable matches a reality. Additively Separable Stable Roommates presents a more complex challenge than its traditional stable roommates counterpart, but can be tackled by referencing the existing taylor linear programming model which provides a way to determine if a stable match can exist. A key contribution of this paper involves establishing the conditions under which a stable match becomes possible, providing valuable insights on the necessary characteristics for such matches to occur. These conditions, tied to the concept of half-integrality, suggest the possibility of approximating stable matches that additively stable roommates problems may offer. Hirschberger et al.'s concept of nearly stable matchings also plays a key role here in understanding how close an approximate stable match may be to a stable one. Finally, this paper involves examining the results of running the taylor linear programming model on various data sets to see how well it can predict stable matches that additively stable roommates problems may offer. A key finding here involves observing how well the model can capture the structure of the roommates' preference lists and the desirability of their potential matches. We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. An earlier proof by George Andersen that the centroid of a cloud is unique and serves as the class's center, relies on analyzing the cloud's mean space. This proof however falls apart when the cloud contains a diversity of spaces with vastly different dimensions. This research aims to prove that a cloud does indeed have a unique center, by first demonstrating the cloud's completeness under a specific topology, and then leveraging this result to establish the cloud's center as a unique space. The selection of the center space is achieved by defining a specific topology on the space of all metric spaces, and showing that a space which minimizes its distance to all other spaces within the class, also minimizes its distance to the class's center, much in the same way that the centroid minimizes the average distance to the class's center. An alternative approach to finding the center, involves showing that a space which minimizes its distance to all other spaces within the class, is also the limit of the cloud as the gauge approaches zero. The validity of these claims relies on a previously unproven conjecture, which states that a space which is homeomorphic to a space with a specific scale, also has a distance that is proportional to the original space's distance, multiplied by the new scale. The correctness of this conjecture can be established by looking at the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance, as an example of a complete metric space. Additionally, this research introduces a new cloud composition method, known as the 'glueing' operation, and proves that it maintains the class's completeness and allows for the reconstruction of a space from a collection of subspaces. A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results. This design has potential applications in various mm-wave applications, particularly in giga-bit wireless local area networks and radar systems. Note: Due to the limited nature of the research described here, the actual frequencies involve operation in either Cyprus (in 24 GHz band) or the United States (in 24 GHz and 37 GHz bands). Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This proof-of-concept study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding process into a reward-based problem, in which a decoder aims to minimize error rates, with multiple decoding approaches available through different neural network architectures. Our results show that this approach remains viable even after introducing artificial noise into the decoding process and that it remains effective for complex decoding tasks with moderate levels of noise. In contrast, other potential solutions like simple neural networks face limitations when faced with increased noise levels in decoding, highlighting the superiority of our approach that combines reinforcement learning with neural networks for fault-tolerant decoding. In the context of fault-tolerant quantum computing, this research represents a significant breakthrough, paving the way for the application of reinforcement learning in decoding, a concept that was previously considered speculative. Furthermore, this innovation may also translate to other quantum error correction methods, such as the quantum LDPC codes. Additional files are listed below. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to measure the relative phase of light in a two-cavity network. The approach is taken with minimal assumptions regarding the dynamics of the cavity system and incorporates a specific type of quantum filter for real-time analysis. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that this method can achieve measurements with greater precision than traditional techniques, even in the presence of thermal noise. The effectiveness of this method is evaluated in terms of its ability to achieve the "Heisenberg limit," the maximum precision possible in measuring a physical parameter, a goal shared by many quantum metrology techniques. The precision achieved by our method is compared to that of another quantum jump metrology scheme, highlighting its superiority when specific conditions are met. Finally, a practical application of the method is proposed and the challenges associated with implementing it in an actual experiment are outlined. The close relationship between quantum information and quantum information processing makes this method suitable for practical use. The integration of quantum feedback control in real-time quantum metrology offers promising avenues for further research, including the application of active control techniques to other sophisticated quantum experiments. The continuous monitoring of quantum systems also holds potential for the development of precise quantum sensors. The development of quantum feedback control has opened new avenues for enhancing the precision of real-time quantum experiments. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. Au$+$Au collisions exhibit suppressed yields of high-energy particles, particularly at forward angles, which is consistent with the activation of partons within the targeted region. Additionally, photon-hadron correlations in Au$+$Au collisions show a notable decrease in hadrons with high momentum, both in the jet and the jet vicinity, and also in regions not directly influenced by the jet. This suppression is more pronounced at higher trigger photon energies and in Au$+$Au collisions with lower center-of-mass energy. When accounting for existing nuclear effects, Au$+$Au collisions appear to experience an increased absorption of high-energy particles, which is roughly in the range of 20$\pm$10% per nucleon-nucleon collision and also dependent on momentum. These observed interactions provide evidence of parton-medium interactions and their energy loss within the targeted region. Furthermore, the data suggest that partons within Au$+$Au collisions experience increased losses not seen in $d$$+$Au collisions, marking a notable phenomenon known as parton re-scattering. This phenomenon is more prevalent in Au$+$Au collisions of lower energy and targets parts of the jet that were previously thought to be less affected. Furthermore, the data indicate parton re-scattering to occur even at the most forward angles, which further demonstrates the partons within the targeted region becoming 'thermalized' within the medium. This phenomenon remains observable even after accounting for nuclear effects and parton energy loss, which suggests that parton re-scattering remains a notable phenomenon in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. In summary, these findings provide further understanding of parton interactions within the targeted region of Au$+$Au collisions and reveal parton re-scattering as a notable phenomenon, which may also contribute to the formation of a quark-gluon plasma in high-energy collision systems. Furthermore, these findings stress the importance of parton re-scattering in the study of parton energy loss and interactions within the targeted region of high-energy collision systems, which was previously considered to be less affected by jet phenomena. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias that can help the model handle OoD scenarios more effectively.

This rich representation is the key to overcoming the optimization - robustness trade-off, as evidenced by the success of methods like ReDyNet and RND. By employing our approach, models constructed from the rich representation were able to demonstrate superior performance on OoD tasks, surpassing results obtained through direct use of the support set. Moreover, this method facilitates the creation of highly robust models on a variety of challenging tasks, achieving a notable edge over the current state-of-the-art in terms of robustness. The source code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/alexrame/rich.

Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when it detects extremely faint signals. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, showcasing its capability to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere at the speed of milliseconds. The test involved passing a laser beam through a turbulent medium that mimics the atmosphere's effect, with the result being a speckle pattern that obstructs our view. By converting this speckle pattern into a signal that can be controlled, we have effectively demonstrated the functionality of the FAST system at speeds of 1.25 microseconds, a notable improvement over previous results. This breakthrough has prompted us to refine FAST's design to operate at even higher speeds, with the goal of one million times faster per frame. The improved FAST (pFAST) algorithm is an optimized version that can effectively eliminate the atmosphere's distortions at speeds of millions of times per second, a pace that aligns with the capabilities of upcoming advanced telescopes, such as the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). A notable aspect of pFAST's design is its reliance on machine learning for the rapid identification of atmospheric distortions, a technique that can effectively replace traditional optical systems known as image deconvolution, with the goal of directly observing exoplanets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before. A key result of our laboratory test is the successful implementation of the pFAST algorithm at high speeds of 1.25 microseconds, a notable improvement over previous results, with the improved pFAST (pFAST2) algorithm an optimized version that can effectively eliminate the atmosphere's distortions at even higher speeds of millions of times per second, a pace that align with the capabilities of upcoming advanced telescopes, such as the ELT. pFAST2 employs a machine learning approach for low-latency atmospheric distortion correction, with the goal of directly observing exoplanets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations are performed, utilizing Monte-Carlo simulations, to showcase the benefits of this model, as evidenced by its similarity to the Hull-White one-factor model's Bermudan swaption prices on Bloomberg, and by the favorable results of its analytical swaption prices compared to those of the Hermite polynomial-based model. Additionally, the analytical approach is proven to be substantially faster. Furthermore, the analytical swaption prices of the deterministic-shift model are found to be very close to those of the Hermite polynomial-based model, and both sets of prices are observed to yield accurate outcomes when back-tested against data from 2007-2009. Lastly, the analytical swaption prices of the proposed model are revealed to be relatively insensitive to its calibration errors. To validate the analytical swaption prices of the deterministic-shift model, a novel technique is developed to derive closed-form solutions for LIBOR decompositions, which are subsequently used to break down a Bermudan swaption's value into its underlying components, thereby explaining the reason behind the analytical swaption prices being greater than those of the Hull-White one-factor model. Finally, the analytical swaption prices of the deterministic-shift model are found to be exactly reproducible, and their associated values for various notional amounts are provided in table form. Several related issues, such as the extension of the proposed model to the multi-factor analysis, are left as potential avenues for future exploration. To facilitate the practical application of the proposed model, the related computer code is made publicly accessible through my website. Moreover, I would like to extend my gratitude to Bloomberg for granting me access to necessary data, and to Mathworks for kindly providing me with necessary software at a discounted rate. Meta-analyses that utilize meta-regression to analyze multiple dependent studies beyond simple pairwise combinations are impeded by the inability to account for clustering effects in estimating residual variance. Two previously proposed estimators address this issue by incorporating an unbiased cluster estimate of residual variance in the context of single-parameter meta-regression. We extend this work to bivariate meta-regression models, presenting estimators that generalize the prior work and maintain asymptotic consistency, unbiasedness, and computability without numerical methods. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that our estimators perform exceptionally well, often producing accurate results even in small sample sizes. The gain in performance is particularly noticeable for smaller effect sizes, where the impact of residual variance is more pronounced. The proposed estimators successfully generalize the concept of "sandwich" estimators to the context of clustered meta-data and provide a viable alternative to established estimators, thus facilitating a more comprehensive approach to data analysis. The approach is further validated through the analysis of actual data from two real-world studies involving pain relief efficacy in the presence of placebo, which showcases the utility of the proposed estimators in yielding reliable results. The proposed methodology is made freely available through the R package metaCRbear. The package includes functions to generate the bivariate data used in our example analysis, which can also be applied to a broader range of clustered meta-data analysis use cases. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to inaccurate estimates of collision velocities and post-collision motion. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interaction, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using physical collision time steps. Our method was then integrated into an existing simulation framework for particle-resolved turbulence simulations, where we showed that using physical collision time steps does not compromise the stability of the simulation. Furthermore, we performed a 2D simulation of turbulent flow with particles of varying densities, where we demonstrated the method's ability to accurately model low-density particle collisions without artificially inflating collision time steps. This method enables a significant reduction in computational cost for large-scale particle-resolved turbulence simulations. Our study's findings also provide a method for accurately simulating dense particle collisions within astrophysical flows. With further optimization, this algorithm has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of particle-resolved turbulence simulations. Our research includes a publicly available code for replicating the study's results, which can be accessed via a GitHub repository. This code combines the ITAP code with our integration method and incorporates several enhancements for enhancing computational efficiency, including using GPU acceleration and adaptive spatial resolution refinement on a hexahedral mesh. Additionally, we employed the MePP tool for simulating particle collisions, which is based on the Morton power-law scheme for predicting closest approaches between particles. This approach ensures that particle collisions are more accurately simulated over extended time periods, thereby enabling more precise control over collision time steps. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed approach demonstrates significant advantages over traditional checkpointing methods in terms of runtime efficiency while maintaining the ability to correct errors with minimal reprocessing costs. Our comprehensive evaluations, involving both realistic simulations and actual experimental trials, have consistently shown the approach to be effective in preserving data integrity, as well as offering superior performance compared to the floating-point arithmetic-based method. Moreover, this method is found to be more efficient than other error-correction approaches while providing enhanced scalability and performance at extremely high speeds (over 80% improvement at 4096 threads). Ultimately, this method is deemed suitable for a broad range of HPC applications due to its exceptional runtime efficiency, as well as its ability to correct errors and preserve data integrity with minimal overhead. Our proposed approach is further demonstrated through an in-depth analysis of its performance in the realistic scenario of running the 3D FFT-Benchmarks on a massive 512-node system, where it consistently achieved crash consistency across all nodes within a remarkably short 30 microseconds. Our results provide substantial support for algorithm-based fault tolerance in HPC systems, as they offer both efficient runtime performance and a reliable guarantee of data integrity even in the event of crashes. Our study also offers a versatile framework for algorithm-based fault tolerance that can be adapted to numerous other HPC applications with minimal modification. Lastly, we acknowledge the potential for further optimization, as well as explore other possibilities for enhancing the performance of algorithm-based fault tolerance through various approaches. Furthermore, we investigate the use of BWT to compress the data of FFT applications, as well or even in addition to the existing compression methods, in order to further reduce the storage requirement and checkpoint overhead of these applications. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the technical challenges and potential research avenues in the area of algorithm-based fault tolerance. Moreover, we openly distribute the source code of our simulation tool, named AB

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), which leverages information networks to generate a hierarchical structure for any given document collection, effectively utilizing network interconnections in a scalable manner. By combining topics with a hierarchical model, HDTM effectively captures meaningful topics and their high-level categories, enabling more accurate document categorization and semantic exploration. In our experiments, HDTM demonstrated superior performance on document classification and clustering, outperforming traditional models by up to 14% in accuracy and consistently improving existing information hierarchy methods. For example, when applied to the Wikipedia network, HDTM was able to discover a hierarchical structure with 5 distinct levels, revealing a 14% improvement in categorizing categories, and demonstrating a 10% improvement in clustering related categories side by side. In particular, HDTM achieved notable advancements in clustering unannotated documents, enhancing network-assisted search by 1.7 and database querying by 1.4 times. In the realm of information networks, HDTM offers a revolutionary solution, and we anticipate its integration into search engines and database management systems to great benefit. In addition to its practical applications, HDTM contributes significantly to the pursuit of comprehensive information hierarchy generation, expanding the capabilities of existing models and facilitating the exploration of unseen web content. The proposed approach is also adaptable to various application fields and can be utilized with different information networks, as demonstrated by our evaluation using both Wikipedia and a healthcare database. In summary, HDTM is a pioneering solution that generates a hierarchical structure for any given document collection, effectively utilizing network interconnections in a scalable manner, and we expect its incorporation into practical systems and theoretical frameworks to yield substantial benefits. We conducted a comprehensive test of the flux-based statistical model for three-body systems, primarily focusing on the hard collisions of $e^+e^-$ at LEP energies. This specific environment allows us to evaluate the flux model with high precision because the outcomes of such collisions are well-documented and their rates are well-predicted using established three-body theory. To test the flux model, we compared its predictions with the actual measured rates for several well-defined processes involving high-energy particle collisions. This comparison revealed that the flux model accurately accounts for experimental measurements with a high level of agreement, exhibiting a prediction accuracy of better than 5% for most cases. Furthermore, the flux model demonstrated an exceptional level of specificity in the prediction of rare events, exhibiting a 5% discrepancy only for rates lower than $10^{-6}$ in frequency. This exceptional performance of the flux model highlights its capabilities in predicting even the most infrequent outcomes of high-energy particle collisions, thereby enabling more accurate assessments of rare physical processes. This pioneering work paves the way for a broader integration of the flux model in quantum field theory, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying physics of high-energy particle collisions. This integration also opens up new possibilities for the application of flux-based statistical models in modern particle physics research, thereby potentially expanding our understanding of the subject. Needless to say, the precision of the flux model in predicting experimental outcomes for various physical processes, especially its exceptional performance in predicting rare events, presents a new benchmark for theoretical physicists to strive for in their calculations of high-energy particle collisions. This new standard of theoretical precision in particle physics predictions may potentially reveal previously overlooked details of the underlying physics, thereby contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of the subject. To achieve this, the flux model can serve as a valuable tool, enabling a more refined estimation of theoretical versus experimental discrepancies in particle physics predictions, thereby shedding light on the extent to which experiments are approaching their ultimate limits in accuracy. To further demonstrate the flux model's capabilities in predicting experimental outcomes for rare physical processes, we have also investigated the behavior of $J/\psi$ photoproduction, a very rare event in high-energy particle collisions, and found that the flux model accurately accounts for this phenomenon with a discrepancy of only 3.1%. This exceptional performance of the flux model in predicting rare events, such as $J/\psi$ photoproduction, highlights the potential of this theoretical framework to contribute to a more precise understanding of the underlying physics of high-energy particle collisions, particularly in cases involving the interaction of rare particles
