We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings. 
Then, incorporating the simplified continuous logic hyperdoctrine into this equivalence relation framework reveals that it corresponds to a category whose objects and morphisms signify subobjects and corresponding mappings between them. 
Ultimately, we identify a suitable topological structure to represent this category and demonstrate that it constitutes a topological hyperdoctrine. 
This arrangement offers an interpretation of continuous logic through a topological structure, reflecting the category theory framework, and may potentially be extended to accommodate additional syntactic constructions for continuous logic, such as least fixed points. 
Furthermore, this structure could serve as a foundation for a category theory-based semantics for continuous logic and potentially analogous frameworks for other infinitary logics. 
Additionally, it is possible that the category theory framework could be incorporated into a broader structure, such as a certain class of topological categories, and that this incorporation could be achieved through a functor that preserves certain properties. 
Finally, the subobjects in this arrangement can be viewed as a form of "properties," and thus, the proposed topological structure can be regarded as a structure for a property theory, and the category theory framework can be interpreted as a formulation of property theory, including a topological structure component and a logic component that is continuous in relation to the metric structure. 
The interplay between these two components can provide a promising framework for a future theoretical structure in mathematics. 
It is also noted that the incorporation of a topological structure for subobjects is a general approach that was first observed in the case of groups and can apply to other categories as well. 
Lastly, the proposed topological structure could serve as a structure for a category that includes a wide range of theorems, such as the Frege-Herbrandt switch, Tarski's greatest, and probably numerous other theorems related to the choice of greatest, and it is observed that these theorems demonstrate a uniform metric structure, and it remains to be seen whether this metric structure can be eliminated without compromising their truth. 
The relationship between these hyperdoctrine frameworks and the choice between greatest and least is a fundamental aspect that remains to be fully understood.

Our findings reveal a combined polarization level of $1.8 \pm 0.3$%, obtained after summing the polarization vectors from a large region, under the assumption of circular symmetry. Analysis of the synchrotron radiation suggests an average polarization level of $\sim 2.5$%, while the forward shock region indicates a nearly 5% polarization. A dynamic interface separates diverse fluids in motion, generating intricate patterns associated with various types of flows. To tackle the resulting intricate math problems, scientists have developed a technique to simplify the interface, preserving key details about its topology. This process converts the complex math problems into more manageable equivalents, enabling researchers to better understand how the dynamics of the interfaces evolve. We propose a new method to further characterize the topology of such simplified interfaces, using a reduced representation of the interface that retains essential features. This approach allows us to accurately measure the geometry of the interface, even in highly distorted situations, and identify the features that make the topology of the interface unique. As an example, we apply this development to the study of droplet collisions, where the new method enables the classification of the resulting droplets based on a measure of their distorted geometry, thereby supplementing the conventional classification. Moreover, we observe that the new measure provides a wider understanding of the droplets' behavior, such as their behavior in diverse droplet collisions and the formation of rings. This development paves the way for a more comprehensive understanding of the topology of the interface in a wide range of phenomena governed by fluid dynamics. Additionally, the techniques used to characterize the topology of the interface have broad applications, including the reconstruction of the dynamics of the interfaces, feature detection, and the design of patterns. Alternatively, the reduced representation of the interface can also be used to generate designs, such as those seen in micromounts, through a process that incorporates their topology. Furthermore, we demonstrate a new method to generate patterns, such as those seen in picture postcards, that incorporate the topology of the interface, resulting in a wider range of designs than those generated using the original features of the interface. This example illustrates the potential of the new measures of the topology of the interface to the field of design. Additionally, we propose an extension of the topological skeleton that includes not only the interface but also the regions above and below it, enabling a more comprehensive characterization of the topology of the interface and several new applications, such as the design of patterns using the topology of the interface in three dimensions. This development provides a more complete understanding of the topology of the interface, and we demonstrate its potential through the design of patterns, such as those seen in micromounts. Furthermore, we apply the new measures of the topology of the interface to the study of droplets that undergo a process in which they split into multiple droplets, and find that the topology of the interface plays a critical role in determining their behavior.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme U shapes, exhibited higher star formation rates and older stellar populations, as indicated by H-alpha analysis. Our research also showed that U galaxies, especially those in groups and clusters, tend to have higher star formation rates and younger stellar populations compared to S galaxies. Similar patterns were found in 'jellyfish' galaxies, displaying tidal features and increased star formation. This transition from S to U shapes may be a precursor to such tidal interactions and resulting morphological evolution. Furthermore, our analysis suggested that U galaxies are more efficient in driving gas out of their disks, as evidenced by a stronger star formation efficiency slope in U galaxies. This process may lead to a spiral-to-peculiar galaxy transformation, possibly induced by a group or cluster environment. Conversely, U galaxies might be more susceptible to tidal interactions due to their already disturbed galaxy structure. Our findings indicate that U galaxies undergo significant changes, both in their star formation activity and morphological appearance, driven by an external process, such as a group or cluster environment. Ultimately, this process may lead to the demise of a disk galaxy through a transformation into a peculiarily shaped, star-forming galaxy. To test our hypotheses, we propose key observational indicators for the U galaxy class and a theoretical framework that necessitates a new generation of long-term, wide-field surveys to capture the U galaxy's dynamic behavior. Moreover, our classification system may be employed to monitor individual U galaxies and track the evolution of their tidal features over time. Finally, our research offers an opportunity to bridge theoretical and observational astrophysics through a more in-depth analysis of the U galaxy's candidate prototypes, whose data we plan to distribute publicly alongside our code. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, this momentum is zero. Additionally, for each phonon mode, the total momentum is proportional to the frequency. Measurements of Raman scattering across a relevant range of frequencies reveal a linear relationship between momentum and frequency for the involved phonon modes, consistent with the idea that these modes exhibit chiral characteristics. This phenomenon is anticipated to be observable in other $A$Bi$_{2}$ compounds as well. We are re-examining the fundamental characteristics of thermal turbulence in fluids, specifically its power spectrum, and the origins of fluctuations within it. These fluctuations form a steady-state distribution governed by the Novikov function, which can be utilized to calculate the likelihood of exceptional events. This theory is applied to both water and helium fluids, and by comparing the results with actual data, we are able to determine the critical factors that influence turbulent dissipation in these fluids. Furthermore, this theory enables us to explore unexplored regions of the $\varepsilon$-$\nu$ parameter space for both fluids, where $\varepsilon$ represents the energy dissipation rate and $\nu$ is the kinetic viscosity. These investigations also provide deeper insights into the nature of the $\varepsilon$-equation, particularly its applicability and limitations in these two-fluid systems. An important correlation is identified, linking the fluctuations in the energy dissipation rate to the inverse of the Taylor microscale, thereby extending the applicability of the Kolmogorov scaling hypothesis to the entire turbulent spectrum. Our analysis, however, reveals a sharp boundary at the Taylor microscale, beyond which the statistical properties of turbulence are dissipated and no longer governed by the Kolmogorov scaling hypothesis. Additionally, we are also re-examining the Carr-Miles Brownian motion model, which describes the sequential combination of two Brownian motions, and developing a method to generalize this model for an arbitrary number of sequential Brownian motions. This generalized model provides an accurate representation of the universal turbulent spectrum, and can be applied even in the absence of thermal noise, thereby revealing the purely stochastic origins of the forward spectral slope in the inertial range of turbulence. Finally, we are also addressing a long-standing uncertainty surrounding the forward spectral slope of turbulence, and providing a solution to the apparent contradiction between the $-7/3$ slope predicted by the Carr-Miles model and the $-3/2$ slope observed in actual turbulent data. This discrepancy can be resolved by considering the contributions of non-interacting sequential Brownian motions, and accounting for the effect of memory loss, thereby leading to a new expression for the forward spectral slope of turbulence. This newly derived expression provides a precise match with the observed $-3/2$ slope in actual turbulent data, and can be extended to determine the entire turbulent spectrum. Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, whose field-theoretical properties and computational models are explored. This contrasts with another phenomenon where a magnetoelectric interaction traps a charge equal to $\pm e/2$ upon exposure to a magnetic monopole, commonly referred to as the Witten effect. The time-reversal symmetry being explicitly violated, as in the case of certain zeeman fields, can be substituted by an alternative mechanism - the topological magnetoelectric effect, thus providing a means to directly observe it. Furthermore, a novel phenomenon is discovered, where a time-reversal-symmetric insulator can develop a half-integer quantum Hall effect in the presence of a magnetic field, whose hallmark is a non-integer Hall conductivity. This newly found class of insulators can be created by introducing a time-reversal-symmetric superfluid or ferromagnet into materials exhibiting a topological magnetoelectric effect, resulting in a stable manifestation of a topological insulator, even when coupled with a magnetic field that would otherwise trigger a transition to a trivial state. The proposed mechanism has potential applications in various experiments, where a stable half-integer quantum Hall effect can be achieved at low temperatures, along with a substantial Hall effect compared to a typical quantum Hall effect. The proposed concepts can be observed through extensive numerical analyses based on a 3D tight-binding model, thus providing a realistic representation of the phenomena. The proposed mechanisms offer novel pathways for realizing various topological properties, along with a means to directly observe them, thereby significantly advancing our understanding of topological insulators. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality. Additionally, we note that modulating the time delay not only increases the diffusion coefficient but also induces intermittent behavior, thereby generating diverse temporal patterns. These findings hold true across multiple system configurations. Since systems exhibiting delayed nonlinearity are widely studied in various fields, including physics, biology, medicine, and engineering, our research is likely to have far-reaching implications for understanding anomalous diffusion phenomena. Furthermore, we explore the practical applications of chaotic diffusion, highlighting how modulating the time delay could potentially enhance diffusion-related processes in fields such as drug delivery and tissue engineering. These observations prompt new theoretical investigations into the links between laminar chaos, Arnold tongues, and diffusive behavior, opening up new avenues for research in this area. Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By assuming a proximal gradient alignment mechanism, we propose a manifold-identified proximal gradient algorithm (MIPGA) that estimates the underlying structure while maintaining a proximal gradient pace. We demonstrate that MIPGA's iterative step is a hybrid of Newton and proximal gradient components and analyze its global convergence to a stationary point. We also examine a second strategy that directly incorporates a manifold identification mechanism for nonsmooth optimization problems. Specifically, we analyze the performance of an identified manifold proximal gradient algorithm (IMPGA) formed by integrating a Newton component with a proximal gradient component aligned with the identified structure. We show that IMPGA achieves a faster convergence rate than proximal gradient methods while providing a clearer theoretical structure than manifold identification methods. Two numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the performance of these algorithms. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/minimist/MIPGA. We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ that satisfy the equation $abc = 0$, the ideal generated by $I$ and the elements $a$ and $b$ will inevitably include the zero element. This new definition aligns with the standard definition of a $1$-absorbing prime ideal when the ring $R$ has the characteristic $2$. It is proven that if $I$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ with a finite number of elements, then $I$ does not cover the entire ring $R$, and the set composed of non-unit elements within the ring $R$ but outside of $I$ is either finite or identical to the entire ring $R$. Furthermore, properties of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals that contain the element $1$ in a ring $R$ were explored. It is proven that such ideals are identical to the existing $1$-absorbing prime ideals that contain the element $1$ in a ring $R$. Additionally, it is proven that if a prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is not a $1$-absorbing prime ideal but is weakly $1$-absorbing, then the set composed of non-unit elements within the ring $R$ but outside of $I$ only contains elements whose ring multiplication is $1$. Finally, the relationship between weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and the existing weakly prime ideals in a ring $R$ was explored. It is found that every weakly prime ideal in a ring $R$ is identical to a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal. It is proven that these two classes of ideals are identical in a ring $R$ if and only if the ring $R$ has a characteristic of $2$. This relationship between weakly prime ideals and weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals can be seen as an extension to an existing theorem. Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary technology, expertise, and
financial resources for sophisticated equipment. While advanced automated road
evaluation is possible with modern devices, these can be expensive and only yield
useful results with substantial training data and skilled operation. For widespread
adoption and efficiency, it's crucial that such systems are both affordable and
technologically simple to manage. This paper explores the potential of transfer
learning for fully automated, rapid road condition assessment in various countries
using minimal, affordable hardware such as smartphones. Our analysis utilizes
images of road surfaces gathered from multiple sources worldwide to create a
universal database for training purposes. Several models based on LeNet-5 and
ResNet-50 architectures were fine-tuned and evaluated on this extensive image
dataset, showcasing the feasibility of using low-cost, handheld devices for
road condition evaluation in diverse, unknown environments. The results indicate
that with fine-tuning, models can achieve satisfactory results on new, unseen
data without being re-trained from scratch on specific local datasets. This
findings have significant implications for implementing widespread, effective
road condition evaluation in a variety of settings. The work presented here may
also be applied to other infrastructure assessment use cases with similar issues.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints in both the state space and a domain-agnostic latent space to facilitate this correspondence.  Additionally, it ensures temporal alignment using a normalized position estimator.  Once the correspondence is established, the learned expert demonstrations can be directly transferred and applied to the target domain, empowering imitation.  The approach is validated through various experiments across a diverse range of complex domains.  Notably, it succeeds in tasks that prior imitation algorithms failed to accomplish.  The novel framework offers a domain-independent and versatile solution for imitation tasks and can be seen as a new approach to learning generalized policies.  The code is publicly available at https://github.com/learn-imitate/learning-imitation-from-observations.  Video supplements can be found at https://learn-imitate.github.io/. A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars formed in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on the initial star formation phase and the environment of the accretion disk around a Population III protostar to resolve a discrepancy in a previous numerical simulation where a second protostar had fragmented the disk. We conducted a new numerical simulation under the same conditions but found that in the presence of an exponentially amplified magnetic field, the disk's fragmentation was completely prevented. The amplified magnetic field led to the suppression of the disk's instability, ultimately preventing the formation of protostars. As a result, all mass in the disk will accrue to a single primary protostar, eliminating the possibility of secondary stars forming via disk fragmentation. However, if the initial amplification of the magnetic field is limited or localized, the disk may remain fragmented, giving rise to multiple Population III protostars. The key takeaway is that the early environmental conditions of the accretion disk around a Population III protostar have a profound impact on determining the final number of stars formed in a given system. Additionally, we observe extreme mass accumulation on the primary protostar in a relatively short period of time - specifically, all mass in the 1000 solar radius accretion disk accrues to the protostar within the first 1.35 orbital periods at 10 astronomical units, resulting in a mass increase of 530,000 times, solidifying the role of the magnetohydrodynamic effect in determining the initial mass function of the first stars. Furthermore, we note that the initial mass loss of the protostar in the initial phase may be substantial and could be directed both into the atmosphere and the accretion disk due to radiative heating and hydrodynamic forces, ultimately driven by the rapid contraction of the star. A subsequent equilibrium may then be reached where further mass loss is balanced by mass accumulation from the surrounding disk, allowing for the eventual cessation of mass growth and the initiation of a more stable core-collapse phase. The dynamic interplay of mass in the system may also be influenced by additional physical processes such as the thermodynamics of the surrounding plasma and the radiative energy output of the protostar. This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. At its core lies the comparison of sequential data segments. The process involves first mapping these segments to suitable Hidden Markov Models via the Baum-Welch algorithm, followed by a simplification of the probability distributions associated with these models. The resulting representation is then analyzed through a clustering method or an outlier detection tool to pinpoint anomalies. Notably, the use of Hidden Markov Models could be replaced by alternative models, such as dynamic Bayesian networks, without affecting the overall method. The proposed algorithm operates in an unsupervised setting, eliminating the need for manual data labeling. The feasibility of this method is demonstrated through its application to simulated and real-world log data. Furthermore, the paper explores the scalability of this algorithm by applying it to the analysis of membrane biologies, a technique which may also be applied to other large datasets. The proposed algorithm shows promise for a broad range of applications. The source code for this algorithm has been made publicly available at https://github.com/timvalin/gla under the terms of the MIT License. A corresponding Python package, gauge_likelihood, can be installed via pip: pip install gauge-likelihood. The predicted output files from these resources contain a prediction score, which can be used to visualize the original data with annotations indicating the likelihood of anomalies. The package further includes pre-trained models for stick-figure data, such as walking patterns, and real-world log data, facilitating the exploration of these examples. The time complexity of this algorithm can be expressed as O(n N N^2) and the space complexity as O(N^2), where n represents the number of data points, N represents the length of the time series, and the constants 2 are insignificant. The algorithm has been optimized for reduced memory usage, enabling its application to sequences exceeding available memory. The optimal model size for these optimizations is when the number of hidden states equals the square root of the number of possible observations. The feasibility of this algorithm was confirmed through its performance on a walking pattern. Moreover, the algorithm can operate in an online setting, either by applying it to sequential data segments of a predetermined length or by adapting the algorithm to accommodate changing data lengths. The latter option involves applying the algorithm in small chunks. The algorithm has been confirmed to be anomaly-resistant and capable of accurately detecting unusual patterns even in the presence of similar sequences that contain anomalies. The reliability of this algorithm was confirmed through its performance on a walking pattern.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. Results show that this estimator outperforms other estimators in reducing mean squared error while remaining unbiased and efficient. The theoretical findings are supported by the empirical results, demonstrating GMLE's efficacy in various contexts. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in modern databases. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Our study builds upon OSDP by taking into account inter-record dependencies. The results of our research indicate that a substantial amount of sensitive information can be disclosed, particularly in cases involving dependencies between data records. Furthermore, our findings outline specific circumstances under which certain privacy protection mechanisms may be ineffective. To rectify this issue, we propose an enhanced mechanism, referred to as the Dependent Expected Mechanism (DEM), which significantly reduces privacy breaches when data records are dependent upon one another. Unlike previous mechanisms, DEM, combines the probabilities of individual data records rather than treating them as independent entities. Our study evaluates DEM's efficacy through numerical examples and reveals that it significantly decreases privacy breaches and database log growth, thereby achieving better accuracy in resultant prediction models. Additionally, DEM's performance is bolstered by our proposed compensation strategy, which enables effective utilization of sensitive data at the individual level. The validity of our approach is substantiated through experiments conducted on real-world datasets. In these experiments, DEM consistently outperformed the traditional log mechanism in achieving better utility and privacy balances. Specifically, our results indicate that DEM achieved a 34.16% improvement in log growth and a 76.47% improvement in privacy breaches for the Internet Traffic dataset. Similarly, our results showed a 32.35% improvement in log growth and a 66.67% improvement in privacy breaches for the Protein Data dataset. Consequently, our research contributes to the development of dependable data privacy methods by addressing previous shortcomings in the OSDP framework, particularly the assumption of independent data records, and introduces an enhanced mechanism, DEM, which significantly outperforms previous approaches in achieving better utility and privacy balances, particularly in cases involving dependencies between data records. The proposed mechanism, DEM, serves as a versatile tool that can be applied to various datasets to achieve a more accurate dependence-based data privacy method. Furthermore, our study highlights the practical implications of data dependencies in maintaining dependable data privacy, thereby laying the groundwork for future research in this field. We investigated this phenomenon in the AS 209 gas disk using the ALMA CO N=1-0 and N=2-1 observations. However, we found no correlation between the CO line surface brightness and the millimeter dust emission in the outer disk. This rules out the hypothesis that the outer disk's dust emission is solely powered by the CO ground-state line opacities. We found that the C18O N=1-0 emission is strongest just outside the CO deficit zone, indicating that the C18O emission may be primarily driven by gas that drifts away from the center of the disk. In order to resolve the nature of the CO deficit, we performed a model of the AS 209 disk gas surface density using data from multiple spectral lines. This model showed that the CO surface density exhibits a sharp decline at 230 au, which is consistent with a change in the gas radial density. However, this change in the gas radial density is not seen in the C18O or dust emission. While our observations do not allow us to determine whether the CO deficit is primarily due to a depletion or a low-temperature or low-density condition, our results show that the outer disk's dust emission is not solely powered by the CO ground-state line opacities. Additionally, our data indicate that the C18O emission is largely driven by gas that is shifted to lower frequencies due to chemical changes. We suggest that future highdynamic range observations of the AS 209 disk at higher spatial resolution could help to clarify these findings and allow us to directly compare the gas and dust surface densities outside the CO deficit zone. If the low surface density model is confirmed, this would imply that planetesimals form more efficiently in the presence of a CO gap, which could be a critical factor in the planetary core mass accretion efficiency. The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency. ETA features a user-friendly interface, enabling researchers to share and combine analysis tasks, such as evaluating the performance of multi-channel high-resolution time-interval analyzers or calculating correlation distributions for event pairs. With its versatile design, ETA facilitates a wide range of applications, including but not limited to physics, electronics, and wireless sensor networks. Furthermore, ETA can serve as a teaching tool for introducing the principles of object-oriented programming, with numerous examples and source code files making it an accessible and versatile tool for the scientific community. ETA is an open-source software tool, distributed free of charge, and can be downloaded from the project's website at http://eta-tool.org/. Additionally, an extensive library of analysis tasks can be found on http://eta-task.org/. ETA is an open-source software, and our team welcomes contributions and collaborations, especially in the areas of wireless sensor network support and introducing programming basics, with relevant contact information provided at http://eta-tool.org/contact.html. We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context remains an unsolved problem. The proof relies on specifying a suitable class of admissible trajectories, for which we establish a key estimate helping to address the issue, via a method involving the Fourier transform's finite-dimensional approximation. This research draws from an initial approach outlined in a 2019 paper by Cardinal and Sankar. The note concludes by discussing potential further explorations.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the masses of these structures based on their radial velocity dispersion revealed that they are actually not gravitationally bound. Furthermore, we found that these structures' ages, when compared to their actual age spreads, appear excessively large. It is also worth noting that these structures, while seemingly homogeneous, can exhibit identical characteristics if composed of randomly selected stars from separate clusters, indicating that these structures might be mere coincidences. These findings call for a cautious interpretation of these structures' significance in understanding the star formation history of the Milky Way galaxy. By comparing these findings to simulated data, we observed that the observed distribution of these structures is not exceptionally rare, occurring in about 5% of randomly selected stars from the sample. Thus, while these structures might lack the interconnectedness previously assumed, they still hold intriguing and unconventional characteristics that can be further explored to understand unusual star formations in the galaxy. Meanwhile, it is essential to approach claims of new, interconnected stellar structures being discovered having a shared origin being a bit more cautious in their interpretation. Additionally, future studies could employ artificial intelligence for precise structure detection in the galaxy and can observe the changes in these structures over time using emerging technologies. These new technologies could allow the observation of these structures forming in the galaxy due to a process called "star formation bursts" which could lead to a better understanding of the galaxy's formation history. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle this challenge. Leveraging a fashion-focused language-image contrastive pre-training framework, VICTOR effectively learns to capture the nuanced compatibility of individual garment items with an outfit. By employing a multi-head attention mechanism that compares the features of three entities - the query item, the outfit, and a dummy item - VICTOR extracts semantically rich latent features, which in turn facilitate the decoding of compatible item representations. Through extensive testing on a well-curated dataset, we demonstrate the superiority of VICTOR over state-of-the-art models and even a robust pre-trained transformer model that's commonly applied in fashion. Furthermore, we highlight the practical potential of VICTOR by applying it to real-world Outfit Maker scenarios. The source code for this project is openly available at https://github.com/stevejpang/VICTOR.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility of holes in GaN can be enhanced through matching its lattice structure to certain II-IV-N compounds. We performed first-principles calculations to determine the effective mass of holes in GaN, ZnGeN$_2$, and MgSiN$_2$ by analyzing their band structures along the wurtzite crystallographic direction. Our calculations show that matching the lattice structure to MgSiN$_2$ could reduce the hole effective mass and increase the hole wavefunction overlap, thus enhancing the hole mobility in GaN. Notably, a similar improvement is observed when matching the lattice structure to ZnGeN$_2$, and both predictions suggest the potential for enhancing hole mobility through strain engineering. Moreover, combining this strain-induced optimization with reducing built-in electric fields in GaN could lead to a significant improvement in integrated gallium nitride electronics performance. Therefore, our study is expected to contribute to the development of highly efficient gallium nitride transistors. Moreover, our study identifies the pair bonding in GaN as the primary source of its high effective mass, which agrees with earlier findings and further emphasizes the significance of optimizing hole transport in gallium nitride through strain induction. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. Our method is informed by the techniques of signal processing and past work in graph embeddings. Our findings indicate that SpliMe outperforms existing temporal KGE methods, and in addition, we identify issues with how static model performance on temporal data is typically evaluated, and provide two solutions to address these problems. Our work is supported by comprehensive experimental results. They demonstrate the plausibility of utilizing static models on their own to effectively handle temporal knowledge graphs, and suggest possible ways to enhance static models without requiring temporal information. This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely yield insistent complications as we attempt to resolve the core question: can any graph that is strong shift equivalent to a row-finite graph also be represented as such. Another key area for exploration as suggested by Bates' and Raeburn's companion work is how strong shift equivalence is related to gauge-invariant ideals. These ideas are expected to lead to significant breakthroughs in the field. Moreover, a new demonstration is provided that proves the weak shift equivalent graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent, revealing the related notion of weak shift equivalence, and this, in turn, implies stable Morita equivalence. This discovery potentially presents a more manageable approach to the previously mentioned core question as it introduces the possibility of reducing the inquiry to a simpler concept: can any graph that is strong shift equivalent to a row-finite graph also be represented as such, and can any graph with a strong shift equivalence class that contains a row-finite graph also be represented as such. Lastly, the concepts of transitive strong shift equivalence and compactly transitive strong shift equivalence are introduced and demonstrated to have associations with stable and compact stable Morita equivalences, respectively. These ideas are expected to lead to several new observations. Additionally, the ideas presented within this note serve as a new approach which can be utilized to provide further insight to the previously published results of Guentner et al. and the recently published results of the book 'Commutative C*-algebras', along with the recent results of the paper 'C*-algebras and Compact Operators'). In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions. Our findings reveal novel, anisotropic characteristics of heavy quark dissociation. Moreover, we have observed that, in the presence of a strong magnetic field, the dissociation probability can be significantly impacted by the direction-dependent real component of the heavy quark potential. Our research lays a foundational framework for similar investigations involving lighter quarks and gluons. Furthermore, these concepts can be extended to other complex systems. Please note that our work is currently under review in the Physical Review D journal.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities. Notably, our best model now does significantly better than the current best systems on several challenging question-answering datasets. Moreover, to make sure the models actually use the knowledge graph information, we came up with a new way to test the models, which measures their performance in scenarios where relevant information is missing. All the code and knowledge graphs we used are publicly available, so others can try our approach and build on it as well. Based on extensive experiments, our method consistently outperformed existing systems on four different question-answering datasets. Moreover, to ensure the quality of our models, we developed a new testing method that simulates real-world scenarios where essential knowledge is missing, and our results show a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we made sure our models' performance could be replicated by others by providing the knowledge graphs, which contain all the necessary knowledge used during training, and our code is also publicly available to facilitate replication. Our best model, which combines a language model with the knowledge graph layer, achieved a 9.5% improvement in question answering accuracy on the FiD dataset and showed even better results on other datasets. Furthermore, to verify the effectiveness of our knowledge graph layer, we tested its combination with various existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, and found that it significantly improved their performance, especially on questions that require additional knowledge to answer accurately. Based on our analysis, our knowledge graph layer did especially well on questions related to geography, on questions with missing entities that need to be filled, and on questions that require additional knowledge to answer accurately. Moreover, to integrate our knowledge graph layer with existing language models in a reversible way, we came up with two new methods that let the models learn from the knowledge graph without forgetting their original skills. Our results show that the models with our knowledge graph layer achieved better performance than those without it

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link degree of X is O(log |X|). The basis of this algorithm is rooted in Lubotzky, Samuels, and Vishne's groups from 2005 that created the first discovered high dimensional expanders.

Incorporating our methods also reveals a novel sparsification algorithm for high dimensional expanders, maintaining its key local spectral characteristics, offering an area of independent interest. The link between X and Y's structure can be seen as an analogy to Navier-Stokes equations where the 'fluid' of complex X is compressed into the 'fluid' of complex Y under certain constraints.

Finally, our work is tied to a long-standing open question regarding whether Tanner graphs of LDPC codes form high dimensional expanders by showing that if they do, then our algorithm can generate a sparsified version of the code while maintaining its ability to decode correctly, a property known as efficient sparsification for high dimensional expanders. The question is tied to P vs NP and has remained unsolved since the early 2000s. The efficient sparsification property can be seen as an analog to the Gilbert-Varshamov bound which shows that certain graphs associated with error-correcting codes achieve optimal rate in the transmission of noisy information. The connection to Navier-Stokes equations and the transmission of noisy information through these codes also speak to the role of these high dimensional expanders in the broader context of computational neuroscience and quantum computing. The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also ultraperipheral collisions of nuclei. These latter interactions are particularly intriguing as they enable the investigation of photon-photon interactions and the subsequent creation of vector mesons. Specifically, new data obtained from lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV were analyzed and presented. The focus was on measuring the nuclear modification factor of J/$\psi$ mesons produced in the forward direction, utilizing both rapidity and rapidity difference as reference points. When focusing on the forward direction, a notable suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons was observed, with the nuclear modification factor ranging from 0.76 to 0.45 as the forward rapidity increases from 3.25 to 4.90. These findings are in line with the predictions offering a dual interpretation: either an interpretation grounded in the coherent photon-nucleus interaction or an incoherent one. Furthermore, the data suggest that the nuclear modification factor for J/$\psi$ mesons is consistently decreasing as the energy increases in the photon-nucleon interaction. To further understand these findings, the nuclear modification factors for various particles as a function of their rapidity were examined. The analysis reveals that the nuclear modification factors for charged particles exhibit a U-shaped pattern, with particles at rapidity of about 2 showing the smallest modification factors. The data for exclusive mesons such as $\phi$ and $\Upsilon$ are currently being prepared for publication, with the aim of gaining a deeper understanding of the underlying photon-nucleon interactions. To achieve this, the nuclear modification factors for these particles as a function of the photon-nucleon $t$-channel will be presented for the first time. Furthermore, the data will be compared to theoretical models, such as the photon-nucleon interaction modified by the nuclear gluon distribution and the photon-nucleon interaction modified by the nuclear shadowing effect. The analysis is ongoing, with the aim of determining which interaction model best explains the observed data. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data, with a key challenge being data quality. Many end-to-end data processing pipelines are in need of a diagnostic or "data debugging" tool that can effectively identify data issues. Leveraging a formal framework based on Shapley values, our proposal outlines a general approach for measuring the contribution of individual data items in facilitating the diagnosis of data problems. A practical implementation of this idea, known as DataValue, is described in detail and demonstrated through hands-on experiments showcasing its utility in addressing data-related challenges encountered during the development of two widely-used visual data platforms. The results highlight the effectiveness of DataValue in helping developers pinpoint problematic data records and assess their impact on model training. With its versatility, DataValue can be applied in a wide range of diagnostic applications, ranging from machine learning to business intelligence and other data-intensive analytics applications. The source code for DataValue is publicly available at https://github.com/extension-mml/shapley-importance. A live demo of the tool can be accessed at https://mml-extension.github.io/shapley-importance/. Extension mechanisms for DataValue, such as the integration of various diagnostic techniques, are documented at https://mml-extension.github.io/shapley-importance?menu=diagnostics#available-diagnostics. The performance of DataValue can be evaluated using the benchmark dataset downloaded from https://github.com/extension-mml/shapley-importance#eval-benchmark. A tutorial on DataValue is available at https://mml-extension.github.io/shapley-importance?menu=tutorials. It should be noted that DataValue is a versatile diagnostic tool, and the described application of Shapley importance is just one possible approach to diagnostic analysis, with other methodologies, such as Bayesian Surprises, also potentially useful in addressing data problems. Furthermore, DataValue's efficiency in handling large datasets can be improved in the future by incorporating data sampling, which is a limitation of the tool in its current implementation. Moreover, DataValue is designed to integrate various diagnostic techniques, such as Explainable AI, but a thorough evaluation of Shapley importance in the context of machine learning diagnostics is needed in the future to further analyze its effectiveness, stability, and areas for improvement. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, shifting from a low-pressure state characterized by an in-plane net magnetization to a high-pressure state lacking this magnetization. The goal of this research is to delve into the  in-plane net magnetism's anomalous Hall effect and its corresponding properties in Mn$_3$Sn under pressure. Theoretical calculations using the Heisenberg model and an extended Berry-phase theory across multiple phases reveal that the magnetization's complete disappearance at 10 GPa contradicts expectations for an increased anomalous Hall effect. Instead, we find that inside the magnetically ordered phases, the Hall effect is notably different from an ordinary paramagnetic contribution, and it shares a direct correlation with the  in-plane net magnetization's magnitude in the three-dimensional material Mn$_3$Sn under pressure. The material's anomalous Hall resistance shows a systematic response to pressure, and it exhibits an inverse logarithmic relationship up to 10 Gpa. The main characteristics of Mn$_3$Sn's anomalous Hall effect, such as its temperature-dependent behavior inside the magnetically ordered phases and its overall magnitude, can be switched on and off in response to pressure, showcasing a unique dynamic interplay between magnetism and the anomalous Hall effect. The material's time-reversal symmetry-breaking properties also change with pressure, and an extensive analysis using theoretical models and density functional theory reveals that Mn$_3$Sn's atomic arrangements under pressure undergo significant and significant triangular lattice distortion. capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation Extraction
(RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring this vital
knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By employing RE, a substantial
amount of high-quality semantic relationships can be obtained for machine learning
purposes. Although RE presents a challenging task, advancements in NLP research along
with the incorporation of machine learning techniques and deep neural networks (DNNs)
have significantly improved its effectiveness. In recent years, studies utilizing DNNs have
achieved superior outcomes compared to preceding studies. This article serves as a
comprehensive overview, focusing on RE utilizing DNNs. It delves into DNN architecture,
key challenges, recent advancements, and the existing data resources, in addition to
outlining future research directions. Furthermore, to facilitate replication, this article
includes an exhaustive review of employed methods and used data sets. We hope that
this paper shall provide valuable insights to researchers working on RE using DNNs. We
intend for it also to contribute to the growth of the RE community, encompassing
DNNs, while maintaining a separate thread for general RE questions. Finally, we aim
for it to be a valuable resource for novel researchers in the realm of RE using DNNs.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary. Our discussion includes the scenario where the Steklov constant is zero, and we establish an asymptotic expression for the large-$r$ behavior of the eigenvalue in that case. Next, we broaden our considerations to second-order linear differential equations with specific potentials and develop corresponding Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problems, again extensively examining the primary eigenvalue in this new context. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download. Furthermore, a medical hypergraph reconstruction application is used to demonstrate the practical implications of this work. To facilitate this task, we also contribute two new datasets: CUI-4M and CUI-8M, totaling millions of edges and nodes. These datasets offer a benchmark for evaluating hypergraph reconstruction methods, with a variant of our approach consistently outperforming baselines by a substantial margin in accuracy. It is worth noting that the CUI-4M and CUI-8M datasets have properties that facilitate the evaluation of hypergraph reconstruction, a task that is currently limited by the availability of datasets. Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, and found their prices to be remarkably resilient when measured against a range of variables. These volatile price movements were minimal, averaging just 0.3% daily volatility for Bitcoin and 0.6% for Ethereum. Furthermore, our research revealed that the prices of cryptocurrencies are not significantly influenced by typical financial market fluctuations, suggesting a high degree of independence. Notably, the prices of cryptocurrencies are highly correlated with each other, indicating a common underlying factor driving their stability. Our analysis also shows that the stability of cryptocurrencies may be attributed in part to their use in transactions, with a notable rise in the price of Bitcoin observed prior to the pandemic, followed by a sharp decline in 2020 due to widespread economic disruptions. These effects were less pronounced for other cryptocurrencies. Our study provides solid empirical support for the concept of cryptocurrency stability, thereby addressing a long-standing concern holding back widespread adoption of these digital assets as a medium of exchange.

methodological innovation leverages the solution of a related integrable 
nonlinear equation, the Zakhararv-Shabat system, through inverse scattering. 
Estimates derived from this approach address critical challenges in weak noise 
scenarios, yielding precise probability bounds and mean-square quantizations 
at various time points and levels of disorder. Moreover, our work resolves long-
standing limitations of the KPZ universalization paradigm by showing that for 
any given disorder level and small enough time, the solutions of the KPZ equation 
can be mapped to high probability approximations of random Gaussian fields. 
Finally, our analytical framework solves the broader mathematical problem of 
establishing precise nonlinear fractional derivative estimates, a task that 
includes resolving the previously unsolved inverse problem for the Klein-Gordon 
equation. The estimates we derived are precision-tuned, thereby setting a 
precision-tuned precision threshold that any viable theory of the KPZ equation 
must surpass. Our work also opens the door to analytical calculations of a 
wide array of higher-order fractional derivatives, thereby potentially 
revolutionizing multiple fields including finance and medicine. Additionally, 
our numerical validation, accomplished by integrating analytical calculations with 
a specially designed iterative numerical method, demonstrates that the 
probability distributions of solution values at various time points and levels 
of disorder converge to precise continuum limits as the underlying lattice is 
disccretized at sufficiently fine scales. Lastly, our work presents precise 
precision thresholds for the KPZ equation and its stronger variants, yielding a 
precise definition of the critical threshold for universalization, a threshold 
that must be surpassed for the KPZ equation to achieve full universality. Our

Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations. Two possible wave types, comprising about $10%$ of the measurements, are identified - the compressive turbulence wave and the magnetosonic wave. These two waves exhibit distinct characteristics, with the compressive turbulence wave showing signs of a quasi-statistical equilibrium. Additionally, researchers observe an intriguing relationship between the fluctuations of the spacecraft potential and the Lat/Long coordinate in one specific regime, which may be an indication of a distinct physical phenomenon associated with the plasma. These data and related observations contribute significantly to an improved comprehension of the plasma turbulence in the solar wind. They also stimulate speculation about a potential role of magnetic field tension in maintaining the stability of the solar wind plasma at sub-ion scales. Lastly, these measurements underscore the importance of considering the plasma as a multi-fluid system even down to very small frequency ranges. This latter approach provides more accurate and stable results. These results are obtained by assuming that certain assumptions related to the plasma and a specific model are approximately correct. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points. The physical approximation exhibits similarities with both the geometrical and physical approximations but performs best in scenarios with minimal turbulence and rarefied geometries. A comprehensive comparison of the models' predictions is made with numerical solutions from a validated code, revealing that the physical approximation accurately represents turning point behaviors, closely matching the numerical solutions despite some deviations elsewhere. A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are employed to improve the low-rank decomposition model's efficiency and computation speed. Ultimately, the sparse matrix-derived saliency map is segmented to pinpoint defect regions. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects. The associated coding is available at https://github.com/ChinaWhitond/FabricDefect/blob/main/FabricDefect.py. Additionally, the embedded demo showcases a step-by-step implementation of the proposed method in MATLAB. The data used can be accessed via https://github.com/ChinaWhitond/FabricDefect/tree/main/imageDefect. Three distinct datasets - the Apparel Experience database, the extended Apparel Experience database, and the UTPF database - are utilized for evaluation, which collectively cover 16 different types of defects. The method achieves impressive performance with the following metrics: 96.13% area accuracy, 98.02% precision, 97.19% recall, and 96.52% segmentation IoU for the AEDB; 95.13% area accuracy, 97.19% precision, 96.61% recall, and 95.69% segmentation IoU for the AEDBEXT; 91.12% area accuracy, 96.32% precision, 95.61% recall, and 94.13% segmentation IoU for the UTPF database. These outstanding results validate the effectiveness of this proposed technique. A novel framework for estimating the predictive uncertainty of RL agents from raw image observations is developed, leveraging predictive coding principles and dimensionality reduction techniques. The framework's applications and benefits are demonstrated in various challenging visual navigation tasks across multiple datasets, which are further analyzed to disclose the underlying mechanisms. The study showcases the effectiveness of the framework in promoting the RL agent's exploratory behavior, enhancing adaptation to novel environments, and facilitating smoother navigation with reduced oscillations. The agent's predictive uncertainty estimates are accurate enough for real-time utilization and reveal an intriguing connection with their representation capabilities. Additionally, the framework is found to boost the RL agent's performance when evaluated on unseen episodes and episodes manipulated with shifted distribution, underscoring its regularizing effect that enhances generalizability without the need for additional regularization methods. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed to over one million actions per second on standard hardware.
This accelerated speed enables extensive and precise testing of virtual agents, facilitating more reliable agent evaluations and a more in-depth exploration of the solution space. 
To achieve such exceptional performance, we harnessed modern low-level programming techniques to create a new, highly efficient game environment framework. 
Our speed boost allows for scaling up the size and complexity of game environments where the agent must utilize skills like natural language understanding, problem-solving, and knowledge application to solve the challenges effectively.
The remarkable increase in simulation processing speed empowers the community to conduct more ambitious research, pushing the boundaries of what artificial agents can accomplish. 
The highly optimized text-based game environment can also be applied to other practical domains such as text search, data processing, and web scraping, presenting a versatile tool for the community. 
Finally, we outline future research directions stimulated by our research, where highly optimized artificial agents can be created to excel in various complex tasks.

Researchers analyzed data on Algol ($\beta$ Persei) and found tentative signs of up to five additional companion candidates, which are believed to have orbital periods ranging from 1.863 to 219 years. These signals are consistent across 236 years of data and also matched the first 226.2 years of the data, accurately predicting eclipses for the following 9.2 years. The companion candidates' orbital planes are thought to be aligned due to the stable and unchanging eclipses of Algol since the early observations of Goodricke (1783). The findings provide further evidence of other binary stars that are similar to Algol and share the distinctive characteristics of "blue large amplitude photometry" (BLAP). The suggested companions are an extension of the earlier discovery of a companion candidate with an orbital period of 87.3 years, first proposed by Irwin (1952). The new findings are also remarkably consistent with the earlier predictions made by Irwin, which can be attributed to the aligned orbits of the companions, the stable eclipses of Algol, and the detection method using eclipse time shifts, which is an independent validation of Irwin's initial observations and predictions over the past 289 years. The suggested companions were confirmed by various tests, which revealed that the signals are significant and could not be artificially created by noise in the data. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This modified variance, combined with the established monotonicity of action, enables us to replicate Glassey's result and prove a general, optimal blow-up criterion. Furthermore, we derive new, non-optimal but explicit criteria for potential blow-up in solutions with positive energy. A significant body of existing literature has concentrated on developing a comprehensive understanding of solutions in this context; our work extends and unifies these efforts, enhancing our knowledge of solution behavior. A particularly intriguing area for further research arises when considering solutions in domains exterior to multiple obstacles, and we provide relevant estimates for solutions with positive energy in this scenario. Lastly, a substantial number of open questions remain unsolved; hence, we plan to address only a few of them in this brief summary and hope to contribute to the advancement of related research in the future. To address this disparity, this research investigates Cargo's security architecture and the transmission of vulnerability risks within the ecosystem. We developed a knowledge graph model to visualize and analyze Cargo ecosystem dependencies, as well as to identify vulnerability dissemination between popular libraries. Our study reveals that a substantial portion of Cargo ecosystem dependencies contain security vulnerabilities and propagate risk to other dependencies, emphasizing the need for regular dependency updates to mitigate security vulnerabilities in the Cargo ecosystem. We provide comprehensive knowledge graph visualizations and code samples to facilitate future research on Cargo ecosystem security architecture and vulnerability transmission. We are the first to publish a formal study on Cargo security architecture, showcasing the importance of in-depth ecosystem analyses to address unique technical characteristics and inform security governance approaches tailored to specific ecosystems, such as Cargo. This research serves as a starting point for future research on Cargo security architecture and vulnerability transmission, highlighting the potential to analyze and propagate vulnerabilities among downstream dependencies, as well as exploring novel graph algorithms to prioritize vulnerability mitigation and maximize security governance effectiveness. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud KNN search can be efficiently optimized by transforming the operation into a simple index calculation. Secondly, the multilayer perceptron can be efficiently optimized by approximated matrix inversion and data dimension reduction. Additionally, we find that the GCN's sparsity can be leveraged for further optimization. By applying these insights, we propose an efficient GCN (EffGCN) that achieves a significant speedup of 204.8 times over the existing state-of-the-art method, while retaining superior accuracy as proven through extensive experiments. The source code of EffGCN can be accessed at https://github.com/ICYLAB/EffGCN. Experimental results demonstrate that EffGCN surpasses various baseline methods in terms of execution speed while maintaining superior model accuracy. Specifically, EffGCN is capable of achieving a 204.8 times speedup relative to PointGCNs+ while retaining nearly identical accuracy on semantic segmentation, or outperforming AutoGCN in object detection while achieving a speedup of 10 times with equivalent accuracy. Furthermore, EffGCN significantly outperforms KNN-GCN in three-dimensional classification, with a speedup of approximately 11 times while maintaining superior model accuracy. EffGCN's enhanced computational efficiency isaccomplished without a reduction in model accuracy through the application of mathematical optimizations and the redefinition of the graph convolution, which trasfers the multilayer perceptron into an efficient linear transformation that can be computed directly from the data, thereby achieving a notable speedup. Additionally, EffGCN's efficient computation of graph convolution isaccomplished through the redefinition of the multilayer perceptron, which is replaced by an efficient linear transformation that can be computed directly from the data, and the efficient handling of the sparsity of the graph, which isaccomplished through the application of matrix reduction and the efficient inversion of matrices, thereby achieving a notable speedup. EffGCN's efficiency is evaluated through a variety of tests on point cloud datasets, including the semantic segmentation of the semantic3d dataset, object detection on the SENSOR dataset, and the 3D classification of the threeD dataset. We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks that embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object classes. As our backdoored classifier is designed to recognize the inherent concepts of trigger images rather than specific patterns, it can be triggered by semantically similar images with distinct appearances, making our attack more applicable and resilient to countermeasures in real-world scenarios. Our experiments show that even with limited Trojan patterns, our approach can adapt to new trigger images within the same category and evade sophisticated defense strategies effectively. Our study proposes a dynamic trigger embedding method to minimize storage requirements and improves the versatility of Trojan attacks on diverse image classification datasets. Additionally, our approach facilitates the creation of stealthier Trojan attacks that evade strict testing criteria. Our code is publicly available on GitHub for reproduction of our results.
