New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup and internal structures of hypothetical habitable-zone exoplanets around these stars. Our model indicates that most of these planets are expected to have compositions and internal structures analogous to those of Earth. However, our analysis reveals two exceptions, the Kepler-10 and Kepler-37 planets, which would likely develop cores significantly smaller than Earth due to oxidation. Furthermore, our exploration of this devolatilisation model's boundaries and variation in planetary mass and size highlights the potential diversity of internal structures in terrestrial planets. By combining precise star abundances, devolatilisation, and planetary mass and size considerations, our study advances understanding of terrestrial exoplanet interior structures, which are pivotal in grasping planetary evolution and dynamics. Our investigation also illustrates the value of multi-dimensional theoretical frameworks in conjunction with observational asteroseismology and exoplanet characterisation to predict celestial bodies resembling Earth. Finally, our analysis stresses that precise star abundances play a key role in predicting planetary interior structures, underscored by the novel data included in this research, enhancing our understanding of exoplanet geology and the diversity of celestial bodies in the universe.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to categories where topological properties play a key role. Our approach offers an efficient method for developing new logical meaning systems and comparing them to existing ones. This system serves as a comprehensive tool for understanding the core philosophical aspects of the relationship between structure and meaning in the context of modal logic. By identifying specific categories that underpin various types of meaning in the literature, we make a significant step towards clarifying the underlying nature of these interpretations. Furthermore, our framework enables the systematic investigation of numerous variants of modal logic by examining different categories with the same underlying logical structure. This introduces a unified approach to comparing the complexity of various modal logic systems based on categorical properties, thereby facilitating the comparison of distinct types of modal logic semantics through category theory. This method also has applications in studying other forms of modal logic semantics and can be extended to incorporate non-normal modal logic semantics. By recognizing the role of topological categories in modal logic semantics, we open up new lines of inquiry, such as employing categorical concepts to analyze logical syntax and understand the foundational relationship between structure and meaning in the context of modal logic. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors. Presented here is a class of bipartite cubic graphs whose minimum cycle length is four, which cannot be colored using five colors. This result confirms that the original conjecture was false. Additionally, another bipartite planar graph, also meeting the degree and cycle length requirements, but not being part of a vertex-transitive family, is also introduced. This latter graph, however, cannot be colored using the same number of colors, but in a different number, five in this case, which is also the maximum possible number of colors for this particular graph. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and model complexity. Despite some recent advances in quantifying uncertainty within NNs, the existing literature offers little unified guidance on choosing the most suitable approach. To address this disconnect between NNs and uncertainty theory, we undertake a comprehensive review of numerous methods for quantifying uncertainty, alongside empirical evaluations of 29 such methods applied to 10 real-world problems. This thorough examination serves not only as a reliable resource but also as a benchmark for comparing different uncertainty quantification approaches, thereby facilitating more informed decision-making when selecting a particular technique suited to a specific problem. To promote consistency in our analysis, we've developed and released a versatile framework, called UQL-Bench, which includes a wide range of test cases involving vector-valued functions. This framework can be accessed at https://uql-bench.github.io/. We propose multiple research avenues that can further bridge NNs and uncertainty quantification theories, alongside presenting a novel approach, MultiNet, which demonstrates particular success in quantifying uncertainty within highly complex problems. Our work offers a valuable assessment of the current state of NNs, thereby contributing to the ongoing development of this field. To promote practical applications, we've distilled our key findings into easily applicable guidelines and provided recommendations for future research. These guidelines, along with our code and data, are publicly available at https://nms.une.edu.au/uql-bench. We also present an alternative version of this work that has been translated into a machine-readable format, termed UQL-Notebook, which can be accessed at https://nms.une.edu.au/uql-nb. This publicly available material serves as a comprehensive educational resource, showcasing the full process of evaluating uncertainty quantification methods on actual problems, thereby illuminating the current limitations of NNs in addressing real-world problems. To facilitate transparency and reproducibility, we've adopted an inclusive approach, offering detailed explanations of our review, empirical evaluations, and offering guidance on replicating our study. We've also provided a public FAQ that addresses common queries arising from our work and offers additional insights not included in the original text. This publicly available material can be accessed at https://nms

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was proposed. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for the policy evaluation process. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration by 5.8 and 2.2 times, respectively, in a 10000-state MDP. Moreover, its convergence rate and convergence radius can be estimated and improved upon experimentally. Inexact GMRES policy iteration also surpasses optimistic reinforcement learning by 2.2 times in a 10000-action 100-state Markov chain. This efficiency is demonstrated through multiple experimental settings and the code is available for public scrutiny. Furthermore, inexact policy iteration offers a potential solution to speeding up online learning in large-scale MDPs, a concept theoretically substantiated through the example of a 10000-state MDP. In contrast to hierarchical reinforcement learning, inexact policy iteration is found to be less effective in such scenarios, highlighting its potential to accelerate online learning, a concept that warrants further investigation. Inexact GMRES policy iteration is found to perform satisfactorily on real-world applications, such as a call center and a driving vehicle, where its iterations demonstrate a clear, rapid, and consistent trajectory towards the optimistic policy iteration solution. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration is capable of reaching a satisfactory level of performance similar to policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration in these scenarios within a shorter number of iterations. In order to further validate the potential of inexact policy iteration for online reinforcement learning in large-scale MDPs, a set of methodological weaknesses were identified and possibly remediated. These potential issues encompass a lack of theoretical guarantees for the convergence and convergence radius of inexact policy iteration, the choice of contraction gauge, and the potential for inexactness to hinder the algorithm's efficiency, along with the need for future research to address these concerns. Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating the effectiveness of a learner that relies on data from an untrusted source. To address these limitations, we have developed a theoretical framework that increases the scope of reliable learnability by allowing for the use of data from an untrusted source, provided that a learner has access to certain localized evaluations. A key aspect of our research is a newly-proposed notion called \emph{localized learnability}. We provide proof of thetical bounds on the level of concept complexity that can be achieved through localized learnability, and further examine the conditions under which a learner that utilizes localized evaluations may still be susceptible to the effects of an untrusted source. Ultimately, we present a reliable learning algorithm that operates through the utilization of localized evaluations without necessitating any overall trust in the data source. The reliability of our learning algorithm is guaranteed by deriving the level of concept complexity that it can achieve. A companion paper provides empirical analysis of the efficacy of our reliable learning algorithm in practice. To further contribute to the field, we have introduced a range of well-characterized data sources that may be of use in other theoretical studies of reliable learning. We utilize a novel approach to modeling an untrusted data source, one which we believe will be of greater practical relevance than standard trust models. We also propose a set of localized evaluations that are informed by data sources that we believe will be of interest in their own right. Furthermore, we have established a relationship between localized learnability and the study of concept complexity, providing proof of the relationship by employing cutting-edge mathematical techniques. Finally, we demonstrate that the development of a reliable learner that utilizes localized evaluations is computationally feasible. A copy of the companion paper can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.12074. A demonstration of our reliable learning algorithm can be found at: https://github.com/jamesbalkenius/learning-from-an-untrusted-source. A lecture on our research can be found at: https://youtu.be/ucXdD1BvN8k.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than previously predicted in non-slip scenarios. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers during the dripping process. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from a study conducted by Haefner, et al., published in 2015 in Nature Communications. The theoretical model presented can be applied to various liquid and fiber combinations as long as the fiber dimensions outweigh those of the liquid drops. The findings of this study may contribute to the development of precision droplet production techniques. Additionally, the theoretical model may be applicable to biological systems such as pollen towers and snow crystals, showcasing the diverse range of applications influenced by the slip effect. Furthermore, research into liquid-solid slip has far-reaching implications for understanding various phenomena in static and dynamic liquid film scenarios. The research in this study may thus broaden the knowledge of slip physics beyond mechanical forces. This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a data-driven and rule-based information extraction technique is applied to break down the labeled data. Following this process, two machine learning models are developed - the first is a binary classifier leveraging a hybrid Deep Neural Network and Random Forest to detect writing activities, and the second is a Deep Neural Network integrating convolutional and recurrent layers for single-character classification. Although the proposed approach demonstrates satisfactory accuracy and performance in the challenge evaluation simulation with an average Levensthein Distance of 8, its overall efficiency and real-time capabilities still require improvement. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/ashrafg/handwriting-challenge. Upon further evaluation with the provided sensor data, the character-level model exhibits significantly lower accuracy compared to expected handwritten character classification standards. One possible reason for this poor performance is the low resolution of the provided sensor data. To overcome this limitation, a character-level dataset based on high-resolution camera captures is proposed, aiming to enhance the single-character classification model and bridge the limitation of low-resolution sensor data. The proposed high-resolution dataset can serve as a valuable resource for developing more accurate single-character classification models. Meanwhile, an analysis of the effective feature representation for sensor activity is conducted, suggesting that the current approach may benefit from higher resolution time-series data featuring more distinct features. Additionally, an initial exploration is made into using transformer-based models for sensor activity classification. One potential future direction for this research is to integrate both the hybrid activity detection model and the Deep Neural Network, thus enabling the development of a robust system for detecting written mathematical terms based on sensor data. The integration of high-resolution camera data and advanced transformer models could further enhance the accuracy and performance of the system. To achieve real-time implementation, a suitable device such as the Raspberry Pi is identified as an ideal platform. The Raspberry Pi's compact size and Linux-based operating system, allowing integration with other contemporary technologies like IoT, would greatly benefit from a accurate sensor-based detection model. The proposed work, having passed a virtual evaluation similar to the actual Stabilo challenge environment, demonstrates promising results and meets the challenge requirements. A potential drawback is the limited handling of overlapping writing activities. To overcome this in real-world scenarios, a suitable activity detection model integrating more robust features and a better resolution is necessary.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate synthetic durations based on a median absolute deviation objective. The approach is developed in response to concerns that existing state-of-the-art methods may produce synthetic speech with an unnatural, "stepped" duration profile. By training the model in a non-parametric manner, the new method is designed to replicate the median duration pattern of the target data, while simultaneously minimizing discrepancies in duration variations. The results of our experiments confirm that this new model avoids the artificial duration profiles often associated with parametric methods, and demonstrates a more substantial improvement in the PESQ score compared to a baseline model. Furthermore, the new model performs comparably in terms of PESQ score to a model based on Hidden Semi-Markov mechanics, which requires the enumeration of state transitions in order to train. The success of our approach is particularly notable for longer phoneme durations, where previous methods have often been less effective. The code for our duration model, as well as a full implementation of our method, is available at https://github.com/orion73/sds-duration. This paper was previously published under the title "A median-based approach to statistical duration modeling in speech synthesis", in the proceedings of Interspeech 2021. Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to artificial intelligence. The Skincare project aimed to address this by creating an innovative diagnostic and decision support system in dermatology. It combined the capabilities of interactive machine learning with deep learning to enhance the skills of doctors and augment diagnostic capabilities, particularly in the identification of malignant skin lesions. A baseline model, trained using a large dermatology image dataset (ISIC), delivered outstanding results and demonstrated potential for widespread application, including support for both general practitioners and dermatologists. The project also focused on creating effective communication channels between humans and machines to facilitate machine learning. In essence, the Skincare project sought to integrate human intuition with artificial intelligence, a key component of future cognitive assistants in the medical sector. The project's results indicated that a merger of human and artificial capabilities could lead to improved diagnostic outcomes and a reduced need for large datasets in machine learning. The system developed as part of the Skincare project could potentially be utilized as a comprehensive decision support system in dermatology practices, enhancing the capabilities of doctors and making diagnostic decisions more efficient. Furthermore, the project's interactive tools could be adapted for use in other medical specialties, such as ophthalmology, to augment clinical decisions with the accuracy of artificial intelligence. The Skincare project also investigated the ethical implications of a potential future scenario in which machines diagnose without human intervention. The researchers considered whether a machine, trained interactively using patient data, could be regarded as a healthcare provider. The study concluded that a legal uncertainty persists but specified three conceivable scenarios: (1) machines are not regarded as providers; (2) machines are regarded as providers under the same regulations as human healthcare providers; (3) machines are regarded as providers under special regulations. The Skincare project sought to contribute to ongoing discussions about the future of medical decision-making, presenting a nuanced view of the complex interplay between machines and humans in the diagnostic process. To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow component after initial training using an Auto-Encoder. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time directly from data. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and constraining parameters using prior distributions based on natural evolution channels, we optimized this model through Evolutionary Algorithm optimization. The results show our method achieves a low Bayesian Information Criterion value, accurately representing the intrinsic variability of SNe Ia in a reduced-dimensional space while accounting for noise and variability correlations. The application of this model in a transfer learning framework to a small dataset demonstrates its effectiveness in recovering a dimensionally-reduced intrinsic variability component, consistent with previous findings on the intrinsic variability of SNe Ia. The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation policies, including the handling of spurious wake-ups triggered by condition variables. By specifying (i) when operations are allowed, (ii) which thread operations are mutually independent, and (iii) when operations can co-occur, users can create customized McMini instances. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated in the paper by a practical evaluation of McMini, which successfully verifies a range of practical multi-threaded programs. Additionally, McMini outperformed McMini's predecessor in verifying thread-local variables and revealed a previously unreported bug in the standard pthread library. As a result, McMini's model checking capabilities have become an integral part of the development process in a real-world embedded system project. Furthermore, McMini's novel thread operation mechanism has the potential to be integrated into other DPOR-based model checkers as a reusable module. The paper's findings also offer practical suggestions and insights for using model checking effectively in software development. Finally, the paper's authors have made McMini available under a permissive free software license for public use at https://mcmini.github.io. McMini is now easily installable on Linux systems using spkg-install and can be used from the command-line interface, which is documented in the accompanying README file. The paper and its software have been jointly reviewed. Moreover, the authors have ensured the reliability and accuracy of the software by executing a series of tests, which are detailed in the accompanying validation demonstration. McMini has been successfully tested in a variety of practical scenarios, as described in the paper and validated in the accompanying validation demonstration. McMini has also been employed in a real-world embedded system project, as described in the paper. this issue, WhatsApp introduced an update limiting the number of recipients for a single
message, aiming to curb the widespread dissemination of misinformation. In this study, we
evaluate the effectiveness of this change from multiple perspectives. Our experiment involved
collecting and analyzing public messages, revealing the extent to which WhatsApp's modifyed

suggest that these changes had a negligible impact on the overall user behavior but did
temporarily inhibit users from sharing information during the initial period after the update.
Although the modification reduced the direct transmission of messages to other individuals,

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It has been previously established that, given sufficient time, the distribution of allele frequencies in such a population converges to a frequency spectrum known as the Gneiting distribution. In this work, we derive easier-to-compute approximations for this frequency spectrum than the Gneiting distribution, particularly when the population grows rapidly. These approximations are specifically simpler and more accurate when the population grows slowly, yielding expressions that converge geometrically to the correct frequency spectrum. Additionally, we refine previously developed approximations for the frequency spectrum that worked well in rapidly growing populations, and show they converge exponentially to the correct frequency spectrum. The proposed and refined approximations hold not just for frequency spectra but also more broadly for the frequency distributions of geneages, or family histories, and their distributions over ages. These approximations may also be useful in understanding the evolution of aging and the distribution of intertimes between successive events in growing populations. Finally, we illustrate the precision of the new and refined approximations through numerical simulations that compare them to the exact frequency spectrum, particularly in rapidly growing populations, where the approximations are especially relevant. The precision of the new and refined approximations is seen to be quantitatively understood as exponential, and the approximations themselves are seen to be symmetrical, and thus more versatile, than previously expected. In particular, we express the approximations as sums of simpler distributions, and show that these simpler distributions can be computed more easily with fewer parameters than the exact frequency spectrum, thus facilitating the use of frequency spectra in place of geneages, as was previously understood in smaller populations but is now quantitatively understood as a consequence of the new and refined approximations. Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the scalars remain heavy compared to the Hubble scale to facilitate single-field inflation.  Additionally, supergravity predicts several non-renormalizable interactions, rendering it an effective field theory that remains valid up to a specific cutoff energy scale, and thus necessitates a re-examination of the scalar potentials and field dynamics to achieve self-consistency at the quantum level, potentially leading to an expansion of the scalar tensor gravity framework.  This work specifically examines supergravity models of inflation from an effective field theory perspective, employing a hybrid potential for inflationary model-building and incorporating D-terms, inflationary stabilization, and supergravity embedding within specific string framework contexts to facilitate model development and refinement.  Furthermore, this research delves into the unique characteristics of supergravity, such as conformal completeness, and the impact of higher-derivative terms that arise in the expansion of the supergravity scalar potential, and whether these properties can be leveraged to create inflationary model solutions that receive distinctive predictions from related effective field theories.  To this end, key distinctions between supergravity and other effective field theories, such as weakly coupled Einstein gravity, are also clarified.  Finally, this research concludes by examining the technical issues related to compound stability, stable de-Sitter solutions, and the behavior of tachons within supergravity, often resolved in the framework by introducing a mediator field, and assessing the relevance of these problems for the supergravity candidate status of this theoretical framework.  The potential solutions to these challenges, such as moduli stabilization via supersymmetric Minkowski limit, and the role of tachyon condensation in supergravity in both a stable de-Sitter and an anti-de-Sitter phase are also discussed.  Lastly, the possibility of supergravity tachyon condensation leading to a stable de-Sitter phase is also explored in relation to supergravity model-building for inflation.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This technique can be applied to other materials and circuits, beyond the scope of this study. Moreover, we establish a relationship between the technique's sensitivity and the resolution of the setup. This presents an opportunity to improve the sensitivity by enhancing the focus of the terahertz beam, leveraging either a tighter probe or a more localized terahertz focus. This could yield significantly higher resolution or sensitivity in analyzing objects much larger than those examined here. Finally, we discuss potential future applications of this research, such as near-field terahertz nanoscopy in quantum computing, where it could contribute to developing more robust devices by accurately evaluating the dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in complex microcircuit architectures. Such precision is essential for building quantum processors out of superconducting quantum circuits and similar technologies. In particular, we see a potential future where we use the technique to analyze the dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in larger-scale quantum computing systems, such as a 1,000 qubit or larger-scale quantum processor. However, this presents a challenge due to the need for improved local termination of the terahertz signal to reduce loss, likely involving optical or other forms of communication with the qubits. This presents an interesting area for future research and development. Finally, we acknowledge that while near-field scanning terahertz nanoscopy holds great potential for evaluating qubits and other quantum circuits, it may not always be applicable or practical. Certain materials or designs may not be amenable to analysis by this method or may require modification to be evaluated properly. In particular, we see a potential future where we use terahertz infrared spectroscopy instead of near-field scanning terahertz nanosscopy to analyze the dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in quantum computing systems, such as using a 1 mm wavelength terahertz infrared beam to examine the dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in silicon microstructures

One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. A high-performance, low-overhead estimation protocol has been developed to minimize reflection power loss without requiring on-off amplitude control. The proposed solution exploits a common structure within the system, significantly reducing pilot transmission overhead by decomposing the cascaded channel into separate user-specific and shared components. The challenge of highly coupled estimation variables is overcome through the use of optimization-based estimation methods utilizing channel covariance. An alternating optimization algorithm has been developed to efficiently solve the resulting non-convex problem, with an efficient initialization technique ensuring a local optimal solution. The research further introduces a successive convex approximation algorithm for optimizing the protocol's pilot transmission factors, yielding improved accuracy. The authors conduct comprehensive simulations, which demonstrate that the new approach yields significantly better performance compared to existing state-of-the-art protocols. The gap between the best possible performance and the researched approach has been quantified, with the latter performing very close to the ideal, showcasing the new approach's efficiency and effectiveness. The research finally presents a Jurisdictional analysis, defining and initializing the Jamming Power Matrix, whose eigenvalues and singular values are analyzed, and presenting an inverse JPM based on the Rayleigh distribution, thereby characterizing the new approach's performance and providing a comprehensive understanding of the approach's behavior. The widespread use of machine learning has led to increased interest in meta-learning, which enables a system to acquire knowledge more efficiently. In this research, we demonstrate how meta-learning can be applied to the development of mathematical skills by modeling a child's ability to learn to count based on verbal cues. By leveraging a practical task, our approach showcases the feasibility of using machine learning to simulate cognitive development in a realistic scenario. Furthermore, our model is adaptable to different types of learning: guidance that facilitates easy learning of counting, or guidance that mimics a child's natural learning process with gradual exposure and inconsistent feedback to improve resilience to errors. With the goal of promoting generalization to more complex mathematical concepts, we apply techniques like transfer learning, incorporating additional information about the quantity of items in a visual representation. Evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and the accuracy of number-word associations, confirm that the guided model excels at learning to count quickly and accurately, whereas the unguided model's performance improves gradually over many trials. Moreover, our findings show that the guided model can utilize knowledge gained from verbal cues to learn the meaning of numbers in a visual context. These outcomes validate the use of machine learning as a valuable tool for simulating cognitive development and could have practical implications for education, allowing teachers to tailor learning experiences to a child's learning style and enhancing their resilience to errors. Additionally, our model provides a means for automatically adjusting learning experiences to match a child's learning style and abilities, thereby reducing the need for extensive knowledge about the child's cognitive profile. Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively. Additionally, we delve into the divisorial analogues of the Minkowski theorem for line bundles and the Brunn-Minkowski inequality for curves and line bundles. Furthermore, we derive a divisorial version of the Heron constant and conclude by establishing a new inequality for the topological Euler characteristic of algebraic surfaces. Our analysis also reveals the divisorial divisors with Euler characteristic close to the Heron constant. Lastly, we explore the connection between the Heron constant and the beta invariant, leaving its resolution as a conjecture. We provide ample supporting evidence for our proposed dividend, with some results applicable beyond algebraic surfaces, extending instead to algebraic varieties of dimension any n >= 2. Our work thus reveals a novel set of connections between divisorial algebraic geometry and convex geometry, offering ample avenues for further exploration and generalization. Lastly, we conjecture that our results can be extended to the case of dimension any n >= 3, particularly in the divisorial form of the Heron constant and the Brunn-Minkowski inequality for curves and line bundles. A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge back to reasonable values following market disruptions. This methodology yields individual stock and market index trend indicators, which are unaffected by trading volume and instead rely solely on the sequence of transaction times and corresponding prices. As these dynamic price models already incorporate trading influence, our approach actually minimizes the impact of trading volume, producing results valid for multiple market conditions. We compare the performance of our approach, focusing on the S&P 500 future, against traditional indicators, revealing its substantial benefits during significant market events like 2008 and 2010. Following backtesting efforts, our approach shows the potential to generate consistent profits, even during stressful times, with a notable 62% success rate in predicting weekly volatility increases. We encourage investors to leverage this trend analysis in their daily trading decisions, focusing on daily and weekly time frames for optimal returns. A live demo, featuring interactive trend analysis for the S&P 500, can be accessed at trendforecast.net. The source code for this analysis has been publicly donated on GitHub: https://github.com/TrendForecast/trend-forecast/blob/main/trend_forecast.py. This donation includes a full suite of tools necessary to replicate our results and generate new insights. We hope this donation enables and fosters a sense of responsibility among the AI development community, promoting the transparent and accountable development of new technologies. Moreover, the trendforecast.net website serves as a publicly accessible platform, providing live trend predictions and investing guidance to a broad audience and promoting education about the benefits of trend analysis. By showcasing the effectiveness of dynamic price models in predicting market trends, our approach may inspire experts to adopt trend analysis as a valuable market analysis tool. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure from the server. Notably, our method offers a trade-off between attack resilience and latency, revealing a linear relationship without compromising user privacy. Our research implies that FLVoogd can balance performance and robustness while preserving user confidentiality. Ultimately, it serves as a reliable and trustworthy framework for securing general federated learning applications across various platforms. The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being inherently conflicting. Thermochemical CO2 dissolution in a massive atmosphere leads to the presence of stratospheric CN molecules, whereas the breakdown of N2 by solar UV radiation in a small atmosphere prevents CN molecule formation. These key distinctions allow the identification of a H2 envelope mass fraction, especially in the 0.1 to 0.3 Earth mass fraction range, through the characterization of a planet's atmospheric composition, offering a novel way to assess the habitability potential of temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets. Furthermore, the distinctive CN bands in the small atmosphere spectra are indicative of a more extensive set of gas solubility equilibria, encompassing CO. These unique spectral features can be utilized to verify the extension of the equilibrium pressure of these gases to higher pressures, thereby enabling the extension of the internal energy assessment of the planet to its pressurized core, thus facilitating more accurate habitability assessments. Our analysis relates the transition from small to massive atmospheres by considering the gas thermal composition transitions (characeterized by the critical pressures of 0.7, 1.5, and 3 bar respectively) as a thermal filter that effectively separates the atmosphere from the planet's denser interior, with the transition from a small to a massive atmosphere occurring at pressures exceeding 10 GPa, thereby necessitating a liquid water ocean presence. Consequently, characterizing the most massive envelopes in temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets, especially those with masses up to 3 Earth masses, may reveal a higher fraction of planets with habitable liquid water oceans, thereby increasing the prospects for temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets as targets for astrophysical biosignature searches in the coming decade. Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability similar to that of symmetric Hopfield networks for spatial patterns. Furthermore, our study reveals the model's capability to efficiently acquire sequences of binary images and generate neural spike-train data. Our model adheres to spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) principles, offering a theoretical framework for the systematic design of biological neural networks capable of long-term, robust sequence storage. The model's robust sequence storage capability exceeds that of traditional Hopfield networks, particularly in terms of the number of sequences. The model's sequences also demonstrate a high level of robustness across various noise levels and an impressive capacity for sequence length. The model's binary storage efficiency surpasses that of the linear learning rule in the 1-bit vector quantization technique used in linear neural networks and deep learning models. A thorough theoretical analysis has been conducted to evaluate the model's storage capacity for sequences. Our work offers a novel solution for the systematic design of spiking neural networks capable of sequential data processing, particularly in robust sequence memory applications, and offers a theoretical framework for the development of biological neural networks capable of long-term sequence storage. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents, such as invoices, is gathering a large, high-quality dataset for the task. Our proposed approach, called Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This efficient labeling strategy significantly reduces overall labeling costs while still training accurate document analysis models. Our experiments with publicly available datasets for invoice analysis and self-supervised document understanding confirm that selective labeling can cut labeling expenses by tenfold or more without compromising model performance. Furthermore, this cost-effective method also accelerates model development and enables greater experimentation with different data sets, a key advantage. The proposed approach is capped by an optimal "break-even point" where the cost of labeling becomes negligible in relation to the costs of collecting data, essentially transforming selective labeling into a form of active learning to expedite model deployment. To facilitate widespread adoption, we've adapted selective labeling to work with a wide range of existing vision-based model architectures and provided comprehensive implementation details to ensure ease of use. Additionally, we've created a publicly accessible labeling tool for easy data labeling and an open-source repository containing all code and data to replicate our results. The proposed selective labeling approach is a versatile solution to the data labeling bottleneck affecting many visually rich document understanding models, offering a cost-effective alternative to traditional active learning methods. It can be utilized by any party looking to train a high-quality document analysis model without incurring the high costs of complete annotation. To this end, we've made the model, data, and code fully accessible at https://selectivelabeling.com. Please contact the corresponding author at your convenience.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how varying the bonding configuration at the interface impacts the electronic properties. Across the examined configurations, we observed that the energy levels at the interface in InAs are positioned higher than those in EuS. Furthermore, we discovered novel states that arise from the interaction between the two materials, and are localized at the interface due to charge transfer. The arrangement of atoms at the interface significantly influences both the energy position and distribution of these states. Additionally, we have computed the magnetic properties of the system and found that the interface's electronic structure correlates with the'sp' component of the exchange split energy levels in EuS. The results obtained can guide the design of magnetic tunnel junctions and other quantum devices that rely on the magnetic properties of the EuS/InAs interface. The code used to generate the figures in this research is available for download on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/JoanDuarte-Santafe/tree-main/tree/main\EuS_InAs\_interface. Please note that this project is part of broader research that involves simulating magnetic tunnel junctions, and the data presented here can be extended to study such devices. To view the related work, visit https://github.com/JoanDuarte-Santafe/tree-main/tree/main\MTJ\_simulations.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Initially proposed by Borel and Wadge in the 50s, this system involves comparing two sets by comparing their highest uniform Borel reductions, which can be determined through an iterative process applying uniform continuity and then comparing the resulting functions uniformly. By focusing on the largest uniform Borel reductions, which can be found using a highest fixed point on a complete uniformity base, we achieve greater computational efficiency in determining Wadge classes. This leads to a significant reduction in symbolic representation of Wadge classes, from $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$ to $2^{\aleph_0}$. Moreover, this classification system retains key properties of the original classes, including closure under countable union and Catalán's code. To further refine the classes, we established a corresponding system of Wadge classes for closed sets, which can also be effectively classified. These findings demonstrate a balance between the simplicity of basic Borel classes and the high degree of structural detail of Wadge classes. To showcase the applicability of these results, we proved a long-outstanding open question in the theory of effective topological spaces, namely that there is no recursive collapse of the Borel spaces to basic Borel spaces. This proof marks a significant achievement in the research on effective topological spaces. Furthermore, we proved a generalised version of a significant result first found by Montalbán, which states that there is no effective collapse of the Baire spaces to basic Borel spaces, thereby also resolving a long-outstanding question whether there is an effective topological space whose Wadge class does not belong to the basic Borel space. These findings expand our knowledge of the theory of effective topological spaces. To achieve these results, we developed novel techniques for computing Wadge classes, including an alternate description of Wadge classes using a single application of uniform continuity, instead of the usual double applications, and also introduced a concept of 'fusion trees' which allow efficient computing of Wadge classes by merging different uniform continuity trees. Additionally, we presented a new method based on name structure that allows effective computation of Wadge classes, thereby providing an alternative to the standard Borel Wadge classes. These innovative techniques not only facilitate the effective classification but also offer additional insights into the topological space itself. To test the effectiveness of our classification system, we performed a thorough computation of Wadge classes

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively decreasing training costs. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables both fine-grained architecture preservation and weight pruning during the training process of CNNs. This results in a substantial decrease in the computational parameters, memory consumption, and training time without an increase in testing accuracy. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/achang2019/CNNDPR. Also, a demo video can be found at: https://youtu.be/jN3M4yCVT4k. It will automatically download the pre-trained models and generate the pruned CNN models for YOLOv4 and YOLOv5 at various parameter reduction rates for your reference. We've successfully employed ClickTrain to prune YOLOv4 and YOLOv5, achieving notable reductions in computational parameters, memory consumption, and training time while sustaining testing accuracy. Specifically, ClickTrain pruned YOLOv4 to require 0.091 times the original number of parameters, 0.13 times the original FLOPs, 3% of the original memory, and 2.45 times faster training time, all while preserving 0.96% less in YOLOv4's testing accuracy. Likewise, Clicktrain pruned YOLOv5 to require 0.075 times the original number of parameters, 0.1 times the original FLOPs, 2% of the original memory, and 3 times faster training time, all while preserving 0.93% less in YOLOv5's testing accuracy. Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by an extremely vast number of states and actions, as well as a difficult-to-compute transition matrix. To resolve these challenges, we develop an algorithm that combines policy iteration with subgradient ascent. We show that this approach allows the CMDP to converge to a solution at a rate proportional to $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$, where T represents the number of iterations, provided that a specific condition is met. This method also offers an efficient way to reduce the dimensionality of the CMDP by exploiting its structural properties when applicable. We successfully apply our algorithm to critical problems with such a structure: multi-product inventory control and multi-class queue management, achieving results superior to state-of-art methods. Keywords: CMDP, Constrained Markov Decision Process, Inventory control, Multi-class queue, Primal-dual approach, Subgradient ascent, Policy iteration, Structural reduction. This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but certain symbols, like the square root symbol, can't be processed this way due to them having internal lines. What's more, handwritten mathematical symbols can sometimes be connected by an overzealous writer. To tackle these issues, we've developed an advanced symbol segmentation method, encompassing both horizontal and vertical segmentation, as well as an approach to rectify incorrectly joined symbols. The effectiveness of our full strategy was tested on the CTS dataset and the ICDAR 2013 Special Challenge dataset. In nearly all cases, our full strategy outperformed the alternative, an equivalent approach to offline handwritten mathematical recognition. The datasets we used were based on mathematical symbols grouped into categories rather than individual characters. This means that recognizing a handwritten mathematical symbol involves not just recognizing the symbol itself but also its context. The categories for the CTS dataset include  84 symbols and for the ICDAR 2013 Special Challenge dataset there are 58 symbols. The results from our research indicate high overall recognition rates for both the CTS dataset and the ICDAR 2013 Special Challenge dataset. Furthermore, we've also successfully recognized some handwritten mathematical expressions by combining the recognized symbols. The recognized mathematical symbols were then translated into a text-based format, specifically using LaTeX. The entire process was done automatically without any manual intervention. The output from our approach can be seen as a series of LaTeX code blocks which can then be converted into a variety of formats, including PDF, HTML, and RTF. The conversion process involves rendering the LaTeX code in a virtual environment, typically through a program like MikTeX for Windows or TeX Live for macOS and Linux. The virtual environment can either be a local installation or accessed remotely via a service like CodeSnippets. A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that has a symplectic resolution with equivariant symplectic properties. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. The growth characteristics serve as a theoretical prototype for the duality concept we introduced between a 7D black hole and superconformal quantum mechanics. The new framework offers a clear theoretical explanation for the exponential growth of BPS state degeneracies in 7D black holes. Moreover, it provides a precise theoretical replica of the asymptotic behavior of the Hilbert scheme's Euler characteristic. Finally, the analysis is extended to higher-dimensional analogs of the hyper-Kahler cone, specifically to the conifedration of ALE spaces with A_n symmetry, to investigate the associated BPS spectrum and its characteristic exponential growth behavior. Necessary details are provided about the relevant conifedations and their geometric and cohomological properties. The 7D black hole and its associated BPS states serve a suitable theoretical example for the analysis, accurately replicating key features, such as the asymptotic exponential growth of BPS state degeneracies. Moreover, the framework offers a precise theoretical replica of the Euler characteristic of the conifedration, a codeformation theory connection that may be of independent interest to mathematicians. Lastly, the associated BPS spectrum and its characteristic growth behavior are computed for the general case of N=8 superconformal quantum mechanics, a 4D black hole, and its 3D analog, revealing a general structure in their BPS state degeneracies and exhibiting a wide range of characteristic growth behaviors. The theoretical replica accuracy, however, depends on specific details of these models, rather than their underlying geometric interpretations. Thus, the utility of the geometric interpretations is demonstrated, and their potential for further theoretical insights is illustrated. We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our research reveals that the disparity in epidemic behavior between homogeneous and heterogeneous networks is surprisingly small, yet the latter's complex structure can lead to a lower overall infection rate. Unlike non-clustered networks, the presence of robust community structures in the network tends to cause a secondary outbreak of infections, resulting in two distinct periods of variability. Specifically, the large fluctuations in the early stages of an epidemic within local clusters pose significant challenges to forecasting its spread. Crucially, our analysis suggests that bridging elements within the network have a substantial impact on predictability, with increased distances from the initial infection source to these nodes corresponding to decreased accuracy in forecasting the epidemic's progression. Furthermore, our research investigates how different disease response mechanisms influence variability, revealing that diverse reaction mechanisms can yield disparate infection rates at the conclusion of an epidemic. Importantly, our understanding of network architecture is invaluable in predicting epidemic behavior and can be leveraged for practical applications, such as decision-making in public health policy. Additionally, our discussion also highlights the potential applications and extensions of our research.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. To address these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. In doing so, our novel method has numerous benefits, primarily in reducing the gap between the approximated posterior and optimal policy distribution. Furthermore, our approach optimizes exploration within action spaces by targeting areas with higher expected returns. To achieve this, a new leapfrog operator has been developed for simulating Hamiltonian dynamics. Consequently, our approach has shown a significant enhancement in achieved return while reducing safety constraint breaches by systematically discarding unsafe action alternatives in safe reinforcement learning environments. Furthermore, our empirical studies have demonstrated that the Hamiltonian Policy, when applied to standard continuous reinforcement learning tasks, leads to enhanced policy outcomes and reduced variance in performance, thus verifying the effectiveness of our approach. It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the twin primes, characterized by this relationship, as $6k-1$ and $6k+1$. We aim to demonstrate that there are infinitely many pairs of these twin primes. We begin by defining two functions, $\varphi_1(p)$ and $\varphi_2(p)$, which yield the counts of all integers within the range from $1$ to $p$ that are expressions of either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will show that these functions adhere to specific conditions related to prime factors, and then (following a step similar to the approach in the proof of the Prime Number Theorem), establish a formula that approximates the product of these functions as $p$ approaches infinity. We will then utilize this result, along with complementary functions $\psi_1(p)$ and $\psi_2(p)$ that track the counts of numbers in the same range which are expressions of either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$ but with a remaining factor greater than $1$, to arrive at a representation of $\log_6(p)$ in terms of the sums of these functions. We will then utilize this representation to introduce an altered metric for $\log_6(p)$, one which is biased towards the higher twin primes, and (leveraging Chebyshev's bias approach) demonstrate that it approaches infinity as $p$ approaches infinity. We will then utilize this result to arrive at a formula for the difference between the logarithms of the larger and the smaller prime in each pair, one which approaches infinity as $p$ approaches infinity. Consequently, this implies that there are infinitely many pairs of these twin primes, and (mutatis mutandis) the same approach may also yield a proof for the Prime Number Theorem. We also note that this metric may not yield the most efficient approach to solving these problems, and that other, more efficient approaches may exist. Finally, we arrive at a distinct, yet equivalent formulation for the Twin Prime Conjecture, one which is both simpler and more intuitive than the original conjecture. We then combine this distinct formulation with Chebyshev's bias approach, arriving at a proof for the Twin Prime Conjecture. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot via a layered controller structure, leveraging sonar sensors for collision avoidance and an extended state observer to integrate sensor data, even in harsh environments. A specific protocol, the A* search algorithm, powers the initial navigation route, while a control layer applies adjustments as needed to assure a secure and stable driving experience. Both theoretical and experimental evaluations have demonstrated the efficacy of this method, revealing satisfactory results in various indoor environments. Furthermore, the controller's stability and robustness were validated through related mathematical analyses. Experimental data show a successful implementation of the method on a mobile robot, fusing sonar sensors to accurately navigate and avoid obstacles within a secure environment. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characterization using its reflectance spectrum between 0.8-2.4 $\mu m$, particularly in the unexplored 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ range, as we attempt to identify the spectral absorption features that correspond to its icy composition. Our findings reveal the presence of crystalline water ice, coinciding with existing observations. Nonetheless, using simple models consisting of intimate water ice mixtures, we fail to attain a comprehensive match of absorption bands, especially considering the spectral continuum, thus indicating the existence of additional components beyond water ice opacity models. Assuming a reference water ice model, our calculations reveal the proportion of water ice on Nereid's surface to be around 60%, paving the way for future studies involving a thorough understanding of Nereid's surface spectroscopy, potentially incorporating other spectral data including polarimetry and low-phase angle spectrophotometry to develop a more precise theoretical framework of its surface composition, thereby shedding light on its formation and evolution. Additionally, this research may contribute to a better understanding of other irregular satellites, potentially linking Nereid's irregular orbit to its broken binary past, thus making its surface spectroscopic analysis an indispensable tool in uncovering the historical break-ups of satellites from their parent planets' moons. As a result, our analysis emphasizes the significance of spectroscopic analysis of irregular satellites, particularly through a comprehensive phase angle coverage, to uncover the events of binary satellite disruptions. Existing theories suggest the ample evidence for moon-breaking events from the Saturnian system, and with a thorough analysis of spectroscopy, we anticipate the revelation of moon-breaking events from the Uranus and Neptune systems as well. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the suitability of spectroscopy as a tool to detect recent moon-breaking events, and the extensive surface spectroscopic data of irregular satellites, including methanol and water ice spectra, that can be employed to uncover the historical moon-breaking events from their parent planets. Moreover, our research emphasizes the theoretical concept of the missing spectrum, an unexplored region of spectral analysis between 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$, as the most crucial aspect of spectroscopic analysis, and the necessity to develop a spectroscopic model that can be used to determine the surface composition of celestial bodies through their reflectance spectrum between 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions can struggle with developing reliable policies when offline data accuracy varies, or 'policy flipping' occurs where a patient is given a different treatment in new data compared to the original training set. To address this, our approach uses a pessimistic model ensemble that incorporates uncertainty and limits the likelihood of policy flipping, thus optimizing the pessimism. Ensembles can be seen as a specialized case of our approach, however they fail to adequately address the issue of policy flipping. We prove the pessimism of our approach to be strictly higher than that of the best possible ensemble, however it remains the best alternative. A Bayesian learning framework is developed to find the most pessimistic ensemble, which in many cases can be reduced to a quadratic programming problem. Our approach successfully handles scenarios of varying policy flipping severities, and through simulation and real-world data analysis, the pessimism of our approach is shown to exceed that of the best possible ensemble by a significant margin, thereby increasing the likelihood of a stable and reliable policy. The method has been implemented in a package called offlineDTR available on CRAN.

We show that when these interactions disrupt the energy pattern, they can trigger multiple related patterns of superconductivity. These new superconducting patterns can exist even if individual electrons move freely within the band. In a lattice structure, we can isolate these effects by looking at changes around a single atom site. Our findings apply broadly to both clean and disordered systems. Additionally, we predict that in a specific type of lattice, called the honeycomb lattice, we can observe multiple related superconducting patterns without entering a more complex "Fock state." This means that even when interactions are weak, we can still see multiple related superconducting patterns. Finally, we show that these multiple related superconducting patterns can coexist with other types of superconducting patterns found in systems with exceptional points. However, these coexisting patterns may break apart when coupled to a less orderly material. The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid. Additionally, we discuss the origin of the functional equation and its connections to previous works by Erdos, Rényi, and others. Furthermore, we explore the a-adic solenoids from a group theoretic perspective, establishing relationships between their properties and the characteristics of the group itself. The connections between the a-adic solenoids and groups are examined through the lens of category theory, with particular focus on functors and their actions on the a-adic solenoids. Finally, we illustrate the significance of the a-adic solenoids by demonstrating their use in the analysis of a different class of random variables, known as Rademacher functions. The a-adic solenoids provide a unified framework for understanding the results of previous researchers, including Steindl, and offering new insights into the properties of the associated Rademacher functions. Lastly, we present a comprehensive list of properties for the a-adic solenoids, which characterize this unique class of groups and solenoids. These properties, which arise from the group theoretic perspective, are distinct from the properties derived solely from the probability theory, thereby demonstrating the versatility of the a-adic solenoids from both theoretical and analytical points of view. The a-adic solenoids can be viewed as a bridge between the group theoretic perspective and the analytical perspective, thereby emphasizing their importance in the theoretical framework. Additionally, we illustrate the relevance of the a-adic solenoids to other areas of mathematics, which provide new pathways for solving existing problems and investigating new mysteries in the field. The key outcome of our research is the realization that the a-adic solenoids are inherently connected to the distribution of random sums, which is a fundamental concept in probability theory. The underlying idea is that the character groups of the a-adic solenoids provide a unique tool for analyzing and understanding the characteristics of random sums. Therefore, the a-adic solenoids can be viewed as a unique group structure that provides a theoretical framework for predicting the distribution of random sums, which has far-reaching applications in the field of probability theory. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research fields such as ecology, microbiology, and landscape ecology. Clustering methods can effectively analyze such data by grouping locations based on the similarity of their constituent elements. This study compares various clustering techniques applied to binary data, including the use of latent class mixtures, hierarchical clustering, and a random forest-based method. Hierarchical approaches allow for the examination of results at multiple levels, whereas techniques employing information theory can provide clear distinctions between groups. We employed these methods to integrate ecosystem service data from various spatial scales and explored the results through comprehensive visualization. Ultimately, the study finds that the combination of latent class analysis and random forest testing represents an effective approach for presence-absence data sets. However, the suitability of this strategy or an alternative technique depends on the specific characteristics of the data and the research questions at hand. By utilizing a real-world dataset from landscape ecology, the study demonstrates the practical application of these clustering methods to identify distinct ecosystem service patterns at multiple spatial scales. This enables decision-makers to make more informed decisions about the management and protection of essential ecosystem services. Furthermore, the research highlights a novel application of random forest, which can effectively analyze the similarity between locations, particularly when assessing the contribution of individual variables to this similarity. This finding holds practical value for researchers who require a thorough understanding of the underlying processes involved in clustering. The study is part of a broader effort to develop a suite of statistical tools for the effective analysis of presence-absence data, as well as other types of binary data in landscape ecology. This research is expected to broaden its scope to other fields, such as microbiology and ecology. The techniques examined in this study are currently available through the R package RPackage_sebastien. It incorporates a novel depth-guided attention module to enhance feature extraction, a composite loss function for improved optimization, and a self-encoding mechanism to enhance feature discrimination. This unified structure outperforms other state-of-the-art methods on the Aachen Bimodal Dataset and the NYU-Dataset. The source code will be publicly available. It achieves this effectiveness without the need for built-in modalities-specific designs, making it a more efficient approach. The proposed method performs well even on images with low-quality depth or those containing modal-related artifacts. The integration of depth and RGB information enables the detection of hidden or occluded objects, demonstrating the significance of combining modalities in this context.
