A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary format is symmetrical. In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored and several fundamental questions about the resulting sets of integers and fractions are answered. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem using a precise formula, by ascertaining if an integer, N, can be expressed as a division between two identical symmetrical numbers, A and B. Upon determining representability, we pinpoint an upper limit on the value of the smallest numerical component. We then prove that a certain set of numbers has a higher frequency of occurrence within the set of all natural numbers, N. We achieve analogous results when examining quotients of numbers whose binary format is anti-palindromic, meaning the second half mirrors the reverse of the first. In addition, several numerical data points, as well as a related open question about integer divisibility, are provided. It is contemplated that resolving this related question will yield a frequency comparison between the sets of integer and fractional results obtained from the quotients of symmetrical and anti-symmetrical numbers, N. Finally, a possible generalization of these results to higher-dimensional vector spaces is suggested. We theorize that the properties identified here can be replicated in more advanced vector spaces with the incorporation of the use of modular arithmetic. Furthermore, a potential application of these results in computational biology, specifically through the use of a tool called Lambda Calculus, is mentioned. It is proposed that the symmetry properties identified in this research may assist scientists in understanding the inherent nature of mathematical objects, thus shedding light on the relationship between semantics and syntax. In other words, it is contemplated that the results of this research may reveal insights into the inherent nature of mathematical objects, thus providing a potential link between the syntax and semantics of mathematics. In contrast, a simpler approach, based on the properties of binary trees, is also offered to explain the results obtained in this research. We demonstrate that the symmetry properties identified in this paper can be understood through the analysis of binary trees, thus paving the way for future generalizations of these results to other fields of mathematics, theory of which was first introduced by R.H. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional reconstruction challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively addresses these issues by integrating three essential aspects: a compatible X-ray source theory, a non-convex image reconstruction process that incorporates data from various energy levels, and a statistical denoising approach tailored to the specific characteristics of the sensor in use. The model's mathematical formulation comprises an energy functional that balances these factors, which are further optimized using an alternating optimization technique. The proposed approach was tested on simulated and real-world data and compared to traditional reconstruction methods, which do not account for polyenergetic X-rays or device-specific denoising techniques. The results demonstrate the superior image quality produced by the proposed model, which surpasses those of the comparison methods in terms of accuracy and resilience to distortion caused by various energy levels, as well as device noise. The code used for these experiments is publicly accessible at a specified repository URL. The proposed sensor-specific denoising approach shows promise for enhancing the quality of CT reconstructions, whereas the X-ray source model may also be applied to other imaging modalities that involve complex X-ray interactions, such as Dual-Energy CT (DECT). The integration of the two techniques may provide a comprehensive solution for accurately understanding and modeling the internal structures of various subjects and objects, which can further aid in device development and testing processes. The combination of the proposed reconstruction model and X-ray source theory may provide a comprehensive solution for accurately understanding and modeling the internal structures of various subjects and objects, which can further aid in device development and testing processes. The integration of the two techniques may also enhance precision and accuracy in these processes. The proposed sensor-specific denoising approach shows promise for extending its applications to other fields and devices. The combination of the proposed reconstruction model and X-ray source theory may also contribute to broadening its applications. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study introduces a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training, skipping the time-consuming step of obtaining detailed annotations. Evaluation confirms the efficacy of this method, with produced lines and pages resembling real-life handwriting. Compared to other baseline generation methods, such as writing synthesis, language model guided generation and dataset augmentation, our approach delivers the most accurate results, according to the employed metrics. Specifically, it boasts a 13 character error rate 7% lower than writing synthesis and a 10% better line quality metric compared to dataset augmentation. Moreover, to mimic the intricacies of real-world datasets more accurately, a novel metric is introduced that emulates the varied lengths and content distribution of actual handwritten documents. Leveraging this new approach, the top-1 tested Character Error Rate (cher) was reached at 14.0, a notable achievement. The proposed method comprises two key components: (i) a program that can explain its behavior and (ii) a handwriting generator guided by the program. While prior studies have employed similar architectures, this study enhances their design with critical modifications. Firstly, the program, comprising letters, is enabled to repeat its applications (repeat) and also considers unobserved parts of symbols (context). Secondly, the evaluator, originally solely concerned with fitting observed data, is now influenced by a language model that evaluates generative program fitness from two angles: program accuracy and handwriting similarity. Lastly, instead of merely optimizing the program to best fit observed data, a search strategy is employed that allows the top programs to be selected based on a broader range of criteria, including unseen test data, a language dictionary and a language model, all while ensuring the top programs are closely related (similar writing styles). The developments outlined above result in programs that excel at real-world datasets in two public repositories, surpassing earlier BPL-based generation methods in terms of character error rate. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient. In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models characterized by uncertain variable domains and unknown interference factors. Following the probabilistic distribution framework, we formulate this as a problem of determining the minimum probability of a decision function's failure, subject to certain constraints. Initially, we simplify this calculation by rephrasing the problem as a linear programming optimization, but due to the problem's computational complexity, we instead rely on a simplified representation of the uncertainty to provide a more manageable approximation of the original problem, ultimately yielding a more accessible calculation. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through both a theoretical analysis and an examination of its application to a real-world problem. Specifically, we examined a situation in which we wished to determine a minimum-safe route for a driver to take, while maintaining adequate battery life in their phone. Our analysis shows that while fully accounting for a phone's battery life as an uncertain factor provides a reliable approximation of its remaining battery life, this reliability comes at a computational cost, rendering it impractical to calculate precisely within a reasonable time frame. Nevertheless, our approach successfully identifies a reasonably accurate route for the driver, while maintaining a manageable computational load. Furthermore, we observe that while our approximation relies on a simplified representation of the uncertainty, this simplification does not provide a minimum-excess safety margin for the driver's route. Instead, we propose a post-processor that helps to identify a route with both a minimum-excess safety margin and a reasonable computational load. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments, in which we examine its performance on progressively more complex networks, while maintaining a reasonable computational load. Ultimately, our study provides a robust framework for decision functions to quantify and ensure performance reliability in the presence of credal Bayesian networks, along with a practical solution that balances performance, reliability, and computational load. Specifically, our decision function's excess risk, which measures the difference between its expected loss and the minimum-excess safety margin it maintains, is shown to be directly proportional to the logarithm of its computational load, which implies that there is an optimal balance between performance reliability and computational load. In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position, thereby preserving its periodic matter wave pattern. Notably, the oscillations fade primarily due to wavepacket dispersal; yet, by assuming the impurity behaves as a bright soliton, the decay can be largely countered. Furthermore, the accelerations give rise to an additional energy component, which is transferred from the impurity to the condensate, in addition to generating phonons within the condensate. The effective energy exchange between the impurity and the condensate is determined by the spin-orbit coupling strength. The presence of a spin-orbit coupling gives rise to a novel energy transfer mechanism, in contrast to non-existence of such energy transfer between a single component BEC and a non-interacting impurity atom. The effective energy exchange is optimally enhanced when the impurity atom is accelerated at an angle with respect to the condensate's roton minimum. The internal phonon modes triggered by acceleration decay rapidly yet retain their spin component, while the impurity atom's energy is partially transferred to the condensate and partially remains as the impurity's energy. The rate of energy transfer from the impurity to the condensate surpasses that in solid matter by a factor equal to the $\tilde{m}/m$. Here, $\tilde{m}$ is the effective mass of the impurity atom due to its interaction with the condensate, while $m$ is the impurity atom's free mass. The rate of energy transfer from the impurity to the phonon modes in the condensate is contingent upon the impurity-phonon coupling strength and the impurity's energy spread. The energy preserved by the impurity can be optimized under neutral conditions and is heavily dependent on the $\tilde{m}/m$ ratio. Moreover, the smallest possible fraction of the impurity's energy is lost as thermal energy in the condensate, which is largely due to the impurity-condensate interaction. This interaction gives rise to an effective thermal barrier that prevents the impurity's energy from being fully transferred to thermal energy within the condensate. In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance determined by the shortest path between distinct elements. The elements of this subset are divided into distinct sets based on their distance from the code. Given the quadrangle's graph has a diameter of four, both the minimum distance and maximum distance from a vertex to its closest code element cannot exceed four. If the minimum distance is four, it signifies the code is a partial ovoid or partial spread; a code is fully classified as an ovoid or spread if it also has a maximum distance of two. A neighbour-transitive code is defined as having an automorphism group that transitively acts on both the code and its closest neighbouring elements. The study focuses on classifying neighbour-transitive codes admitting insoluble automorphisms in thick classical quadrangles and finding neighbour-transitive codes of minimum distance four in the classical quadrangle W_3(q). The study further classifies neighbour-transitive codes in the classical quadrangle W_3(q) and the tropical generalised quadrangle. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on the few-femtosecond timescale with this type of XANES spectroscopy, allowing for in-depth examination of electronic dynamics close to the Fermi level.

The model demonstrates a straightforward approach to elucidating how each of these processes affects changes observed in XANES measurements.

The findings suggest that redistributing electrons drives most fluence-dependent changes observed at high X-ray fluences. This paper introduces a completely integrated CMOS temperature sensor, covering a voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V. The sensor employs a bi-metal thermal converter to monitor temperature changes via a digitally controlled, externally-trimmable resistance network. A temperature extraction circuit utilizes a digitally-scaled, background-calibrated algorithm to achieve high resolution and reduce dynamic power consumption. Featuring a fully on-chip adaptive voltage regulator, the sensor allows operation across a wide temperature and voltage spectrum with minimal external components. Experimental results from a 0.13$\mu$m test chip demonstrate its effectiveness, with a measurement error of 1.4°C and a resolution of 0.24°C. The sensor consumes 24.5µW at 25°C and 1.8V, with a conversion time of 30ms and a energy cost of 1.06nJ/Conversion. Additionally, the sensor's Q-value reaches 81.2 and its thermal sensitivity amounts to 0.63°C/V. Due to its low power profile, the sensor can also be used in systems with power-gating capabilities. Moreover, the sensor features a small 36x24µm die area, making it suitable for a diverse array of temperature-related applications. With a measurement accuracy of ±1.4°C and a high resolution of 0.24°C, this sensor outperforms several temperature sensors in terms of resolution, while its low power consumption and small area size place it among the leaders in terms of power efficiency and compactness. Moreover, its wide voltage operation range facilitates its integration into diverse voltage-ranged analog and digital circuitries. Furthermore, background calibration has eliminated traditional temperature sensor challenges like drift and accuracy degradation due to process variations, thereby ensuring high accuracy throughout its entire temperature range. Moreover, its converter-related energy consumption is remarkably lower than previously reported systems with similar resolution. Additionally, this chip's capability to adapt to changing supply voltages has made it suitable for a wide range of applications with varying supply voltages. Finally, despite having a high resolution, the sensor features a fast conversion time of 30ms, making it suitable for various high-resolution temperature monitoring applications in embedded systems. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired hybrid entangled states, which are a combination of both discrete and continuous variables. We present two methods of implementing this technique, each utilizing a different technique to create the desired polarization entangled states: the first based on single photons and linear optics and the second using a two-mode squeezer. By examining both implementations and discussing the benefits and limitations of each, this research provides an understanding of entanglement preparation and its practical implications, highlighting an interface between diverse types of entangled states and potentially providing an alternative method for generating polarization entanglement through a heralded approach. By harnessing this technique, it is possible to obtain polarization entanglement without postselection, thereby enabling a more practical and efficient preparation of entangled states for use in quantum information sciences and technologies. In particular, this research demonstrates a method for generating the desired polarization entanglement by harnessing single photons through a heralded approach, thereby overcoming a long-standing limitation associated with optical quantum computing and other applications that rely on postselection, which can now be avoided by employing the proposed technique. This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight. For sequences of points in R^d the authors present algorithms under the L_2 norm that achieve previously known competitive ratios but allow for Steiner points to be added to substantially improve the competitive ratio in terms of ε. However, the authors also prove that eliminating the dependence on n in dimensions d ≥ 2 is not possible, while providing improved lower bounds under the L_1 norm: Ω(ε^(-2)/log ε^(-1)) in the plane and Ω(ε^(-d)) in R^d for d≥3. Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This work presents a more practical viewpoint, contending that feature extraction comes with expenses varying across distinct features. Moving beyond existing binary misclassification assessments, this study proposes a more realistic approach by adapting the widely utilized F1-score metric to account for costs in feature selection. To optimize this adapted F1-score, the research introduces an innovative heuristic, demonstrating its efficiency through comprehensive simulations involving up to 100 features. Furthermore, the models' robustness to pseudolearning attacks in simulated scenarios is assessed, with the findings indicating a stable performance within a certain feature range for the proposed method. To streamline the training process, the research applies technical enhancements, including data aggregation and model trimming, yielding superior results. Finally, the study confirms the efficiency of the proposed method through a comparison with existing state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its superiority in terms of precision, F1-score, recall, and accuracy in IoT device classification. The novel approaches developed in this research are envisioned to be valuable contributions to the field of IoT device identification, with potential applications extending to data protection and security applications. This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, such as accuracy or F-score, our approach delivers results equivalent to GIZA++ when trained on a dataset 22 times smaller. Crucially, this breakthrough enables comprehensive fine-tuning of GIZA++ on any available dataset, thereby overcoming previous constraints related to dataset size. Additionally, we develop a more efficient model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the European Corpus of Modern English, reducing alignment computation time by half. The source code for these methods is openly available on GitHub. Our work aligns with the GANER framework for responsible ML development, promoting the reuse and understanding of existing ML models through minimal yet effective modifications. We adhere to the GANER principles by suggesting minor adjustments to the training process of a widely used, commercial MT system to achieve top-notch results in word alignment. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of metric-driven research and make our alignment metrics openly accessible, also sharing our training code to facilitate the replication of our work. Lastly, we effectively apply our approach to the task of word alignment, showcasing the benefits of MT-based pretraining and highlighting the potential of our model to enhance the quality of other NLP tasks through fine-tuning. Through this research, we achieve three key objectives: first, we develop a word-alignment model that leverages bilingual information from MT systems; second, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on a small dataset; third, we successfully apply the concept of MT-based pretraining and fine-tuning to the task of word alignment, including achieving a 22 times reduction in the required dataset for comparable performance. MT-based pretraining enables high-quality alignment results on a relatively small dataset, and we openly make available the code for replicating our work and distributing our model to others. We also explore the potential of our model to contribute to the enhancement of other NLP tasks through fine-tuning, revealing that a model pre-trained on non-domain-specific data can achieve exceptional results in word alignment with just a small amount of fine-tuning based on domain-specific data. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures. Each player's strategy is handled as a variable in the algorithm, allowing for simultaneous updates with asynchronous communication among players. However, updating each player's strategy is done incrementally using a fixed frequency, which can lead to oscillations; yet we prove the convergence of the algorithm under a relatively mild condition. Moreover, we show that the frequency of updates can be optimized dynamically without pre-determination, and still achieve convergence. Our algorithm is further illustrated and tested on a simple game of demand dispatch. Numerical results show that the frequency of updates can significantly impact the algorithm's efficiency, and even asymptotically reach the equilibrium at an optimal frequency. Additionally, we propose an alternative version of the algorithm at a fixed frequency, which has a more straightforward analysis but requires communication among players by batch, and prove its convergence to the equilibrium via the convergence of the warped resolvent. This research note details a computational model for primordial black holes, which is then employed to investigate the scenario in which dark matter exists in the form of these dense objects. Primordial black holes are hypothetical compact celestial bodies, which are predicted to have been created in the early universe either as a result of gravitational collapse or through other mechanisms. Although they no longer exist in the universe today, as they have since been absorbed by other objects, no concrete evidence has been found to date. A theoretical model has been developed, which is designed to recreate the birth of these black holes and study their properties. This model is an enhancement of a prior computational model, which has been refined to better capture the correct mass spectrum of primordial black holes. Specifically, our simulation is utilized to analyze a region in which the star-forming efficiency in a universe that is only capable of forming stars is a key factor. Our results indicate that the mass fraction of primordial black holes, which is a theoretical component of dark matter, is in agreement with current observational limits. A combination of this model's output with other dark matter theories could potentially explain the observed dark matter density in our universe. Future developments of this model will be directed towards varying initial conditions to examine the influence of parameters on the properties of primordial black holes. Additionally, we aim to integrate the capabilities of POPsyCLE, which is a particle-level simulation tool, to study the formation of structures in a universe that contains primordial black holes as a component of dark matter. A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for delicate biological specimens or sensitive samples due to the inadequacy of available light-detecting capabilities and potential harm from light interaction. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a quantum imaging protocol that achieves all this by leveraging the unique properties of a Michelson interferometer and combining it with induced coherence-based interactions to exploit undetected photons. This innovative imaging technique not only minimizes interaction with the subject but also enables imaging with lower photon flux and longer wavelengths than usual, making it feasible to use weaker light sources and detecting capabilities. As a result, we have successfully taken single-color images of small objects using either a basic or advanced camera. Unlike previous interaction-free imaging techniques that relied on the manipulation of photon probabilities, our protocol specifically extracts spatial information from the one-photon transition probability. Furthermore, we have analytically confirmed that the resolution of our detector directly determines the image quality, and our findings show that a pinhole lens offers the best resolution for our Michelson interferometer setup. Additionally, we have devised a modified version of the detector to filter out only certain wavelength ranges, effectively achieving imaging rates up to 10 times faster than conventional methods using a similar camera. The innovative Michelson interferometer scheme, coupled with induced coherence-based interactions, has opened up new possibilities for imaging a broader range of subjects without undetected photons, and the techniques developed here could be applied to various quantum imaging applications at the single-photon level. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The stick-slip regime transitions into the stationary regime when the surface roughness exceeds a certain threshold, specifically when the asperity size reaches the level of the soap film's curvature. The discovery of the stationary regime has crucial implications, pointing to the existence of a second-order friction transition alongside the already known first-order slippage transition. The onset of this transition can be predicted using a simple flux-weighted average method based on the Arzt model. The proposed model also sheds light on the morphological details underlying this roughness effect and its potential applications in the development of surface-modified materials with tailored friction properties. Additionally, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanics governing complex liquid flows and fails to penetrate at interfaces. The observed friction modes also have analogues in other complex fluids and are relevant to phenomena such as drag reduction, noise reduction, and tribology. Lastly, our research also sheds light on the dynamics of foam collapse and the potential applications of surface-modified materials in the reduction of noise and energy loss. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly improved image quality enhancement, yet these advances have also raised concerns about potential misuse in image steganography. In reversible steganography, the stealer's malicious intent can be challenging to predict, making it essential to employ robust classification models to prevent misuse. Conventional machine learning algorithms may struggle to achieve this goal, especially when dealing with limited and unevenly distributed steganographic data. To address this issue, we propose the use of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), an probabilistic variant of Neural Networks, as a reliable classifier for detecting reversible steganography. By estimating the uncertainty distribution within BNNs, we investigate how it impacts the detection performance and can serve as a confidence metric. Experimental results demonstrate that BNNs excel in predicting the output of steganographic algorithms, even when trained with limited data, thus showcasing their utility in reversible steganography detection. The associated source code is available at https://github.com/jbincx/steganography_bnn. and will be officially released on Pypi under the name 'rstealer', with a demo available at https://steganography-bnn.herokuapp.com/. This work has been accepted at ICIP 2023.

Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling their survival and operation. Disruption of this process is associated with various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons control transportation to target essential areas. We introduce a new optimization model that simulates the material transportation mechanism in complex neural geometries by minimizing congestion. The model adheres to partial differential equations that describe transportation based on molecular-motor-assisted models and is solved in complex tree structures through isogeometric analysis. We test our model by introducing different parameters that mimic traffic congestion, specifically investigating the effects of reduced microtubules and swirling structures on material transportation. Our simulations effectively demonstrate both the optimal material transportation in healthy neurons and the occurrence of congestion in neurons with abnormalities, illustrating the significance of both geometry and microtubule structure in facilitating optimal neural transport processes. Our model provides a versatile framework for testing various cellular transportation mechanisms, enabling the simulation of neural system disorders and the exploration of potential treatments. Furthermore, our approach highlights the potential for optimized material transportation strategies in applications beyond basic cellular biology. Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept is further explored in a research paper, which outlines a novel, chemical-based system capable of exhibiting autonomous Hebbian learning through multiple input channels. This artificial neural network model is based on a simple, chemically-reversible reaction system, emulating a biological neuron's behavior, and is demonstrated to identify patterns in the input data it receives. The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This problem can be represented mathematically as 
$\begin{cases}
  -\Delta_p u + \lambda^{\pm} |x|^{q-1} u = 0 \quad \text{in} \ \  B^o(0,1), \\
  u = 0 \quad \text{on} \ \  \partial B(0,1),
  \end{cases}$ where $B^o(0,1)$ denotes the interior of the unit ball centered at $0$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $q \in \mathbb{R}$ is a constant that can be either greater than $1$ or less than $1$. We employ the Weyl's function in combination with optimal Sobolev embedding theorems to establish upper and lower bounds for the first eigenvalue of this problem under specific conditions on $q$ and $\lambda$. Additionally, we introduce new whole-domain eigenvalue problems for both the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator and the fractional $p$-Laplace operator, and provide further analysis of these estimates through several examples and considerations of smoothness of the first eigenfunction. Finally, we conclude by discussing possible generalizations of these estimates to other types of second-order nonlinear elliptic operators. We note that this research paper relies heavily on the referenced works of Bressan and Wang (2022) and Caffarelli and Vazquez (2006). We mention that part of the results in this research paper were first presented at the 16th EPSA Conference on Differential Equations and Nonlinear Analysis in July 2022. This research paper has been revised to better reflect the current state-of-the-art in this field, and we have added new material, particularly in Section 4, to better showcase the unique aspects of our approach and results.'

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Numerical results are then presented to evaluate the effectiveness of GCNNs in comparison to other traditional Neural Networks. Ultimately, we illustrate that GCNNs offer a effective solution for handling irregular data, but also acknowledge their limitations compared to other more tailored methods when it comes to analyzing graph-specific data. The contribution of this work lies in providing a comprehensive framework that offers insights into the inner workings of GCNNs, as well as a novel perspective on Neural Networks that extends beyond the standard CNN and fully connected NN cases. Additionally, the proposed matched filtering perspective introduces a simplified understanding of the GCNNs, showcasing that a wide range of deep Neural Networks can be viewed as sequentially applied matched filters. Lastly, the study presents a numerical evaluation of GCNNs that can learn and predict non-linear patterns, despite the widespread misconception that deep Neural Networks are limited to analyzing linear patterns. The study also showcases the effectiveness of GCNNs in comparison to fully connected Neural Networks, highlighting practical advantages that arise from incorporating graph structures in Neural Networks. The study further presents results that demonstrate the superiority of GCNNs over various other methods, across different test datasets, and finally highlights practical considerations that emerge when evaluating the performance of GCNNs, revealing non-intuitive patterns such as data regularization and feature selection overfitting that are uniquely inherent to GCNNs. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. This approach has shown significant improvements in accuracy for both syntactic and part-of-speech analysis across multiple languages, particularly in instances where annotated data is scarce. Notably, in one such case, the method has achieved an impressive 41.2% enhancement in UAS. This gain is particularly substantial as it indicates a reduction of over one full percentage point in the existing error margin. Furthermore, the method has shown a relative reduction of 20-30% in the existing error margin in two other languages. The code for this algorithm is available at https://github.com/alecmagnus/dcst.

If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'.

Estimating inter-beat intervals from electrocardiograms is crucial for detecting arrhythmias and analyzing heart function. This research introduces a novel method for interpolating missing ECG beats and estimating intervals using a Tiramisu autoencoder-based approach. Initially, ECG data is pre-processed to convert raw data into a suitable format for analysis. Featuring beat patterns, RR-interval trends, and their derivatives, the optimized input enhances the model's capability to accurately predict intervals. The Tiramisu approach is then evaluated on the Long-Berlin dataset, with results indicating that it outperforms existing methods for estimating inter-beat intervals. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in detecting arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation, by incorporating supplementary R-peak detection and a atrial-fibrillation-synthesis module. By integrating this novel method into a real-time arrhythmia-discriminator device, the study successfully detects atrial-fibrillation during a television broadcast, showcasing the feasibility for use in everyday devices. Additionally, the study highlights the raw-R-gram's potential in analyzing arrhythmias and understanding its connection to the estimation of inter-beat intervals. By achieving low average absolute errors of approximately 16 milliseconds, the Tiramisu approach achieves a significant error reduction of around 48%, surpassing existing methods. The corresponding histogram of errors reveals a concentration of errors around 10 milliseconds, indicating near-perfect predictions. Based on these findings, the study concludes that the Tiramisu approach provides a significant improvement over existing methods for estimating inter-beat intervals from ECG signals. We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done for the free particle in any dimension using a saddle-point expansion. Additionally, a direct numerical approach via solution of the AOUP equations is performed, alongside a method using Legendre-Fenchel transform of the scaled cumulant generating function obtained via a cloning algorithm. Results for the free particle exhibit asymptotically linear behavior on both sides, dependent on a multiplicative factor of the dimension. Conversely, confinement scenarios in two dimensions display distinct behavior when applying active force in either harmonic or anharmonic potentials, each exhibiting varying rate function and mechanism. Moreover, a fluctuation relation for active work distribution is verified in free particles, exhibiting temperature-dependent behavior. Similar verification occurs in cases involving harmonic potential, while in anharmonic cases, verification holds at low active force levels; yet at high levels of active force in anharmonic cases, a distinct effective temperature, derived from the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, is found to govern behavior. Lastly, a precise expression for the effective temperature in anharmonic cases, but without disorder, is derived via analytical calculations, revealing two distinct definitions of temperature that cross-calculate to zero. This research provides precise, analytical solutions to previously numerical or semianalytical problems, offering a deeper understanding of the system's behavior. Moreover, this study presents an innovative method combining the cloning algorithm and Legendre-Fenchel transform to solve large deviation problems, an approach that can be applied to various other systems. Finally, this work examines, via direct numerical approach and replica theory, the behavior of active particles in the presence of disorder, presenting results that can be extended to higher dimensions. This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture and capture high-definition footage of 772 individuals, representing various demographics and styles. Using these multi-view images, we apply advanced 3D mesh modeling to accurately reconstruct and represent diverse human body expressions from multiple viewpoints. The proposed dataset demonstrates exceptional efficiency in learning and reconstructing a complete human model, effectively supplementing existing human body expression datasets such as MPII-Gaze, Multi-PIE, Human3.6M, and Panoptic Studio datasets, which were previously limited to single viewpoints or fewer subjects. Based on HUMBI's capabilities, we outline a new benchmark challenge focused on leveraging pose data to generate highly realistic, photorealistic human body expressions in three-dimensional formats, with a significant emphasis on promoting genuine social telepresence. The HUMBI dataset is accessible at http://humbi-data.net. The benchmark challenge code is accessible at https://github.com/zhkhang/HUMBI_Benchmark_Challenge. Additional information about the dataset and benchmark challenge can also be obtained via email at zhang.khang@ieee.org. Leveraging HUMBI, we successfully developed a novel approach to 3D human body expression reconstruction, addressing existing shortcomings and producing superior results compared to current state-of-the-art models, as demonstrated by our benchmark challenge evaluations. The HUMBI dataset holds immense potential for advancing various areas, including 3D human body expression reconstruction, social telepresence, and human-aware robotics. The benchmark challenge outcomes may also inspire new research directions in these fields, promoting enhanced research in areas such as multi-person pose estimation to facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of human body signals. The HUMBI dataset can be utilized to develop more accurate multi-person pose estimation algorithms by leveraging multiple view images, while the benchmark challenge evaluations provide a comprehensive evaluation of the state-of-the-art models. The HUMBI dataset and benchmark challenge can also be applied to develop novel and effective solutions for social telepresence by utilizing diverse human body expressions from multiple viewpoints. The benchmark challenge evaluations may also uncover existing shortcomings in social telepresence, prompting researchers to devise new strategies to enhance the overall quality of social telepresence. Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and compare it to other prominent cross-lingual transfer methods, demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy and efficient use of resources for task-specific models, and achieving state-of-the-art results for fine-tuning and zero-shot scenarios. The code for this project is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/jase1234/task_reps.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Leveraging shared model benefits while preventing performance decline
is a delicate balance, and our work brings this important consideration to the
attention of the mrl community. Our code is available at https://github.com/affun/mbt.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland. Furthermore, the study reveals that power lines in remote areas can be subjected to excessive loads due to the extended reach of hurricane-generated winds and storm surges. These findings enable the development of a detailed analysis framework for estimating total power losses and identifying vulnerable regions of the power grid. It is hoped that these outcomes will contribute to the development of more effective contingency planning and risk assessment strategies for reducing power losses in the future. Ultimately, it is anticipated that these findings will aid control centers in preparing for and mitigating the effects of hurricane scenarios, and these conclusions are substantiated by the analysis of a specific case study. The novel aspects of this research are the integration of a complex hurricane model, a detailed analysis of storm surges, and the application of a spatial power grid model to estimate total power losses and identify vulnerable regions. These advancements enabler the development of a comprehensive decision-support system for power utilities to effectively plan for and mitigate the effects of hurricane scenarios. To validate these outcomes, the study presents a series of hypothetical hurricane scenarios that simulate the movement and variation of the storms in a 10-year period. The analysis of these scenarios confirms that storm-related flooding can cause additional load reductions and increase the likelihood of transmission line overload. This approach enables us to generalize the theorem for functions u, where u is defined by u(x,y,z) = a(x,y,z)/r with r representing the distance from a point (x,y,z) to a given set of points x_i, y_i, z_i (i=1,2,3), and a being an arbitrary polynomial in a given domain. We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, revealing connections to both the Cantor set and the Mandelbrot set. Through initial studies, we establish the existence of two unique invariant measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, providing an understanding of entropy approachability. Furthermore, our work reveals a critical aspect: the entropy approachability threshold can fail under certain conditions, specifically when the algebraic degree of certain self-maps associated with the encoding sequences exceeds a certain limit, notably when it reaches $\sqrt{2}$, yet also when it remains below this limit if certain sequences are prohibited. We validate the development of newly defined 'forbidden sequence' parametric families of invariant measures with maximal entropy for the generalized baker maps, as well as for more intricate models involving coupled maps in 2D and 3D spaces, which are represented by coupled baker maps, particularly when the sequences of transitions between these maps adhere to a certain language characterized by a low rate of binary symbol change, known as 'binary entropy'. Finally, our work discloses novel sources of complexity, or entropic, behavior in these generalized baker map systems, which are found to exhibit either ergodic or non-ergodic behavior, depending on specific conditions, as well as the development of unique 'plateau' phenomena observed in the time-series of 2D and 3D system trajectories, which are found to occur outside of these 'binary entropy' constraints. We provide analytical calculations for the measures with maximal entropy in these systems, providing frameworks for evaluating either the uniqueness or non-uniqueness of these measures in 2D and 3D spaces, as well as the degree of ergodicity in these systems. Additionally, our work includes a detailed observation of how trajectories behave under the generalized baker map, revealing a complex interplay of stability and chaos that is not fully captured by traditional approaches to entropy approachability. To showcase the breadth of this new approach, we also find that similar mechanisms governing the breakdown of entropy approachability also exist in other systems, such as the Dyck system, as well as certain 1D and 2D area-preserving map systems with a period of $3n$ that involve a particular combination of mode changes and interactions,

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, WN has been adapted with a pitch-dependent modification by incorporating a neural network estimating the pitch for each sample, resulting in a more robust model for periodic signal generation. To further improve the model's periodic signal processing capability, a novel dilated convolution operation with a periodic kernel has been introduced in QPNet, which enables the discovery of local periodic patterns. Due to the high computational requirements of autoregressive models like WN and QPNet, a sample-wise approximation is applied for inference acceleration. The effectiveness of the proposed model is confirmed through the generation of quasi-periodic waveforms at unseen frequency ranges using only a single neural network. Numerical evaluations reveal that QPNet surpasses WN and the baseline periodnet in terms of the correlation between generated waveforms and the target pitch. Additionally, the generated waveforms demonstrate higher fidelity based on the frequency spectrum. The code for this project can be accessed at https://github.com/tomohrano/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet. The generated waveforms are available at https://quasiperiodic.github.io/. The generated waveforms can also be heard through audio demos at https://tomohrano.github.io/quasi-periodic-wavenet/. The proposed model has been successfully applied in vocal learning, including the generation of chanted melodies and raw waveform signals of pitch 4.3, with a sampling rate of 400 Hz, which exhibit a spectrum wider than 300 Hz. This model also outperformed prior state-of-the-art periodic generative models, such as periodnet, and WaveNet with pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks, in numerical evaluations and audio quality assessments. Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have shown various successes in real-world applications and scientific research. However, their effectiveness significantly declines when dealing with new users and items or in the absence of user-item interaction data. This research aims to enhance the overall CF approaches by incorporating the concept of biclusters, comprised of sparse and localized user-item preference patterns, to address the issues of preference uniqueness, sparsity, and subjectivity. A novel CF algorithm, called Bicluster-based CF (BiCF), and its improvement with Online Learning (OL BiCF) are proposed to identify and integrate these biclusters into the traditional CF framework. BiCF achieves better performance than current state-of-the-art methods by leveraging biclusters, while OL BiCF adapts to real-time data streams, outperforming baseline CF methods and achieving results comparable to those achieved through Bicluster-based Latent Factor Models. An extensive experimentation process, conducted with four benchmark datasets and two dataset settings, including the Netflix DVD era and the Amazon Video, proved the effectiveness of the proposed BiCF and OL BiCF algorithms. Additionally, the source code and datasets used in this research study have been made available for public access through an open repository. OL BiCF, the improvement of BiCF, displays promising features such as real-time adaptability, ability to perform well on a single dataset, and even outperforms CF methods that require data to be pre-maintained, thus presenting an alternative solution for CF practitioners struggling to handle new users and items or empty interaction matrices. The choice between BiCF and OL BiCF depends on the specific use case, with BiCF being more suitable for offline training and OL BiCF ideal for real-time applications. Future research can utilize the bicluster concept in Information Retrieval and Natural Language Processing domains to tackle issues of locality, sparsity, and subjectivity. Additionally, the integration of CF and Multiple Model Ranking (MMR), a technique requiring user-specific preference weights, can further enhance the BiCF and OL BiCF algorithms, thus expanding the knowledge boundary in this research study. Finally, the CF field lacks a widely-accepted evaluation protocol due to its embedded biases and limitations, highlighted in this research, necessitating a more objective approach to algorithm evaluation and advancement, with potential future contributions in this area. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the solar surface, independent of previous activity indicators. These features were better correlated with reduced sensitivity to certain spectral features, and revealed larger errors at higher solar activity levels. Notably, using the most reliable indicator, the A$_{S}$$ error was reduced to $\sqrt{300}$ compared to $\sqrt{800}$ with the existing S$_{ini}$ indicator, allowing for more reliable detection of smaller Doppler signals, and potentially larger low-mass exoplanets under similar conditions. Furthermore, we found that leveraging short-term active indicators can eliminate seasonal variations in these features, and enable the use of longer data sets to boost detection limits. These results may be applicable to other stars with similar spectral types, and we provide indicators for both active and quiet stars that could be used for analyzing future observations. Additionally, we provide the fitted model in our study, allowing users to calculate the expected spectral features based on a star's characteristics and activity levels, and vice versa. This research was conducted as a junior project by a student in the PhD program at the University of La Laguna under the supervision of Dr. Pablo Moya and Dr. Jonatan Cepa.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly lowers the tunneling rate, making it more likely that tunneling occurs through a weakly attached state rather than a tightly attached one. Consequently, under certain conditions, the reduced tunneling rate can help distinguish between two scenarios: (1) tunneling into a Majorana state attached to a gap edge, resulting in a heated system over time, or (2) tunneling into a tightly attached state associated with a heated system over time. Our simulations, modeling the system within the quantum flux parametric spectrum, demonstrate that distinguishing between these scenarios is feasible without attributing the zero-energy peak to the Majorana state. Furthermore, our calculations of reduced tunneling rates, specifically the Fowler-Nordheim rate and a variable-rate tunneling model, show that the tunneling process is more likely to occur into a heavily coupled state rather than a Minorana state, particularly at higher temperatures. Ultimately, our method's accuracy in distinguishing between the two scenarios depends on the specific ohmic dissipation level in the electrode. Ohm values below a certain threshold ($\sim$25 Ohm) are insufficient for distinguishing, whereas ohm values above this threshold enable clear differentiation, as evidenced by our data beyond the initial threshold up to ($\sim$260 Ohm). Thus, our proposed method provides a viable solution to the paradox between high tunneling rates and ohmic dissipation, paving the way for the development of efficient tunneling techniques at higher dissipation levels. Additionally, our study suggests investigating systems with lower-than-expected ohmic behavior as potential sources of weakly attached states. To further enhance tunneling techniques, our research points to two key areas for future exploration: (1) implementing protocols reducing tunneling into tightly coupled states and (2) optimizing the attachment of resistive electrodes to minimize tunneling into these states. By addressing these questions, our work contributes to the advancement of tunneling spectroscopy and the tunneling physics underlying Majorana-based computing technology. To facilitate further research, our simulation data, weighing the importance of different ohmic behaviors in distinguishing between the two scenarios, is made publicly available. Moreover, our study emphasizes the critical role of distinct ohmic behaviors in tunneling spectroscopy and suggests investigating non-ohmic behaviors in systems with a higher proportion of weakly attached states

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this composition also validates a generalised version of Berman's theorem, which describes topological coKhomology as the opposite of shadows, within this context. Finally, a key aspect of THH, specifically its reduction functors, is translated into bicategorical shadows through the notion of'shadows of reduction', serving as an explanation for their collective preservation of Morita invariance. These concepts, central to higher algebra, are wrapped in a simplified context, aiming to illustrate the underlying ideas in a clear and approachable manner. Ultimately, the theories of SH and topological coKhomology are presented as dual concepts, with the former constituting the category of shadows and the latter the category of co-shadows, thereby forming the category of bicategorical shadows as a quotient of topological Hochschild cohomology. The notion of'shadows of reduction' is demonstrated to be an orthogonal functor, which explains why Morita invariance is preserved through the composition of topological Hochschild homology and reduction functors, a phenomenon also observed in spectrum categories and stable homotopy theory. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability in their pursuit of identifying a unique solution. Conversely, our research aims to harness style-specific information, extracting it from paired images to condense into a two or three-dimensional vector. This style embedding, represented in a compact, fixed structure, can then be utilized to guide a generative model in achieving a desired level of color manipulation. By expressing the mapping between global color pairs as a bi-directional forward and inverse transformation, our conditional generative model achieves notable advancements in efficiency and accuracy, outperforming previous individual forward modeling approaches in several key aspects. Moreover, our novel approach enables the application of global color mappings to unsupervised settings by decomposing the style embedding into invariant and unique components, effectively decoupling the two. This research aims to bridge this gap by integrating the active inference framework with deep learning, allowing complex mental models to be constructed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this integrated method can be applied in autonomous robot navigation without requiring pre-trained models. Our results indicate that active inference facilitates robust and efficient navigation in complex environments despite limited training. Additionally, we show that the mental framework created during navigation is beneficial for predicting future situations. These findings support the use of active inference for generating detailed predictions about the world and guide future research in integrating this theory with deep learning. The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties. Specifically, the paper will center on the role of requirements engineering in formulating what explanations are needed and ensuring these explanations align with user requirements. This marks a pivotal aspect in the XAI process and this paper will provide a starting point for further investigation into this area. Additionally, potential future work will be identified in developing and incorporating user-centered approaches for explaining AI-driven decisions. These approaches will facilitate a deeper understanding of what explanations are most beneficial to who and why, thus enabling more effective XAI practices. Several such possibilities include investigating user perspectives through the use of RE, developing explanation requirements that are adaptable and can be applied across various domains, and applying RE's problem formulation capability to define the XAI problem and develop actionable solutions. These possibilities along with a few more promising research avenues will be presented in this paper. Firstly, the importance of considering the preferences and needs of XAI stakeholders in explanation processes will be addressed. Secondly, the role of requirements engineering in providing a unified language and methodology for handling diverse stakeholder preferences in explanation processes will be discussed. Lastly, the capabilities of requirements engineering in formulating and addressing the complex decision-making transparency requirements of future AI systems will be explored. This paper is a preliminary effort and we hope it will contribute to further research in these areas and more. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. Furthermore, we've established a challenge associated with it, inviting researchers to submit their results, which can be found on our website. The UniToPatho dataset, along with challenge information, can be accessed at https://unito-patho.github.io/. The dataset is freely available for download at https://doi.org/10.18886/unioto_patho. In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We expand upon the initial investigation to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and can tolerate a degree of sequence error. In this case, we identify tight lower and upper bounds for the more general leakage metric through the application of single-letter analysis. The newly derived formulas demonstrate that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates can be expressed in terms of the confusion graph's characteristics, thereby providing a valuable framework for assessing the impact of graph topology on source coding efficiency and leakage. Furthermore, our analysis shows that while a specific deterministic coding strategy still achieves the optimal compression rate, it may fall short of the optimal leakage rate under these relaxed conditions. The presented findings include a derivation of the optimal leakage values for several well-known source models, such as the uniform source and the source with mixing weight. The study also discusses potential extensions to the underlying theory, including the extension to infinite source alphabets. Finally, the presented work is compared to prior research on related problems, such as leakage in continuous-time source coding, where distinct technical approaches were employed. Vice versa, the presented work may also be seen as extending and adapting certain ideas from prior research on related problems, such as leakage in confidential coding. The study specifically identifies areas of common interest between these fields and highlights how certain notions and techniques can be transferred from one field to another. Furthermore, the presentation includes a detailed overview of related prior research and how it relates to the investigated problems. The study also presents possible future research directions, including the extension of the underlying theory to more complex adversarial models. The main text is accompanied by detailed supplementary materials, including additional auxiliary results and constructive coding strategies that achieve the optimal leakage rates.

A new hierarchical generative model called MrSARP is introduced in this research, specifically designed for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) image generation, to produce SAR images at various resolutions simultaneously. The MrSARP model is trained alongside a discriminator that assesses multiple-resolution images together to verify their realism, representing a target at various resolutions. The study demonstrates the applicability of the MrSARP deep generative model in retrieving high-resolution images from lower resolution images of the same target. The cost function of the model is modified to improve its ability to recover input parameters based on multiple-resolution images. The performance of the model is assessed using conventional super-resolution error metrics on simulated data and is compared with conventional up-sampling and image sharpening methods that utilize sparsity. The results show that MrSARP outperforms these methods in recovering high-resolution images from lower resolution images of the same target. The study also includes an investigation of the performance of the model in recovering images from sparse, translated, simulated dataset of the Western Cape, Australia. The results show that MrSARP is able to recover images with acceptable error at a reasonable sparse sampling rate of 16. The study concludes that the new model is capable of resolving multiple scatterers within a limited distance due to its ability to recover images at various resolutions. A numerical analysis is also presented to confirm that the new model resolves the radar target with fewer iterations compared to a conventional sparse phasing approach. The code for the research is publicly available online. The study visually presents the high and low resolution images used in the research, as well as the error metrics. It also includes a series of images showing the evolution of the radar target resolution over several iterations of the MrSARP algorithm.
