A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component.  The framework performs well even at slow circuit repetition rates and with minimal quantum circuit measurements, yielding a reliable energy estimate.  Moreover, we investigate how our approach handles noise during circuit operation, discovering that for short circuits it remains resistant to disturbances.  The outcome of these findings supports the use of the suggested method as an adaptable tool to exploit the mixed capabilities of QAOA within imperfect quantum devices.  Specifically, we discover that for a particular problem, our technique achieves a $420\times$ improvement in circuit access efficiency relative to a conventional global optimizer, while maintaining comparable optimized energies.  The method's efficiency in optimizing circuit parameters with minimal measurements makes it an appealing technique for future quantum algorithms, where numerous circuit evaluations may become prohibitively costly.  The technique's resilience to quantum errors as well as its ability to exploit the unique characteristics of QAOA for near-term quantum applications are particularly relevant under existing and impending quantum hardware limitations.  Lastly, we present a quantum circuit design for solving combinatorial optimization problems, which incorporates our proposed optimizer, and demonstrate its potential to achieve substantial computational benefits.  The scheme could serve as a useful template for the quantum community to validate novel optimizing strategies within actual problem-scenarios, thereby facilitating practical issue-identification and the development of more robust solutions to tackle complex problems effectively.  The code used to generate the results is publicly accessible via the link provided.  Additionally, we have uploaded the dataset containing our results here. A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant sectors and polygons are combined. The algorithm identifies the intersection points of two general ellipses by utilizing Ferrari's quartic solution, and then applies the secant line method to calculate the overlap area through integration of sector and polygon areas. The resulting overlap area is displayed as a function of the semi-major and semi-minor axes of the two ellipses, along with their respective orientations. The approach adopted is analytical, with the recursion of intersection points limited to the roots of a quartic equation. The proposed method boasts recursion-free and symbolic evaluation properties. The predicted areas match closely with geometrically calculated areas for notable cases, such as overlapping circles, to the third decimal place. Furthermore, the approach adheres to symmetry, yielding exact results for the overlap area of two identical horizontal or vertical ellipses. The proposed method has been demonstrated to be accurate through the integration of the calculated overlap areas into the GraphTools suite. The comprehensive validation includes a detailed examination of various test cases, as well as an investigation of the algorithm's performance via a suite of performance assessments. The validation confirms that the method is efficient, stable, and reliable, even when the input parameters approach their limiting values. The method has been successfully applied to a range of ellipses, and the associated source code is freely accessible via GitHub. The method's accessibility is further ensured through the inclusion of instructions outlining how to employ the algorithm, along with an extensive collection of relevant references. The approach devised for calculating the overlap area between two general ellipses has been successfully adapted to the more complex scenario of four ellipses, with the approach having been presented previously in a separate publication. Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. To handle the collapse of the traditional Q-function in continuous time, we derive a first-order approximation and introduce the term "small q-function". The q-function has connections to both the instantaneous advantage rate function and the Hamiltonian. We develop a continuous-time "Q-learning" framework based on the q-function, separate from time discretization, by characterizing its relationship to value functions and stochastic processes via martingale conditions. We apply this theory to create actor-critic algorithms for solving reinforcement learning tasks, either when or not the Gibbs measure density can be calculated. Our algorithms either relate to Jia and Zhou's (2020) Hamiltonian-based policy optimization or serve as its continuous time versions with adaptations for Simpson and Teboes' work (2020). Furthermore, we provide simulations to verify the effectiveness of our continuous-time Q-learning framework. The theory has potential applications in fields such as control, robotics, and economics. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/jaehyuns/continuous_Q_learning. Please note that this research was supported by AFOSR under award number FA9852-19-094. Its preparation was facilitated by the NSF-CNS-FRR under award number 2131131. Both sources provided financial support.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. This finding holds true for materials of any shape or orientation and can be determined experimentally through measurement of surface properties. Furthermore, we analyzed the optimal energy transfer between identical zinc oxide crystals for various orientations and found a significant number of conditions that facilitate this energy transfer. Notably, our studies demonstrate that certain characteristics of acoustic waves can become completely transmitted, even if they would normally be attenuated. This phenomenon could have valuable applications in device development, such as enhancing sensitivity in surface-based sensors by combining multiple sensors. Additionally, we explored the practical limitations of coupling energy between zinc oxide and gallium phosphide materials, and calculated the minimum gap size required for efficient coupling across a wide range of frequencies. This minimum gap size can be much smaller than the wavelength of the acoustic waves involved, and is primarily determined by the materials' properties rather than the frequency. We explore a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton condensates at a microscale, relying on highly coherent fluids of semiconductor-based light-emitting systems. Theoretical research indicates that modern spatial light manipulation technologies can be employed to redirect these polariton condensates through microscale obstacles. To achieve this, we develop a comprehensive framework that integrates the non-linear optics governing polariton behavior with advanced optical metrology capable of shaping polariton waveforms. Our findings demonstrate that polariton condensates can be redirected using microscale lenses and microscopically focused beams, paving the way for novel micro-optical systems utilizing polariton condensates. Moreover, we predict access to previously unattainable spectral properties via the generation of stop bands and anomalous dispersion. To utilize these unique properties, we propose innovative schemes such as polariton spectroscopy and the creation of polariton joliet patterns. Our work lays the foundation for the development of innovative micro-optical systems utilizing polariton condensates, enabling new functions that combine the advantages of both solid-state lasers and conventional micro-optics. </abstract>

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still a mystery. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential to comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual photometric data obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope, with wavelengths of 0.48 and 2.1 microns, are presented during a period of reduced dust activity, revealing a refined upper limit of the planet's radius of approximately 4500 km. Medium-depth transit observations also suggest particle sizes ranging from 0.5 to 1 micron, suggesting extremely high mass loss rates of about 3e8 kg/s, coherent with hydrodynamic escape theories. In contrast, explosive volcanic eruptions or other mechanisms generating this activity would demand exceptional geological activity levels. Combining these results with the maximum possible planetary size, our findings estimate the remaining lifespan of the exoplanet at approximately 370 million years; conversely, incorporating predictions from the hydrodynamic model yields a remarkably reduced lifespan of only 21 million years. In the hydrodynamic model scenario, a dramatic reduction in radius is expected within the exoplanet's remaining lifespan, with the radius decreasing from around 4000 km to below 1000 km. The analysis of grain size and other key factors presents an opportunity to validate theoretical models through observational evidence, with predictions of reduced dust activity levels in the near future, presenting additional avenues for validation. The findings of this study also underscore the importance of timing in the observation of variable dust activity to avoid misleading conclusions. The researchers plan to follow up on these findings with additional data from various instruments, including the James Webb Space Telescope, with a potential to observe the exoplanet at infrared wavelengths, revealing whether the expected decrease in dust activity levels holds true. Moreover, a dramatic reduction in the dust cloud's optical depth is anticipated due to the disintegration of the exoplanet, which is expected to lead to the exposure of a hot white dwarf surface, with temperatures potentially exceeding 10,000 K under certain hydrodynamic model scenarios. In the context of planetary disintegration, the exoplanet K2-22b is considered particularly significant, with a key role in determining the bounds of this phenomenon, which may be relatively widespread among extra-solar planets. We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation, while still capturing the essential physical kinetic effects. The MHD-AEPIC model exhibits comparable performance to traditional MHD simulations with embedded PIC regions, but at a significantly lower computational cost, thereby facilitating longer simulation durations. Our research focuses on the reconnection site within a central MHD domain, where the embedded PIC region simulates reconnection dynamics, demonstrating that this approach accurately replicates the reconnection rates observed in full kinetic PIC simulations. Therefore, the MHD-AEPIC model provides a viable option for studying complex, collisionless magnetic reconnection in intricate scenarios.
